questions.q: Which statement about enantiomers is correct?

options.B: They rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions by equal amounts
options.D: They are also called structural isomers

questions.explanation: Enantiomers have identical physical properties except for the direction in which they rotate plane-polarised light. They are stereoisomers, not structural isomers.

questions.q: Which molecule is NOT chiral?
questions.explanation: Propan-2-ol has two identical CH₃ groups on the carbon bearing the OH, so there are not four different groups and it is not chiral.

questions.q: Which reagents are used to make an ester from a carboxylic acid?

options.A: An alcohol and concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst

questions.explanation: Esterification is a reversible reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, catalysed by a strong acid such as concentrated H₂SO₄, heated under reflux.

questions.q: What is the name of the ester formed from ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol?
questions.explanation: The alkyl group comes from the alcohol (propyl) and the -oate from the acid (ethanoate).

questions.q: Which products form when methyl propanoate is hydrolysed with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: Alkaline hydrolysis gives the alcohol and the sodium salt of the acid. The ester is methyl propanoate so the alcohol part is methanol.

questions.q: What is produced when a vegetable oil is heated with sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.explanation: Saponification: the triglyceride ester is hydrolysed to the sodium salts of fatty acids (soap) and propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol).

questions.q: Biodiesel is made by reacting vegetable oils with

options.B: methanol in the presence of a catalyst

questions.explanation: Transesterification of the triglyceride with methanol (KOH catalyst) gives methyl esters of fatty acids (biodiesel) and glycerol.

questions.q: Which reagent reacts with ethanoyl chloride to form ethanamide?
questions.explanation: Acyl chlorides react with ammonia to form primary amides: CH₃COCl + 2NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ + NH₄Cl.

questions.q: Which product forms when ethanoyl chloride reacts with methylamine?
questions.explanation: Primary amines react with acyl chlorides to give N-substituted amides: CH₃COCl + CH₃NH₂ → CH₃CONHCH₃ + HCl.

questions.q: What is the by-product when ethanoyl chloride reacts with ethanol?
questions.explanation: Acyl chlorides undergo nucleophilic addition–elimination with alcohols, forming an ester and HCl. Unlike esterification with a carboxylic acid the reaction is rapid and not reversible.

questions.q: Which observation is made when ethanoyl chloride is added to water?

options.B: A vigorous reaction with steamy fumes of HCl

questions.explanation: Acyl chlorides hydrolyse violently in water to form the carboxylic acid and hydrogen chloride, seen as white steamy fumes.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of using ethanoic anhydride rather than ethanoyl chloride to make aspirin?

options.B: It is cheaper, less corrosive and does not produce HCl
options.D: It is a gas so is easier to handle

questions.explanation: Ethanoic anhydride is cheaper, safer to handle, less vulnerable to hydrolysis and the by-product is ethanoic acid rather than corrosive HCl.

questions.q: What type of mechanism do acyl chlorides undergo with nucleophiles?
questions.explanation: The nucleophile adds to the carbonyl carbon, then the C=O re-forms as Cl⁻ is eliminated, followed by loss of H⁺.

questions.q: Which compound is a weak acid that reacts with sodium carbonate to release carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids are weak acids but are acidic enough to liberate CO₂ from carbonates and hydrogencarbonates, a test that distinguishes them from phenols and alcohols.

questions.q: Which is a common use of esters?
questions.explanation: Esters have pleasant smells (flavourings and perfumes), are good solvents, and are added to polymers as plasticisers to make them more flexible.

questions.q: The reaction of ethanoic anhydride with ethanol produces
questions.explanation: (CH₃CO)₂O + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + CH₃COOH. One acyl group forms the ester and the other leaves as ethanoic acid.

questions.q: Which statement about the bonding in benzene is correct?

options.A: It has three C=C double bonds
options.B: Each carbon donates one electron to a delocalised π system above and below the ring
options.C: All the carbon atoms are sp³ hybridised
options.D: The C–C bonds alternate between short and long

questions.explanation: Each carbon uses three electrons in σ bonds and the fourth p electron overlaps sideways to form a delocalised ring. All six C–C bonds are the same length, between a single and a double bond.

questions.q: Which piece of evidence does NOT support the delocalised model of benzene?

options.A: All C–C bond lengths are equal
options.B: Benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition
options.C: The enthalpy of hydrogenation is less exothermic than expected for cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene
options.D: Benzene has the molecular formula C₆H₆

questions.explanation: The molecular formula alone does not distinguish between the Kekulé and delocalised models. The other three observations all show that benzene is more stable than a triene and has no separate double bonds.

questions.q: What is the shape of the benzene molecule?
questions.explanation: Benzene is planar; each carbon is trigonal planar (sp²) with bond angles of 120°.

questions.q: Why does benzene undergo electrophilic substitution rather than electrophilic addition?

options.A: Addition would break the stable delocalised ring
options.B: Benzene has no electrons to donate
options.D: Substitution is faster for all hydrocarbons

questions.explanation: Addition would destroy the delocalised π system and lose its stabilisation (about 150 kJ mol⁻¹). Substitution keeps the ring intact.

questions.q: Which reagents are used to nitrate benzene?

options.B: Concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid at about 50 °C

questions.explanation: Concentrated H₂SO₄ protonates HNO₃ to generate the NO₂⁺ electrophile. Keeping the temperature around 50 °C prevents further nitration.

questions.q: Which species is the electrophile in the nitration of benzene?
questions.explanation: The nitronium ion NO₂⁺ is formed from HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻.

questions.q: Which equation shows the formation of the nitronium ion?
questions.explanation: Sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, which loses water to form NO₂⁺. The sulfuric acid is regenerated at the end so it acts as a catalyst.

questions.q: What is the role of sulfuric acid in the nitration of benzene?
questions.explanation: H₂SO₄ is used to generate NO₂⁺ and is re-formed when H⁺ is lost from the intermediate, so it is a catalyst.

questions.q: Why is the nitration of benzene an important industrial reaction?

options.A: Nitrobenzene is used as a fuel
options.B: Nitro compounds are reduced to aromatic amines used to make dyes and pharmaceuticals

questions.explanation: Nitroarenes are reduced (Sn/HCl) to arylamines such as phenylamine, which are starting materials for dyes, and polynitro compounds are explosives.

questions.q: Which catalyst is used in the Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene?
questions.explanation: Aluminium chloride accepts a chloride ion from the acyl chloride to generate the acylium ion electrophile, RCO⁺.

questions.q: What is the electrophile in the Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene with ethanoyl chloride?
questions.explanation: CH₃COCl + AlCl₃ → CH₃CO⁺ + AlCl₄⁻. The acylium ion then attacks the benzene ring.

questions.q: What is the product of the reaction between benzene and ethanoyl chloride with AlCl₃?
questions.explanation: Acylation attaches a COCH₃ group to the ring, giving the ketone phenylethanone, C₆H₅COCH₃.

questions.q: Which conditions are used for Friedel–Crafts acylation?

options.B: Heat under reflux with anhydrous AlCl₃ in a dry non-aqueous solvent

questions.explanation: AlCl₃ reacts with water, so the reaction must be anhydrous. Reflux is used to drive the reaction.

questions.q: In the mechanism of electrophilic substitution, what happens in the final step?

options.B: A proton is lost from the intermediate, restoring the delocalised ring

questions.explanation: The positively charged intermediate (with a partially delocalised ring) loses H⁺ to regenerate the full aromatic system.

questions.q: Why is the enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene (−208 kJ mol⁻¹) less exothermic than three times that of cyclohexene (−360 kJ mol⁻¹)?

options.B: The delocalised electrons make benzene about 152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than a hypothetical triene

questions.explanation: The difference of about 152 kJ mol⁻¹ is the delocalisation (resonance) energy, showing benzene is more stable than if it contained three isolated C=C bonds.

questions.q: What is the molecular formula of methylbenzene?
questions.explanation: Methylbenzene (toluene) is a benzene ring with one hydrogen replaced by CH₃: C₆H₅CH₃, or C₇H₈.

questions.q: What type of reaction is the conversion of nitrobenzene to phenylamine?
questions.explanation: The NO₂ group is reduced to NH₂ using tin and concentrated HCl (or H₂ with a nickel catalyst), followed by NaOH to liberate the free amine.

questions.q: Why is the nitration of benzene kept below about 55 °C?

options.B: To prevent further nitration giving dinitrobenzene
options.C: To stop the sulfuric acid decomposing

questions.explanation: At higher temperatures a second NO₂ group can be substituted, giving 1,3-dinitrobenzene as an impurity.

questions.q: Which bond angle is found in benzene?
questions.explanation: Each carbon atom is trigonal planar with three σ bonds, so the bond angles are 120°.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares cyclohexene and benzene with bromine water?

options.B: Cyclohexene decolourises bromine water; benzene does not
options.C: Benzene decolourises bromine water; cyclohexene does not

questions.explanation: Cyclohexene has a localised C=C with high electron density that attracts Br₂ (electrophilic addition). Benzene's delocalised electrons are spread out and not polarising enough to react without a catalyst.

questions.q: How many σ and π electrons are in the delocalised system of benzene?
questions.explanation: Each of the six carbons contributes one p electron, giving a delocalised system of six π electrons above and below the plane of the ring.

questions.q: Which intermediate forms during the nitration of benzene?

options.C: A positively charged intermediate with a partially delocalised ring (arenium ion)

questions.explanation: The NO₂⁺ electrophile accepts a pair of electrons from the ring, forming a cationic intermediate in which delocalisation is interrupted at one carbon.

questions.q: Which of these nitrogen compounds is the strongest base?
questions.explanation: Alkyl groups push electron density onto the nitrogen (positive inductive effect), making the lone pair more available to accept a proton. In phenylamine the lone pair is delocalised into the ring; amides are not basic.

questions.q: Why is phenylamine a weaker base than ammonia?

options.A: It has no lone pair on the nitrogen
options.B: The nitrogen lone pair is partially delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept a proton
options.C: The benzene ring donates electrons to nitrogen

questions.explanation: Delocalisation of the lone pair into the aromatic π system reduces the electron density on the nitrogen.

questions.q: Which reagents are used to prepare ethylamine from bromoethane?

options.A: Excess ammonia in ethanol, heated under pressure

questions.explanation: Nucleophilic substitution with excess concentrated ammonia in a sealed tube gives the primary amine. Excess ammonia reduces further substitution to secondary and tertiary amines.

questions.q: Why is excess ammonia used when making a primary amine from a halogenoalkane?

options.B: To reduce further substitution of the amine product

questions.explanation: The amine formed is itself a nucleophile and can react with more halogenoalkane. Excess ammonia makes it more likely that the halogenoalkane collides with NH₃.

questions.q: Which method gives the purer product when making a primary amine, and why?

options.A: Reduction of a nitrile, because no further substitution can occur
options.B: Reaction of a halogenoalkane with ammonia, because the reaction is faster
options.C: Reduction of a nitrile, because it uses no catalyst
options.D: Reaction with ammonia, because ammonia is cheap

questions.explanation: Reducing a nitrile (with LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni) gives only the primary amine. The ammonia route gives a mixture of primary, secondary, tertiary amines and a quaternary ammonium salt.

questions.q: Which reagent reduces propanenitrile to propylamine?
questions.explanation: Lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III) (or H₂ with a nickel catalyst) reduces the C≡N group to CH₂NH₂.

questions.q: Which reagents are used to reduce nitrobenzene to phenylamine?

options.A: Tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid, then sodium hydroxide

questions.explanation: Sn/conc. HCl reduces NO₂ to the phenylammonium ion; NaOH is then added to liberate the free phenylamine.

questions.q: Which product forms when excess bromoethane reacts with ammonia?

options.B: A quaternary ammonium salt, tetraethylammonium bromide

questions.explanation: With excess halogenoalkane, substitution continues through secondary and tertiary amines to the quaternary ammonium salt (C₂H₅)₄N⁺Br⁻.

questions.q: Quaternary ammonium salts with long hydrocarbon chains are used as

options.B: cationic surfactants in fabric softeners and hair conditioners

questions.explanation: The positively charged head is attracted to negatively charged surfaces such as fibres and hair, reducing static and softening.

questions.q: What is the product when ethylamine reacts with hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Amines are bases and accept a proton: CH₃CH₂NH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺Cl⁻.

questions.q: What type of reaction occurs between ethylamine and ethanoyl chloride?
questions.explanation: The amine nitrogen acts as a nucleophile towards the acyl chloride, forming an N-substituted amide and HCl.

questions.q: In which reaction does the amine act as a nucleophile rather than a base?
questions.explanation: With a halogenoalkane the lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon (nucleophilic substitution). With acids the lone pair accepts a proton (base).

questions.q: Which is a secondary amine?
questions.explanation: A secondary amine has two alkyl groups on the nitrogen. One is primary, three is tertiary and four is a quaternary ammonium ion.

questions.q: Which is a tertiary amine?
questions.explanation: Trimethylamine has three carbon groups attached to nitrogen.

questions.q: Why are amines soluble in water?

options.B: They form hydrogen bonds with water through the N–H group and the lone pair
options.D: They react with water to form hydrogen gas

questions.explanation: The N–H bonds and the lone pair on nitrogen allow hydrogen bonding with water. Solubility falls as the hydrocarbon chain lengthens.

questions.q: Which compound is produced when phenylamine reacts with excess bromoethane?

options.B: A mixture including N,N-diethylphenylamine and a quaternary salt

questions.explanation: The nitrogen keeps reacting with the halogenoalkane while it has a lone pair, giving successive substitution products.

questions.q: Why does the base strength increase from ammonia to methylamine to dimethylamine?

options.A: The number of lone pairs increases
options.B: Each alkyl group pushes more electron density onto nitrogen, making the lone pair more available

questions.explanation: The positive inductive effect of alkyl groups increases the electron density on the nitrogen lone pair, increasing its ability to accept a proton.

questions.q: The mechanism for the reaction between ammonia and bromoethane is
questions.explanation: The nitrogen lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon and the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, releasing Br⁻. A second ammonia then removes H⁺.

questions.q: Which compound would be formed by reducing CH₃CH₂CN?
questions.explanation: Reduction of the nitrile converts C≡N to CH₂NH₂, so propanenitrile gives propylamine, which keeps all three carbons.

questions.q: Which type of polymerisation forms Terylene (PET)?

options.B: Condensation polymerisation of a diol and a dicarboxylic acid
options.C: Condensation polymerisation of a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid

questions.explanation: Terylene is a polyester made from benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid and ethane-1,2-diol. Each ester link forms with the loss of a water molecule.

questions.q: Which pair of monomers forms nylon-6,6?
questions.explanation: Nylon-6,6 is a polyamide: the diamine and dicarboxylic acid each have six carbons and link through amide (peptide) bonds.

questions.q: What small molecule is lost when a polyamide forms from a diamine and a dioyl dichloride?
questions.explanation: With an acyl chloride, each amide link forms with the elimination of HCl. With a dicarboxylic acid, water is lost instead.

questions.q: Why are polyalkenes such as poly(ethene) not biodegradable?

options.B: The C–C and C–H bonds are non-polar and unreactive, so enzymes and water cannot attack them

questions.explanation: Polyalkenes are saturated hydrocarbons. There is no polar bond for a nucleophile or enzyme to attack, so they persist in landfill.

questions.q: Why can polyesters and polyamides be hydrolysed?

options.A: They contain polar ester or amide links that can be attacked by water, acid or alkali

questions.explanation: The C=O carbon in an ester or amide link is δ+ and can be attacked by nucleophiles such as water or OH⁻, breaking the chain. This makes them biodegradable.

questions.q: Which intermolecular force acts between nylon chains and gives nylon its strength?

options.B: Hydrogen bonding between N–H and C=O groups

questions.explanation: The N–H of one amide link forms a hydrogen bond to the C=O of an adjacent chain, holding the chains strongly together.

questions.q: Which intermolecular forces act between poly(propene) chains?
questions.explanation: Poly(propene) is a non-polar hydrocarbon, so only van der Waals (induced dipole) forces hold the chains together.

questions.q: What is the repeating unit of the polymer formed from HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH and HO–CH₂CH₂–OH?
questions.explanation: An ester link forms between each COOH and OH. The repeating unit contains one unit of each monomer joined by two ester links.

questions.q: Kevlar is a polyamide made from benzene-1,4-diamine and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid. Why is it so strong?

options.B: The rigid aromatic rings and hydrogen bonds between chains hold the straight chains in highly ordered sheets
options.D: The chains are cross-linked by covalent bonds

questions.explanation: The planar rings keep the chains straight and the N–H···O=C hydrogen bonds between chains hold them in rigid sheets, giving great tensile strength.

questions.q: Which statement about disposing of polyalkenes is correct?

options.A: They can be hydrolysed back to their monomers
options.B: They can be recycled by melting and reshaping, or burned as fuel with controlled flue gas treatment
options.C: They biodegrade in landfill within a year

questions.explanation: Addition polymers are thermoplastics that can be remoulded, or incinerated to recover energy. Hydrolysis only works for condensation polymers.

questions.q: What is the general structure of an α-amino acid?
questions.explanation: In an α-amino acid the amine and carboxylic acid groups are attached to the same (α) carbon, which also carries an R group and a hydrogen.

questions.q: Which amino acid is NOT optically active?
questions.explanation: Glycine has two hydrogen atoms on the α-carbon, so it has no chiral centre. All other common amino acids are chiral.

questions.q: What is a zwitterion?

options.A: An ion with two positive charges
options.B: A molecule carrying both a positive and a negative charge, with no overall charge

questions.explanation: At its isoelectric point an amino acid exists as H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COO⁻: the acid group has donated its proton to the amine group.

questions.q: What is the structure of alanine in a solution of low pH (strongly acidic)?
questions.explanation: In acid both groups are protonated: the amine becomes NH₃⁺ and the carboxylic acid stays as COOH, giving a positive ion.

questions.q: What is the structure of alanine in a solution of high pH (strongly alkaline)?
questions.explanation: In alkali the carboxylic acid loses its proton to COO⁻ and the amine group is unprotonated, giving a negative ion.

questions.q: Why do amino acids have relatively high melting points for their molecular size?

options.B: They exist as zwitterions, so strong ionic attractions act between them
options.D: They are gases at room temperature

questions.explanation: In the solid state amino acids are zwitterions, and the electrostatic attraction between opposite charges requires a lot of energy to overcome.

questions.q: Which bond links amino acids together in a protein?
questions.explanation: The COOH of one amino acid condenses with the NH₂ of the next to form a –CO–NH– peptide link with the loss of water.

questions.q: How many different dipeptides can be formed from two different amino acids, X and Y, using one of each?
questions.explanation: X–Y (X's acid group to Y's amine) and Y–X are different molecules, so two dipeptides are possible.

questions.q: Which describes the primary structure of a protein?

options.A: The sequence of amino acids in the chain

questions.explanation: Primary structure is the order of amino acids held by peptide bonds. Secondary is the local folding (helix or sheet), tertiary the overall 3D shape.

questions.q: Which interaction holds the α-helix in a protein's secondary structure?

options.B: Hydrogen bonds between N–H and C=O groups of the peptide links

questions.explanation: The helix is held in shape by hydrogen bonds between the N–H of one peptide link and the C=O of another further along the chain.

questions.q: Which interaction forms between cysteine residues in the tertiary structure of a protein?
questions.explanation: Two cysteine side chains (CH₂SH) are oxidised to form a covalent S–S bridge, one of the strongest links holding the tertiary structure.

questions.q: How is a protein hydrolysed to its constituent amino acids in the laboratory?

options.A: Heating with concentrated hydrochloric acid under reflux

questions.explanation: Peptide bonds are hydrolysed by heating with 6 mol dm⁻³ HCl under reflux for several hours (or by enzymes in the body).

questions.q: In thin-layer chromatography of amino acids, why is the plate sprayed with a developing agent after running?

options.A: To fix the amino acids to the plate
options.B: Amino acids are colourless so a developing agent (ninhydrin) is needed to see them

questions.explanation: Ninhydrin reacts with amino acids to give purple spots, allowing the Rf values to be measured and compared with known values.

questions.q: What is the Rf value of a spot that travels 3.0 cm when the solvent front travels 7.5 cm?
questions.explanation: Rf = distance moved by the spot / distance moved by the solvent front = 3.0 / 7.5 = 0.40.

questions.q: Which statement about enzymes is correct?

options.B: They are proteins whose active site binds a substrate with a specific shape, and they are stereospecific
options.D: They are used up in reactions

questions.explanation: The active site has a specific 3D shape that only the correct substrate (and often only one enantiomer) fits, like a lock and key.

questions.q: How do many drugs work on enzymes?

options.B: They have a shape similar to the substrate and block the active site (inhibition)
options.C: They are substrates that react faster

questions.explanation: Drug molecules designed to fit the active site act as inhibitors, preventing the natural substrate binding. Computers are used to model the fit.

questions.q: Which base pairs are found in DNA?

options.A: A with G, C with T
options.B: A with T, C with G
options.C: A with C, G with T
options.D: A with A, T with T

questions.explanation: Adenine forms two hydrogen bonds with thymine; cytosine forms three hydrogen bonds with guanine.

questions.q: How does cisplatin act as an anticancer drug?

options.A: It forms a coordinate bond between platinum and a nitrogen atom of guanine in DNA, preventing replication

questions.explanation: A chloride ligand on Pt is replaced by a nitrogen on a guanine base (ligand substitution), cross-linking the DNA strands so cancer cells cannot divide. It also damages healthy cells.

questions.q: Which sequence converts ethene into ethanoic acid?

options.A: Hydration to ethanol, then oxidation with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ under reflux

questions.explanation: Ethene + steam (H₃PO₄ catalyst) gives ethanol, a primary alcohol. Heating under reflux with excess acidified dichromate oxidises it through the aldehyde to the carboxylic acid.

questions.q: Which reagent converts a primary alcohol to an aldehyde?

options.A: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), distilling the product as it forms
options.B: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heating under reflux

questions.explanation: Distilling off the aldehyde as soon as it forms prevents further oxidation to the carboxylic acid.

questions.q: Which two-step route converts bromoethane into propanoic acid?

options.A: KCN in ethanol, then acid hydrolysis of the nitrile

questions.explanation: Nucleophilic substitution with cyanide gives propanenitrile (one extra carbon), which is hydrolysed with dilute acid to propanoic acid.

questions.q: Which route increases the carbon chain length by one?

options.A: Reaction of a halogenoalkane with KCN

questions.explanation: The cyanide ion adds a carbon atom. The nitrile can then be hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid or reduced to an amine.

questions.q: Which reagent converts an alkene into an alkane?
questions.explanation: Catalytic hydrogenation adds H₂ across the C=C double bond.

questions.q: Which reagent and conditions convert ethanol into ethene?
questions.explanation: Dehydration (elimination) of an alcohol uses concentrated H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄ with heat, or passing the vapour over hot aluminium oxide.

questions.q: Which reagent converts propan-1-ol into 1-bromopropane?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bromide, generated in situ from KBr and concentrated H₂SO₄, substitutes the OH group for Br.

questions.q: Which is the best route from benzene to phenylamine?
questions.explanation: Benzene is nitrated with conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄ to nitrobenzene, which is reduced with tin and concentrated HCl followed by NaOH to give phenylamine.

questions.q: Which reagent converts an acyl chloride into an ester?
questions.explanation: Alcohols react with acyl chlorides by nucleophilic addition–elimination to form esters and HCl.

questions.q: Which is a key principle of green chemistry in organic synthesis?

options.A: Using as many steps as possible
options.B: High atom economy, fewer steps, less hazardous solvents and renewable feedstocks
options.C: Using toxic solvents to speed up the reaction

questions.explanation: Industrial routes aim to minimise waste and energy use and avoid hazardous reagents. Fewer steps raise the overall yield.

questions.q: Which sequence converts propanone to 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanoic acid?

options.A: KCN/H⁺ to form the hydroxynitrile, then acid hydrolysis

questions.explanation: Nucleophilic addition of HCN gives (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN, and hydrolysis of the nitrile group gives the carboxylic acid.

questions.q: What is the overall yield of a three-step synthesis if each step has a yield of 80%?
questions.explanation: Yields multiply: 0.80 × 0.80 × 0.80 = 0.512, so about 51%.

questions.q: Which reagent converts a nitrile into a carboxylic acid?
questions.explanation: Acid hydrolysis of a nitrile with dilute HCl under reflux gives the carboxylic acid and ammonium chloride.

questions.q: Which reagent converts an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid?

options.B: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heated under reflux

questions.explanation: Aldehydes are oxidised to carboxylic acids by excess acidified dichromate under reflux (or by Tollens' or Fehling's reagents in the test-tube tests).

questions.q: Which reagent converts a ketone into a secondary alcohol?
questions.explanation: Reduction with sodium tetrahydridoborate(III) adds H⁻ then H⁺ to the C=O, giving a secondary alcohol.

questions.q: Which sequence converts 1-bromobutane into butan-1-ol?
questions.explanation: Aqueous hydroxide ions act as a nucleophile, substituting Br for OH. Ethanolic KOH would cause elimination to but-1-ene instead.

questions.q: Which reagent converts 1-bromobutane into but-1-ene?
questions.explanation: In ethanol the hydroxide ion acts as a base and removes a proton, eliminating HBr to form the alkene.

questions.q: Which reagents are needed to convert ethanoic acid into ethanoyl chloride?
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids are converted to acyl chlorides using sulfur dichloride oxide (SOCl₂) or phosphorus(V) chloride.

questions.q: Which product forms when ethanoyl chloride reacts with phenylamine?
questions.explanation: The amine nitrogen attacks the acyl chloride, forming an N-substituted amide (an acylation of the amine).

questions.q: A synthesis starts with ethene and ends with ethylamine. Which route is correct?
questions.explanation: Electrophilic addition of HBr gives bromoethane, which undergoes nucleophilic substitution with excess ammonia to give the primary amine.

questions.q: Why is reflux used when oxidising a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid?

options.B: To keep the volatile reactants and intermediate aldehyde in the flask so oxidation goes to completion

questions.explanation: Reflux condenses and returns vapours so the mixture can be heated for a long time without losing the aldehyde, allowing complete oxidation.

questions.q: Which nucleus is detected in carbon-13 NMR?
questions.explanation: Carbon-12 has no nuclear spin so cannot be observed. The ¹³C isotope (about 1.1% abundance) has spin and gives the NMR signal.

questions.q: What is the reference compound used in NMR spectroscopy?
questions.explanation: TMS, Si(CH₃)₄, is set as δ = 0. It gives a single sharp peak, is inert, volatile and its 12 equivalent protons give a strong signal.

questions.q: Why is CDCl₃ used as a solvent in ¹H NMR rather than CHCl₃?

options.B: Deuterium does not give a signal in the ¹H region, so the solvent does not swamp the spectrum
options.C: It has a higher boiling point

questions.explanation: Deuterium (²H) resonates at a very different frequency, so deuterated solvents give no peaks in the proton spectrum.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of propan-2-ol?
questions.explanation: The two CH₃ carbons are equivalent, giving one peak, and the CH(OH) carbon gives another.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of propan-1-ol?
questions.explanation: All three carbons are in different environments: CH₃, CH₂ and CH₂OH.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹H NMR spectrum of ethanol?
questions.explanation: The CH₃, CH₂ and OH protons are in three different environments.

questions.q: In the ¹H NMR spectrum of ethanol, what is the splitting pattern of the CH₂ peak (ignoring the OH)?
questions.explanation: The CH₂ protons have three neighbouring protons on the adjacent CH₃, so by the n+1 rule the signal is a quartet.

questions.q: Which splitting pattern is seen for a proton with two equivalent neighbouring protons?
questions.explanation: n + 1 rule: two neighbours give 2 + 1 = 3 lines, a triplet with intensities 1:2:1.

questions.q: What does the area under a peak in a ¹H NMR spectrum (the integration) show?

options.B: The relative number of protons in that environment

questions.explanation: The integration trace or ratio gives the relative numbers of equivalent protons causing each signal.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹H NMR spectrum of propanone, and what is the splitting?
questions.explanation: All six protons are equivalent (two identical CH₃ groups) and have no neighbouring protons on an adjacent carbon, so there is one singlet.

questions.q: Which compound gives a ¹H NMR spectrum with a triplet and a quartet in the ratio 3:2?
questions.explanation: Chloroethane, CH₃CH₂Cl, has a CH₃ triplet (split by two CH₂ protons) and a CH₂ quartet, in the ratio 3:2 with no other peaks. Ethanol and ethyl ethanoate have extra peaks.

questions.q: What causes spin–spin splitting in ¹H NMR?

options.A: The magnetic field of protons on adjacent carbon atoms

questions.explanation: Protons on neighbouring carbons can align with or against the external field, slightly changing the field felt by the proton being observed.

questions.q: A ¹H NMR peak at δ 9.5 to 10 ppm indicates
questions.explanation: Aldehyde protons appear far downfield at about δ 9.5 to 10.0. Carboxylic acid protons are even further, at δ 10 to 12.

questions.q: A ¹³C NMR peak at about δ 200 ppm indicates

options.B: a C=O carbon in an aldehyde or ketone

questions.explanation: Carbonyl carbons in aldehydes and ketones appear at the highest chemical shifts, around δ 190 to 220. Ester and acid C=O appear at δ 160 to 185.

questions.q: Why do protons attached to electronegative atoms appear at higher chemical shifts?

options.B: Electron density is withdrawn from them, so they are less shielded from the external field

questions.explanation: Deshielded protons experience a larger effective magnetic field and resonate at a higher frequency, so appear further downfield.

questions.q: How can an OH proton signal be identified in a ¹H NMR spectrum?

options.B: It disappears when the sample is shaken with D₂O
options.D: It is always the largest peak

questions.explanation: The OH proton exchanges with deuterium from D₂O. Deuterium does not show in the ¹H spectrum, so the OH peak vanishes.

questions.q: Which technique would distinguish between propanal and propanone?

options.B: ¹H NMR: propanal shows a peak near δ 9.8 and three environments; propanone shows one singlet

questions.explanation: Both have the same molecular formula and a C=O stretch in the IR. Propanone gives one singlet at about δ 2.2; propanal shows three signals including the aldehyde proton near δ 9.8.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of benzene?
questions.explanation: All six carbons in benzene are equivalent because of the delocalised ring, giving a single peak at about δ 128.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of methylbenzene?
questions.explanation: The CH₃ carbon and four different ring environments (C1 attached to CH₃, C2/C6, C3/C5 and C4) give five peaks.

questions.q: Which compound has a ¹H NMR spectrum consisting of a single peak?
questions.explanation: All twelve protons of Si(CH₃)₄ are equivalent, which is one reason TMS is the reference standard.

questions.q: Which type of radiation is used in NMR spectroscopy?
questions.explanation: Nuclei in a strong magnetic field absorb low-energy radio-frequency radiation when their spin flips.

questions.q: In chromatography, what is the stationary phase in thin-layer chromatography (TLC)?

options.B: A thin layer of silica or alumina on a plate

questions.explanation: The stationary phase is the adsorbent coating on the plate; the mobile phase is the solvent moving up it by capillary action.

questions.q: What is the mobile phase in gas chromatography?

options.B: An inert carrier gas such as nitrogen or helium

questions.explanation: In GC the sample is vaporised and carried through the column by an unreactive gas.

questions.q: On what does separation in column chromatography depend?

options.B: The balance between adsorption to the stationary phase and solubility in the mobile phase
options.D: The temperature of the laboratory only

questions.explanation: Components that adsorb strongly to the stationary phase and dissolve poorly in the mobile phase move slowly; the opposite moves quickly.

questions.q: What is the retention time in gas chromatography?

options.A: The time the sample spends in the injector
options.B: The time taken for a component to pass through the column to the detector
options.C: The time the column is heated

questions.explanation: Each component has a characteristic retention time under fixed conditions, which can be compared with known standards to identify it.

questions.q: Which statement about Rf values is correct?

options.A: Rf values are always greater than 1
options.B: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front, and depends on the solvent and stationary phase used
options.C: Rf values are independent of the solvent
options.D: Rf values are measured in centimetres

questions.explanation: Rf is a ratio with no units, between 0 and 1, and is only reproducible under the same conditions.

questions.q: Why might two different compounds give the same Rf value in TLC?

options.B: They have similar polarity and interact similarly with the stationary and mobile phases
options.C: They have the same molecular mass

questions.explanation: Rf depends on the balance of adsorption and solubility, so compounds of similar polarity can travel the same distance. A different solvent may then separate them.

questions.q: Why is gas chromatography often combined with mass spectrometry (GC–MS)?

options.A: GC separates the components and MS identifies each one from its mass spectrum
options.B: MS speeds up the GC column

questions.explanation: GC alone gives retention times, which are not always conclusive. The mass spectrum of each separated component allows positive identification, used in forensics, drug testing and food analysis.

questions.q: In TLC, why must the spot be above the solvent level at the start?

options.B: If the spot were in the solvent it would dissolve into the solvent reservoir instead of moving up the plate
options.D: To stop the spot being visible

questions.explanation: The sample must travel with the mobile phase up the plate. Immersing the spot would wash it off the plate.

questions.q: Why is the TLC chamber covered with a lid during development?

options.A: To stop the plate falling over
options.B: To keep the atmosphere saturated with solvent vapour so the solvent does not evaporate from the plate

questions.explanation: Evaporation from the plate would change the solvent front and give unreliable Rf values.

questions.q: Which detector output is used to find the relative amounts of components in GC?
questions.explanation: Peak area is proportional to the amount of each component, so the areas give their relative proportions.

questions.q: Which substance is best separated by gas chromatography?

options.A: A mixture of volatile organic liquids

questions.explanation: GC requires the sample to be vaporised without decomposing, so it suits volatile, thermally stable compounds.

questions.q: How can a colourless spot on a TLC plate be located?

options.B: Under UV light if the plate contains a fluorescent indicator, or by spraying with a developing agent such as ninhydrin or exposing to iodine vapour

questions.explanation: Many TLC plates fluoresce under UV so spots appear dark; alternatively, chemical developing agents produce a visible colour.

questions.q: Which equation represents the first ionisation energy of magnesium?
questions.explanation: Ionisation energies are defined for gaseous atoms: one mole of gaseous atoms loses one mole of electrons to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.

questions.q: Which equation represents the lattice enthalpy of dissociation of sodium chloride?
questions.explanation: Lattice dissociation enthalpy is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solid ionic compound is separated into its gaseous ions. The reverse process is lattice formation.

questions.q: Which change has a negative value?

options.A: The enthalpy of atomisation of chlorine
options.B: The first electron affinity of chlorine
options.C: The second electron affinity of oxygen
options.D: The lattice dissociation enthalpy of KBr

questions.explanation: Adding one electron to a gaseous atom releases energy, so the first electron affinity is negative. The second electron affinity of oxygen is positive because the electron is added to an already negative ion. Atomisation and lattice dissociation are endothermic.

questions.q: Which compound has the most exothermic lattice enthalpy of formation?
questions.explanation: Lattice enthalpy becomes more exothermic as ionic charge increases and ionic radius decreases. MgO has 2+ and 2− ions and Mg²⁺ is smaller than Ca²⁺, so the attraction is strongest.

questions.q: The experimental lattice enthalpy of silver iodide is much more exothermic than the value calculated from a perfect ionic model. What does this show?

options.B: AgI has a significant degree of covalent character
options.D: The electron affinity of iodine is positive

questions.explanation: A large difference between the Born–Haber (experimental) value and the perfect ionic model value shows the compound has covalent character: the small, highly polarising cation distorts the large iodide ion.

questions.q: Which process is represented by the enthalpy of hydration?
questions.explanation: Enthalpy of hydration is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions becomes aqueous ions. The whole solid dissolving is the enthalpy of solution.

questions.q: Which ion has the most exothermic enthalpy of hydration?
questions.explanation: Hydration enthalpy is more exothermic for ions with higher charge and smaller radius, because the attraction to the polar water molecules is stronger. Mg²⁺ is small and doubly charged.

questions.q: The enthalpy of solution of a salt can be calculated from which combination?

options.A: Lattice dissociation enthalpy + sum of hydration enthalpies
options.B: Lattice formation enthalpy + sum of hydration enthalpies
options.C: Lattice dissociation enthalpy − sum of hydration enthalpies
options.D: Sum of hydration enthalpies − enthalpy of atomisation

questions.explanation: Dissolving can be treated as breaking the lattice into gaseous ions (lattice dissociation, endothermic) then hydrating those ions (exothermic). ΔH solution = ΔH lattice dissociation + ΣΔH hydration.

questions.q: For which change is the entropy change most positive?
questions.explanation: Entropy rises most when a gas is produced from a solid. The other three changes reduce disorder: freezing, and reactions where the number of gas molecules falls.

questions.q: Which statement about entropy is correct?

options.B: A perfect crystal at 0 K has zero entropy
options.C: Gases have lower entropy than liquids
options.D: Entropy has units of kJ mol⁻¹

questions.explanation: At absolute zero a perfectly ordered crystal has no disorder, so S = 0. Entropy increases with temperature and with the change solid → liquid → gas, and has units of J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: Which expression gives the Gibbs free-energy change?
questions.explanation: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS converted to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ if ΔH is in kJ mol⁻¹. A reaction is feasible when ΔG ≤ 0.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. At what temperature does the reaction become feasible?
questions.explanation: At the limit ΔG = 0 so T = ΔH / ΔS = 178 000 / 161 = 1106 K. Remember to convert ΔH to J mol⁻¹ or ΔS to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: A reaction has a negative ΔH and a negative ΔS. Which statement is correct?

options.A: It is feasible at all temperatures
options.C: It is feasible only below a certain temperature
options.D: It is feasible only above a certain temperature

questions.explanation: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With ΔS negative the −TΔS term is positive and grows with T, so ΔG becomes positive above the temperature where ΔH = TΔS.

questions.q: A reaction has a positive ΔH and a negative ΔS. Which statement is correct?

options.A: It is feasible at all temperatures
options.C: It is feasible only at low temperatures
options.D: It is feasible only at high temperatures

questions.explanation: Both ΔH and −TΔS are positive, so ΔG is positive at every temperature and the reaction is not feasible.

questions.q: Which quantity has units of J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹?
questions.explanation: Entropy and entropy changes are measured in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. ΔH, ΔG and lattice enthalpy are in kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: For the reaction A(g) + B(g) → C(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −199 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG at 298 K?
questions.explanation: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −92 − (298 × −0.199) = −92 + 59.3 = −32.7 kJ mol⁻¹. The ΔS must be converted to kJ.

questions.q: Which statement explains why some reactions with a positive ΔG still appear to occur?

options.A: The activation energy is very low
options.C: ΔG only indicates feasibility, and some products form before equilibrium is reached

questions.explanation: A positive ΔG means the reaction is not thermodynamically feasible overall, but an equilibrium lies to the left so a small amount of product can still form. Negative ΔG does not guarantee a fast reaction either.

questions.q: A graph of ΔG against T is plotted for a reaction. What is the gradient?
questions.explanation: Rearranging ΔG = ΔH − TΔS as y = mx + c gives gradient −ΔS and intercept ΔH.

questions.q: The mean bond enthalpy of Cl–Cl is 243 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the enthalpy of atomisation of chlorine?
questions.explanation: Atomisation forms one mole of gaseous atoms: ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g). That is half the bond enthalpy, +121.5 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: In a Born–Haber cycle for MgCl₂, which term must be used twice?
questions.explanation: MgCl₂ contains two chloride ions, so two moles of gaseous Cl atoms are needed (2 × atomisation of chlorine) and two moles of electron affinity. Magnesium needs the first and second ionisation energies once each.

questions.q: Which statement about the perfect ionic model is correct?

options.A: It assumes ions are point charges with no polarisation
options.B: It assumes the ions are perfectly spherical and the bonding is purely ionic
options.C: It gives the experimental value of the lattice enthalpy
options.D: It applies only to compounds with covalent character

questions.explanation: The perfect ionic model treats ions as perfect spheres with evenly distributed charge and purely electrostatic attraction. Deviations from experimental values show covalent character.

questions.q: Why does the enthalpy of hydration of the halide ions become less exothermic from F⁻ to I⁻?

options.A: The charge on the ion increases
options.B: The ionic radius increases so the attraction to water is weaker

questions.explanation: All halide ions carry a 1− charge. As the radius increases down the group the charge density falls, so the electrostatic attraction to the δ+ hydrogen of water is weaker.

questions.q: The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[A][B]². What is the overall order?
questions.explanation: Overall order is the sum of the individual orders: 1 + 2 = 3.

questions.q: For the rate equation rate = k[A]², what are the units of k?
questions.explanation: k = rate / [A]² = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) / (mol dm⁻³)² = mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹.

questions.q: Which units of a rate constant indicate a zero-order reaction?
questions.explanation: For a zero-order reaction rate = k, so k has the same units as rate: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

questions.q: Doubling [A] quadruples the rate while doubling [B] has no effect. What is the rate equation?
questions.explanation: Rate ∝ [A]² (doubling gives ×4) and B is zero order so it does not appear in the rate equation.

questions.q: In a concentration–time graph, which feature shows a reaction is first order with respect to the reactant?

options.C: A gradient that does not change
options.D: A half-life that doubles each time

questions.explanation: A first-order reactant has a constant half-life: the time for the concentration to halve is the same whatever the starting concentration.

questions.q: Which graph of rate against concentration shows a reaction that is second order with respect to that reactant?

options.B: A straight line through the origin
options.C: An upward curve through the origin

questions.explanation: For second order, rate ∝ [X]², which is a parabola (upward curve) through the origin. First order gives a straight line through the origin and zero order a horizontal line.

questions.q: Which quantity can be found from the gradient of a tangent to a concentration–time curve?
questions.explanation: The gradient of a concentration–time curve at a point gives the rate of reaction at that instant. Drawing tangents at different concentrations lets the order be found.

questions.q: The Arrhenius equation is k = Ae^(−Ea/RT). Which statement is correct?

options.A: A larger Ea gives a larger k
options.B: A higher temperature gives a smaller k
options.C: A is the frequency factor (pre-exponential factor)

questions.explanation: A is the pre-exponential (frequency) factor. Increasing Ea decreases k; increasing T increases k. R is the gas constant, 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: A graph of ln k against 1/T is plotted. What is the gradient?
questions.explanation: Taking logs: ln k = ln A − Ea/RT. Comparing with y = mx + c, the gradient is −Ea/R and the intercept is ln A.

questions.q: The gradient of a plot of ln k against 1/T is −6.50 × 10³ K. What is the activation energy?
questions.explanation: Gradient = −Ea/R so Ea = 6.50 × 10³ × 8.31 = 54 000 J mol⁻¹ = 54.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: A reaction A + 2B → C occurs by a two-step mechanism. The rate equation is rate = k[A][B]. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The rate-determining step involves one A and two B
options.B: The rate-determining step involves one A and one B
options.C: The rate-determining step involves only A
options.D: The rate equation must match the overall equation

questions.explanation: The rate equation reflects the species involved up to and including the rate-determining step. [A][B] shows one molecule of each is involved; the second B reacts in a later, fast step.

questions.q: The mechanism for a reaction is: Step 1 (slow) NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO; Step 2 (fast) NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂. What is the rate equation?
questions.explanation: Only the slow (rate-determining) step controls the rate. It involves two NO₂ molecules, so rate = k[NO₂]². CO appears only in the fast step.

questions.q: Which change increases the value of the rate constant k?

options.A: Increasing the concentration of a reactant
options.D: Adding more of a zero-order reactant

questions.explanation: k depends only on temperature (and the presence of a catalyst). Concentration and pressure change the rate but not the rate constant.

questions.q: The rate constant for a reaction doubles when the temperature rises from 300 K to 310 K. Which statement best explains this?

options.A: The frequency of collisions roughly doubles
options.B: Many more molecules have energy greater than the activation energy

questions.explanation: A 10 K rise increases collision frequency only slightly. The large increase in k comes from the exponential increase in the fraction of molecules with E ≥ Ea.

questions.q: For the reaction 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂, rate = k[N₂O₅]. Initial [N₂O₅] = 0.400 mol dm⁻³ and the initial rate is 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. What is k?
questions.explanation: k = rate / [N₂O₅] = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ / 0.400 = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. First-order k has units of s⁻¹.

questions.q: Which technique is most suitable for following the rate of a reaction that produces a coloured product?
questions.explanation: A colorimeter measures absorbance, which is related to the concentration of the coloured species, continuously and without disturbing the reaction.

questions.q: In the iodine clock reaction, the time t for the colour to appear is measured. Which quantity is proportional to the initial rate?
questions.explanation: A fixed amount of product forms before the colour appears, so rate ∝ 1/time.

questions.q: Which statement about a catalyst is correct?

options.A: It increases the rate constant by raising the activation energy
options.B: It provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy
options.C: It increases the number of collisions
options.D: It shifts the position of equilibrium

questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers Ea by providing a different pathway, so a greater fraction of molecules can react and k increases. It does not affect the equilibrium position.

questions.q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), what is the expression for Kp?
questions.explanation: Kp = product partial pressures over reactant partial pressures, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the equation.

questions.q: What are the units of Kp for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) when pressures are in kPa?
questions.explanation: Kp = p(SO₃)² / (p(SO₂)² p(O₂)) has units kPa² / (kPa² × kPa) = kPa⁻¹.

questions.q: For which equilibrium does Kp have no units?
questions.explanation: Kp has no units when the total number of moles of gas is the same on both sides, as in H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI (2 moles each side).

questions.q: The mole fraction of a gas in a mixture is defined as

options.A: moles of the gas × total pressure
options.B: moles of the gas ÷ total moles of gas
options.C: partial pressure ÷ moles of the gas
options.D: total moles of gas ÷ moles of the gas

questions.explanation: Mole fraction = moles of that gas / total moles of gas in the mixture. Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure.

questions.q: A mixture contains 2.0 mol N₂, 6.0 mol H₂ and 2.0 mol NH₃ at a total pressure of 200 kPa. What is the partial pressure of H₂?
questions.explanation: Total moles = 10. Mole fraction of H₂ = 6.0/10 = 0.60. Partial pressure = 0.60 × 200 = 120 kPa.

questions.q: Which change alters the value of Kp?
questions.explanation: Kp, like Kc, is a constant at a given temperature. Only temperature changes its value; pressure and concentration changes shift the position of equilibrium without changing Kp.

questions.q: For an exothermic reaction, what happens to Kp when the temperature is increased?
questions.explanation: Raising the temperature shifts an exothermic equilibrium towards the reactants, so the proportion of products falls and Kp decreases.

questions.q: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), the total pressure is increased at constant temperature. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Kp increases and the equilibrium shifts left
options.B: Kp is unchanged and the equilibrium shifts left
options.C: Kp decreases and the equilibrium shifts right
options.D: Kp is unchanged and the equilibrium shifts right

questions.explanation: Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (left, 1 mole vs 2), but Kp stays the same because temperature is constant.

questions.q: Adding a catalyst to a gaseous equilibrium at constant temperature

options.C: does not change Kp or the equilibrium position
options.D: shifts the equilibrium to the right

questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but neither Kp nor the position changes.

questions.q: In the reaction PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), 1.0 mol PCl₅ is placed in a vessel and 40% dissociates. How many moles of gas are present at equilibrium?
questions.explanation: 0.40 mol PCl₅ dissociates to give 0.40 mol PCl₃ and 0.40 mol Cl₂, leaving 0.60 mol PCl₅. Total = 0.60 + 0.40 + 0.40 = 1.40 mol.

questions.q: At equilibrium a mixture contains 0.60 mol PCl₅, 0.40 mol PCl₃ and 0.40 mol Cl₂ at a total pressure of 280 kPa. What is Kp for PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g)?
Which statement about partial pressure is correct?

options.A: It is the pressure the gas would exert if it alone occupied the container
options.B: It equals the total pressure divided by the number of gases
options.C: It is independent of the mole fraction
options.D: It is always measured in mol dm⁻³

questions.explanation: The partial pressure of a gas in a mixture is the pressure it would exert alone in the same volume at the same temperature. The partial pressures sum to the total pressure.

questions.q: The sum of the mole fractions of all gases in a mixture is

options.D: equal to the number of gases

questions.explanation: Mole fractions are proportions of the total, so they always sum to 1.

questions.q: For the Haber process, which set of conditions gives the highest equilibrium yield of ammonia?
questions.explanation: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ has fewer gas moles on the right and is exothermic, so high pressure and low temperature favour ammonia. In practice a compromise temperature is used for an acceptable rate.

questions.q: Which quantity is NOT needed to calculate Kp from an equilibrium mixture of gases?

options.A: The mole fraction of each gas

questions.explanation: Kp uses partial pressures, which come from mole fractions and total pressure. The volume is not required (it would be for Kc).

questions.q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), Kp = 50 at a certain temperature. If p(H₂) = p(I₂) = 10 kPa at equilibrium, what is p(HI)?
questions.explanation: Kp = p(HI)² / (p(H₂) p(I₂)) so p(HI)² = 50 × 10 × 10 = 5000 and p(HI) = 70.7 kPa.

questions.q: Kp for an endothermic reaction increases when the temperature rises. Which statement explains this?

options.A: The forward reaction is favoured, increasing the proportion of products

questions.explanation: For an endothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature shifts equilibrium to the right (Le Chatelier), so product partial pressures rise relative to reactants and Kp increases.

questions.q: Solid carbon reacts: C(s) + CO₂(g) ⇌ 2CO(g). Which expression is Kp?
questions.explanation: Solids do not appear in the Kp expression because they have no partial pressure. Only the gases are included.

questions.q: A gaseous equilibrium is set up at constant temperature and the volume of the container is halved. Which statement is correct?

options.C: Kp is unchanged but the partial pressures change
options.D: Kp and the partial pressures are unchanged

questions.explanation: Halving the volume doubles the total pressure and every partial pressure. The system shifts to restore Kp, which is unchanged because the temperature has not changed.

questions.q: Which statement about Kc and Kp for the same gaseous reaction is correct?

options.C: Kp changes with pressure but Kc does not
options.D: Kc has no units but Kp always has units

questions.explanation: Both equilibrium constants depend only on temperature. Their numerical values and units can differ because one uses concentrations and the other partial pressures.

questions.q: What is the standard hydrogen electrode assigned a potential of?
questions.explanation: The standard hydrogen electrode is the reference against which all other electrode potentials are measured and is defined as exactly 0.00 V.

questions.q: Which conditions are used for the standard hydrogen electrode?

options.A: H₂ at 100 kPa, 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺, 298 K
options.B: H₂ at 100 kPa, 0.10 mol dm⁻³ H⁺, 298 K
options.C: H₂ at 50 kPa, 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺, 273 K
options.D: H₂ at 100 kPa, 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺, 273 K

questions.explanation: Standard conditions are 298 K, gases at 100 kPa and solutions of 1.00 mol dm⁻³, with a platinum electrode coated in platinum black.

questions.q: Why is platinum used in the standard hydrogen electrode?

options.B: It is inert and allows electron transfer, and its rough surface catalyses the reaction
options.D: It dissolves in the acid to form Pt²⁺ ions

questions.explanation: Platinum is unreactive, conducts electrons and the finely divided platinum black surface provides a large area that catalyses the H⁺/H₂ equilibrium.

questions.q: Zn²⁺/Zn has E° = −0.76 V and Cu²⁺/Cu has E° = +0.34 V. What is the EMF of the cell Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu?
questions.explanation: EMF = E°(right, positive electrode) − E°(left) = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V.

questions.q: In the cell Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu, which species is oxidised?
questions.explanation: Zinc has the more negative electrode potential so it loses electrons: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ at the negative electrode. Cu²⁺ is reduced at the positive electrode.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the salt bridge in an electrochemical cell?

options.A: To allow electrons to flow between the half-cells
options.B: To complete the circuit by allowing ions to move
options.C: To keep the two solutions at the same temperature

questions.explanation: The salt bridge (often KNO₃ in agar) lets ions migrate so that charge does not build up in either half-cell. Electrons flow through the external wire, not the salt bridge.

questions.q: Which species is the strongest oxidising agent? E° values: F₂/F⁻ +2.87 V; Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V; Br₂/Br⁻ +1.09 V; I₂/I⁻ +0.54 V.
questions.explanation: The most positive electrode potential belongs to the species most readily reduced, so F₂ is the strongest oxidising agent.

questions.q: Which species is the strongest reducing agent? E° values: Li⁺/Li −3.04 V; Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V; Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44 V; Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V.
questions.explanation: The most negative electrode potential means the metal loses electrons most readily, so lithium is the strongest reducing agent.

questions.q: Using E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V and E°(I₂/I⁻) = +0.54 V, which reaction is feasible under standard conditions?
questions.explanation: The more positive couple (Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) is reduced and the less positive (I₂/I⁻) is oxidised: Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻ to I₂. EMF = 0.77 − 0.54 = +0.23 V, positive so feasible.

questions.q: Increasing the concentration of Cu²⁺ in the Cu²⁺/Cu half-cell

options.D: reverses the direction of electron flow

questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu. Increasing [Cu²⁺] pushes the equilibrium right, so electrons are removed from the electrode more readily and E becomes more positive.

questions.q: In conventional cell notation, the vertical double line || represents
questions.explanation: A single line | shows a phase boundary within a half-cell. The double line || represents the salt bridge separating the two half-cells.

questions.q: Which type of cell is a lithium ion battery?
questions.explanation: Lithium ion cells are rechargeable (secondary) cells: applying an external voltage reverses the cell reactions.

questions.q: At the negative electrode of a lithium ion cell during discharge, which process occurs?
questions.explanation: During discharge lithium atoms in the graphite electrode are oxidised to Li⁺, releasing electrons to the external circuit. Li⁺ + CoO₂ + e⁻ → Li⁺[CoO₂]⁻ occurs at the positive electrode.

questions.q: What is the overall reaction in an alkaline hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
questions.explanation: The two half-equations (H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻ and O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻) combine to give 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Water is the only product.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of a hydrogen fuel cell over a conventional rechargeable battery?

options.A: It does not need to be recharged as long as fuel is supplied
options.B: Hydrogen is easy to store at room temperature
options.C: It produces carbon dioxide as a useful by-product

questions.explanation: A fuel cell generates a constant voltage while hydrogen and oxygen are supplied, so it never runs down. Storing hydrogen safely is a disadvantage.

questions.q: A cell has EMF 0 V. What does this tell you?

options.D: Both electrodes are made of platinum

questions.explanation: When the EMF falls to zero the two half-cell potentials are equal: the cell reaction has reached equilibrium and the cell is flat.

questions.q: E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V and E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Copper metal can reduce silver ions
options.B: Silver metal can reduce copper ions
options.C: Neither metal reduces the other's ions

questions.explanation: The less positive couple (Cu) is oxidised and the more positive ion (Ag⁺) is reduced: Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag, EMF = +0.46 V.

questions.q: Why might a reaction with a positive EMF not actually occur?

options.A: Positive EMF means the reaction is never feasible
options.B: The activation energy may be too high so the rate is very slow
options.C: E° values only apply to non-standard conditions

questions.explanation: E° values predict thermodynamic feasibility, not rate. A feasible reaction can be too slow to observe if its activation energy is high. Non-standard conditions can also change the outcome.

questions.q: An atom of ⁵⁶Fe contains how many neutrons?
questions.explanation: Iron has atomic number 26, so 26 protons. Neutrons = mass number − protons = 56 − 26 = 30.

questions.q: Which statement defines isotopes?

options.A: Atoms with the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
options.B: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
options.C: Atoms with the same mass number
options.D: Ions of the same element with different charges

questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same atomic number (protons) and so the same chemical properties, but different mass numbers because of different numbers of neutrons.

questions.q: Which ion has 18 electrons?
questions.explanation: Chlorine has 17 electrons; the chloride ion gains one to make 18. Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ have 10, O²⁻ has 10.

questions.q: What is relative isotopic mass?

options.A: The mass of an isotope compared with 1/12 of the mass of an atom of carbon-12
options.B: The weighted mean mass of an atom compared with 1/12 of carbon-12
options.C: The mass of one mole of an isotope
options.D: The number of neutrons in an isotope

questions.explanation: Relative isotopic mass refers to one isotope. Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of all the isotopes of the element.

questions.q: Chlorine has isotopes ³⁵Cl (75%) and ³⁷Cl (25%). What is its relative atomic mass?
A sample of element X has isotopes of mass 24 (79%), 25 (10%) and 26 (11%). What is the relative atomic mass to 1 decimal place?
In a mass spectrum of chlorine gas, Cl₂, which m/z values are seen for the molecular ions?
questions.explanation: Cl₂⁺ can be ³⁵Cl³⁵Cl (70), ³⁵Cl³⁷Cl (72) or ³⁷Cl³⁷Cl (74), in the ratio 9:6:1.

questions.q: Which statement about the mass spectrum of an element is correct?

options.A: The height of each peak shows the relative abundance of that isotope
options.B: The number of peaks equals the atomic number
options.C: The highest peak is always the heaviest isotope
options.D: The spectrum shows the number of neutrons directly

questions.explanation: Each peak is an isotope at its m/z value and its height (or area) gives the relative abundance, from which Ar is calculated.

questions.q: Why do isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties?

options.A: They have the same number of neutrons
options.B: They have the same electron configuration
options.D: They have different numbers of protons

questions.explanation: Chemical reactions involve electrons. Isotopes have identical numbers of protons and electrons, so the same electron arrangement.

questions.q: Which particle has a relative mass of 1 and a relative charge of 0?
questions.explanation: Protons have mass 1 and charge +1, neutrons mass 1 and charge 0, electrons mass 1/1836 and charge −1.

questions.q: Which species contains the same number of electrons as the Ca²⁺ ion?
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ has 20 − 2 = 18 electrons, the same as an argon atom.

questions.q: What is the formula of aluminium sulfate?
questions.explanation: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ combine 2:3 to balance the charges: 2 × 3+ = 3 × 2−.

questions.q: What is the formula of ammonium carbonate?
questions.explanation: Two NH₄⁺ ions are needed for each CO₃²⁻ ion.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of manganese in MnO₄⁻?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is −2 each: 4 × −2 = −8. The ion has charge −1, so Mn = −1 − (−8) = +7.

questions.q: Which is the correct name for Fe₂(SO₄)₃?
questions.explanation: Three sulfate ions carry 6− in total, so each of the two iron ions must be 3+: iron(III).

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of chlorine in ClO₃⁻?
questions.explanation: 3 × −2 = −6 for oxygen; the ion is −1, so Cl = −1 + 6 = +5. The ion is chlorate(V).

questions.q: Which equation is correctly balanced?
questions.explanation: Two Al atoms give 2AlCl₃, needing 6 Cl atoms from 3Cl₂.

questions.q: Which ionic equation represents the reaction between solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulfate?
questions.explanation: The spectator ions Na⁺ and Cl⁻ stay in solution; the ionic equation shows only the ions that form the precipitate.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in Na₂S₂O₃?
questions.explanation: Na is +1 (×2 = +2) and O is −2 (×3 = −6). For neutrality 2S = +4, so each S is +2 on average.

questions.q: Which species has nitrogen with an oxidation number of +3?
questions.explanation: In NO₂⁻, 2 × −2 = −4 and the charge is −1, so N = +3. NO₂ is +4, NO₃⁻ is +5, NH₃ is −3.

questions.q: Which compound contains chromium with oxidation number +6?
questions.explanation: In CrO₄²⁻, 4 × −2 = −8 and the charge is −2, so Cr = +6.

questions.q: Which formula shows a diatomic element?
questions.explanation: Chlorine exists as Cl₂ molecules. Neon is monatomic, ozone is triatomic and phosphorus forms P₄.

questions.q: How many moles of water molecules are in 36.0 g of water? (Mr = 18.0)
What is the mass of 0.250 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃? (Mr = 100.1)
What volume does 0.150 mol of a gas occupy at room temperature and pressure? (Vm = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹)
What is the concentration of a solution containing 0.0500 mol of NaOH in 250 cm³?
questions.explanation: c = n / V = 0.0500 / 0.250 = 0.200 mol dm⁻³. Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000.

questions.q: A compound contains 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass. What is its empirical formula?
A compound has empirical formula CH₂O and relative molecular mass 60.0. What is its molecular formula?
questions.explanation: Empirical mass = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30. 60/30 = 2, so the molecular formula is (CH₂O)₂ = C₂H₄O₂.

questions.q: Which statement defines the Avogadro constant?

options.A: The number of grams in one mole
options.B: The number of particles in one mole of a substance, 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹
options.C: The volume of one mole of gas
options.D: The mass of one atom of carbon-12

questions.explanation: One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles, the same as the number of atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12.

questions.q: Using pV = nRT, what is the volume of 1.00 mol of gas at 300 K and 100 kPa? (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
questions.explanation: V = nRT / p = 1.00 × 8.314 × 300 / 100 000 = 0.0249 m³ (24.9 dm³). Pressure must be in Pa.

questions.q: Hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·xH₂O, loses 36.1% of its mass on heating to form the anhydrous salt. What is x? (Mr CuSO₄ = 159.6, H₂O = 18.0)
questions.explanation: Take 100 g: 63.9 g CuSO₄ = 0.400 mol and 36.1 g water = 2.01 mol. Ratio 2.01/0.400 = 5.0.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl neutralises 20.0 cm³ of NaOH solution. What is the concentration of the NaOH?
What is the percentage yield if 4.40 g of ester is obtained when the theoretical maximum is 8.80 g?
questions.explanation: Percentage yield = actual / theoretical × 100 = 4.40 / 8.80 × 100 = 50.0%.

questions.q: What is the atom economy for making hydrogen in the reaction Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂? (Ar: Zn 65.4, Cl 35.5, H 1.0)
questions.explanation: Atom economy = Mr of desired product / total Mr of products × 100 = 2.0 / (136.4 + 2.0) × 100 = 1.4%.

questions.q: Which type of reaction always has an atom economy of 100%?
questions.explanation: In an addition reaction all the reactant atoms end up in the single product, so there is no waste.

questions.q: Which of these is a weak acid?
questions.explanation: Ethanoic acid only partially dissociates in water. HCl, HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ are strong acids that dissociate fully.

questions.q: Which equation shows the dissociation of a strong acid?
questions.explanation: A strong acid dissociates completely, shown with a single arrow. The equilibrium arrow for ethanoic acid shows partial dissociation.

questions.q: Which is a base but NOT an alkali?
questions.explanation: An alkali is a soluble base that releases OH⁻ in water. Copper(II) oxide is a base (it neutralises acids) but is insoluble.

questions.q: What are the products when sulfuric acid reacts with sodium carbonate?

options.B: Sodium sulfate, water and carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide: H₂SO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂.

questions.q: Which equation shows the reaction of hydrochloric acid with magnesium oxide?
questions.explanation: A metal oxide (base) reacts with acid to form a salt and water only; no gas is produced.

questions.q: What is the ionic equation for neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong alkali?
questions.explanation: Only the H⁺ and OH⁻ ions react; the metal and non-metal ions remain as spectators in solution.

questions.q: Which is the correct description of a standard solution?

options.B: A solution of exactly known concentration
options.C: A solution of a strong acid

questions.explanation: A standard solution is prepared by dissolving an accurately weighed mass of solute and making up to a known volume in a volumetric flask.

questions.q: In a titration, why is the conical flask swirled while adding the acid from the burette?

options.B: To mix the reactants so the indicator colour change shows the true end point

questions.explanation: Without mixing, local excess of one reagent would give a misleading indicator colour before the whole solution has reacted.

questions.q: Which piece of apparatus is used to measure 25.0 cm³ of solution accurately into a conical flask?
questions.explanation: A volumetric (bulb) pipette delivers one fixed volume with high precision. A burette is used for the variable volume being added.

questions.q: What is a 'concordant' pair of titres?

options.A: Two titres within 0.10 cm³ of each other
options.B: Two titres that are both above 25 cm³

questions.explanation: Concordant titres agree closely (typically within 0.10 cm³) and only these are used to calculate the mean titre.

questions.q: Which equation shows ammonia acting as a base?
questions.explanation: Ammonia accepts a proton from HCl to form the ammonium ion, which is the definition of a base.

questions.q: In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, which species is oxidised?
questions.explanation: Zinc loses electrons (oxidation number 0 to +2). Cu²⁺ gains electrons and is reduced.

questions.q: In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, which is the oxidising agent?
questions.explanation: The oxidising agent accepts electrons and is itself reduced: Cu²⁺ gains two electrons.

questions.q: What is the change in oxidation number of iron in the reaction 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃?
questions.explanation: Iron metal is 0. In FeCl₃ each Cl is −1 so Fe is +3.

questions.q: Which reaction is a redox reaction?
questions.explanation: Magnesium changes from 0 to +2 and hydrogen from +1 to 0. The other reactions have no changes in oxidation number.

questions.q: In a disproportionation reaction

options.B: the same element is both oxidised and reduced

questions.explanation: For example Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HClO: chlorine goes from 0 to −1 and from 0 to +1.

questions.q: Which equation shows the half-equation for the oxidation of iron(II) ions?
questions.explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons. Fe²⁺ loses one electron to become Fe³⁺.

questions.q: When magnesium reacts with dilute sulfuric acid, which species is reduced?
questions.explanation: H⁺ ions gain electrons to form H₂ (oxidation number +1 to 0). Sulfate is a spectator ion.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is +1 (×2 = +2), so for a neutral molecule the two oxygen atoms total −2, giving −1 each.

questions.q: Combining the half-equations Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ and MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O gives which ratio of Fe²⁺ to MnO₄⁻?
questions.explanation: Five Fe²⁺ ions supply the five electrons needed to reduce one MnO₄⁻ ion.

questions.q: Which statement about oxidation numbers in a compound is correct?

options.A: They always add up to zero

questions.explanation: Fluorine, the most electronegative element, is always −1. Hydrogen is −1 in metal hydrides, oxygen is −1 in peroxides, and in ions the oxidation numbers add up to the charge.

questions.q: Which reaction shows the reduction of copper?
questions.explanation: Copper goes from +2 in CuO to 0 in the metal, a gain of electrons.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of electrons in the n = 3 shell?
questions.explanation: Shell 3 has 3s, 3p and 3d subshells: 2 + 6 + 10 = 18 electrons (2n² with n = 3).

questions.q: How many orbitals are in a p subshell?
questions.explanation: A p subshell has three orbitals (px, py, pz), each holding two electrons.

questions.q: What is the electron configuration of a chlorine atom?
questions.explanation: Chlorine has 17 electrons: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 5.

questions.q: What is the electron configuration of the Fe²⁺ ion?
questions.explanation: Iron is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². When ions form the 4s electrons are lost first, leaving 3d⁶.

questions.q: Which is the shape of a p orbital?
questions.explanation: s orbitals are spherical; p orbitals are dumbbell shaped with two lobes.

questions.q: Which element has the electron configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹?
questions.explanation: Copper (29 electrons) has a full 3d subshell and a single 4s electron, an exception to the usual filling order.

questions.q: Which statement about the 4s and 3d subshells is correct?

options.B: The 4s is filled before the 3d because it is at a lower energy, but is emptied first when ions form

questions.explanation: The 4s subshell is slightly lower in energy than 3d when empty, so it fills first (K, Ca). Once filled it is slightly higher, so ions lose 4s electrons first.

questions.q: How many electrons can one orbital hold?
questions.explanation: An orbital holds a maximum of two electrons, which must have opposite spins.

questions.q: What is the electron configuration of the oxide ion, O²⁻?
questions.explanation: Oxygen has 8 electrons; the 2− ion gains two more to reach 10, the same configuration as neon.

questions.q: Which block of the periodic table contains calcium?
questions.explanation: Calcium's highest energy electrons are in the 4s subshell, so it is in the s block.

questions.q: Which element has three unpaired electrons in its ground state?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is 1s² 2s² 2p³. The three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins (one in each).

questions.q: What is the shape of a molecule of BF₃?
questions.explanation: Boron has three bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so the shape is trigonal planar with 120° bond angles.

questions.q: What is the bond angle in ammonia, NH₃?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen has three bonding pairs and one lone pair. The lone pair repels more strongly, squeezing the angle from 109.5° to 107°.

questions.q: What is the shape of SF₆?
questions.explanation: Six bonding pairs and no lone pairs around sulfur give an octahedral shape with 90° bond angles.

questions.q: Which molecule is non-polar despite having polar bonds?
questions.explanation: CO₂ is linear, so the two C=O dipoles are equal and opposite and cancel. In H₂O and NH₃ the dipoles do not cancel.

questions.q: Which is the strongest type of intermolecular force?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding is the strongest intermolecular force. Covalent bonds are intramolecular and much stronger still.

questions.q: Why does ice float on water?

options.B: Hydrogen bonds hold the water molecules in an open lattice in ice, so it is less dense than liquid water
