options.D: Water molecules are heavier in the liquid

questions.explanation: In ice each molecule is hydrogen bonded to four others in a regular open structure that occupies more space than the liquid.

questions.q: Which substance has the highest boiling point?
questions.explanation: Water forms on average two hydrogen bonds per molecule (two H atoms and two lone pairs), more than HF or NH₃, so it has the highest boiling point.

questions.q: Why does the boiling point increase from Cl₂ to Br₂ to I₂?

options.B: The molecules have more electrons so the induced dipole–dipole forces are stronger

questions.explanation: More electrons give larger temporary dipoles and stronger London forces between molecules, needing more energy to separate them.

questions.q: What is the shape and bond angle in a water molecule?
questions.explanation: Two bonding pairs and two lone pairs. The two lone pairs repel strongly, reducing the angle to 104.5°.

questions.q: Which statement explains why sodium chloride conducts electricity when molten but not when solid?

options.A: Electrons are free to move in the liquid
options.B: The ions are free to move in the liquid but fixed in the solid lattice

questions.explanation: Ionic conduction requires mobile ions. In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the giant ionic lattice.

questions.q: What type of bond forms in the ammonium ion when NH₃ reacts with H⁺?
questions.explanation: The nitrogen lone pair provides both electrons for the new N–H bond, which is a dative covalent bond.

questions.q: Which describes electronegativity?

options.A: The energy to remove an electron
options.B: The ability of an atom to attract the bonding electrons in a covalent bond

questions.explanation: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group; fluorine is the most electronegative element.

questions.q: Why is graphite a good conductor of electricity while diamond is not?

options.B: Each carbon in graphite forms three bonds, leaving a delocalised electron that can move along the layers

questions.explanation: In diamond all four outer electrons are used in covalent bonds. In graphite the fourth electron is delocalised between the layers.

questions.q: Which molecule has a trigonal bipyramidal shape?
questions.explanation: Five bonding pairs and no lone pairs on the central phosphorus give a trigonal bipyramid with angles of 90° and 120°.

questions.q: Which property increases across Period 3 from sodium to argon?
questions.explanation: Across a period the nuclear charge increases while shielding stays similar, so the outer electrons are held more tightly and the general trend in ionisation energy is upwards.

questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of aluminium lower than that of magnesium?

options.B: Aluminium's outer electron is in a 3p orbital, higher in energy and more shielded than the 3s electron of magnesium

questions.explanation: The 3p electron is further from the nucleus and shielded by the 3s electrons, so less energy is needed to remove it despite the higher nuclear charge.

questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of sulfur lower than that of phosphorus?

options.B: In sulfur the electron is removed from a 3p orbital containing a pair; the repulsion between the paired electrons makes it easier to remove

questions.explanation: Phosphorus is 3p³ with one electron per orbital. Sulfur is 3p⁴, so one orbital holds a pair and the repulsion lowers the energy needed.

questions.q: Why does first ionisation energy decrease down a group?

options.B: The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, outweighing the increased nuclear charge

questions.explanation: Each new shell adds distance and shielding, so the attraction on the outer electron falls despite more protons.

questions.q: Which element has the largest jump between its second and third ionisation energies?
questions.explanation: Magnesium is 2,8,2. The third electron comes from the inner n = 2 shell, much closer to the nucleus and less shielded, giving a very large jump.

questions.q: The successive ionisation energies of an element are 578, 1817, 2745, 11 577 kJ mol⁻¹. In which group is the element?
questions.explanation: The large jump occurs after the third electron, so three electrons are in the outer shell: Group 3 (13), aluminium.

questions.q: Which element in Period 3 (Na to Ar) has the highest melting point?
questions.explanation: Silicon has a giant covalent structure. Breaking its strong covalent bonds needs far more energy than melting the metals or the simple molecular non-metals.

questions.q: Why does the melting point increase from sodium to aluminium?

options.B: The number of delocalised electrons per atom and the charge on the ions increase, so the metallic bonding is stronger

questions.explanation: Na⁺ with one delocalised electron, Mg²⁺ with two and Al³⁺ with three: stronger electrostatic attraction between ions and the electron sea.

questions.q: Why does sulfur (S₈) have a higher melting point than phosphorus (P₄)?

options.B: S₈ molecules are larger with more electrons, so the London forces between molecules are stronger

questions.explanation: Both are simple molecular. The larger S₈ molecule has more electrons, giving stronger induced dipole–dipole forces.

questions.q: Which statement describes periodicity?

options.A: The repeating pattern of properties across each period
options.C: The number of elements in a group

questions.explanation: Periodicity is the regular recurrence of trends in physical and chemical properties as the periodic table is crossed, period after period.

questions.q: Which equation represents the second ionisation energy of calcium?
questions.explanation: The second ionisation energy is for removing one electron from each gaseous 1+ ion to form gaseous 2+ ions.

questions.q: Which equation shows the reaction of calcium with water?
questions.explanation: Group 2 metals react with water to form the hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

questions.q: Why does reactivity increase down Group 2?

options.B: Ionisation energies decrease because the outer electrons are more shielded and further from the nucleus, so electrons are lost more easily
options.C: The number of outer electrons increases

questions.explanation: Each metal must lose two electrons. Going down the group this requires less energy, so the reactions become more vigorous.

questions.q: Which Group 2 hydroxide is the most soluble in water?
questions.explanation: Solubility of the hydroxides increases down the group, so barium hydroxide solution has the highest pH.

questions.q: Which Group 2 hydroxide solution has the lowest pH?
questions.explanation: Magnesium hydroxide is only sparingly soluble, so the concentration of OH⁻ is lowest and the pH is lowest (about 9 to 10).

questions.q: Which Group 2 compound is used to treat acid indigestion?
questions.explanation: Mg(OH)₂ (milk of magnesia) neutralises excess stomach acid: Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O.

questions.q: Which Group 2 compound is used to neutralise acidic soils?
questions.explanation: Ca(OH)₂ (slaked lime) raises the pH of soil by neutralising acids.

questions.q: What is the product when calcium oxide reacts with water?
questions.explanation: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂, a vigorous exothermic reaction forming an alkaline solution.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number change for the Group 2 metal when it reacts with oxygen?
questions.explanation: Group 2 metals lose both outer electrons to form M²⁺ ions, e.g. 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

questions.q: Which thermal decomposition reaction is correct?
questions.explanation: Heating a Group 2 carbonate gives the metal oxide and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Which equation shows magnesium reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: A redox reaction: Mg is oxidised to Mg²⁺ and H⁺ is reduced to hydrogen gas.

questions.q: What is observed when barium is added to water compared with magnesium?

options.C: They react at the same rate

questions.explanation: Reactivity increases down the group. Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water; barium reacts rapidly.

questions.q: Which statement about the trend in boiling points of the halogens is correct?

options.B: They increase down the group because the molecules have more electrons and stronger London forces
options.C: They are all gases at room temperature
options.D: They increase because the covalent bonds get stronger

questions.explanation: F₂ and Cl₂ are gases, Br₂ a liquid and I₂ a solid at room temperature, because the induced dipole–dipole forces increase with the number of electrons.

questions.q: What is observed when chlorine is bubbled through potassium bromide solution?
questions.explanation: Chlorine is more reactive and displaces bromine: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. Bromine gives an orange solution.

questions.q: Which equation shows a displacement reaction that occurs?
questions.explanation: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide. Bromine is above iodine, so it oxidises iodide ions.

questions.q: Why does the reactivity of the halogens decrease down the group?

options.B: The atoms get larger with more shielding, so the attraction for an incoming electron is weaker

questions.explanation: A halogen reacts by gaining an electron. Down the group the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so the electron is attracted less strongly.

questions.q: Why is cyclohexane added when testing halogen displacement reactions?

options.B: The halogen dissolves in the non-polar cyclohexane layer, where its colour is easier to see

questions.explanation: Bromine appears orange and iodine violet in the organic layer, making them easier to distinguish than in water.

questions.q: Which equation shows disproportionation of chlorine?
questions.explanation: Chlorine goes from 0 to −1 (NaCl) and 0 to +1 (NaClO) in the same reaction. This is how bleach is made.

questions.q: What is the reaction of chlorine with water in sunlight?
questions.explanation: In bright sunlight chlorine oxidises water, forming hydrochloric acid and oxygen. Without sunlight the disproportionation Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO occurs.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of chlorinating drinking water?

options.B: It kills bacteria and prevents the spread of waterborne diseases

questions.explanation: Chlorine (as HClO) kills harmful microorganisms. The risks include toxic chlorine gas and the formation of chlorinated hydrocarbons, which some think may be carcinogenic.

questions.q: What is observed when silver nitrate solution is added to a solution containing iodide ions?
questions.explanation: AgI is a yellow precipitate that does not dissolve in concentrated ammonia. AgCl is white and AgBr cream.

questions.q: Which silver halide precipitate dissolves in dilute ammonia solution?
questions.explanation: AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia, AgBr only in concentrated ammonia and AgI in neither. This distinguishes the three.

questions.q: Why is the solution acidified with nitric acid before adding silver nitrate in the halide test?

options.B: To remove carbonate and hydroxide ions that would also give precipitates with silver ions
options.D: To change the colour of the precipitate

questions.explanation: Ag₂CO₃ and AgOH are also insoluble. Nitric acid removes these ions first so a precipitate confirms a halide.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of chlorine in sodium chlorate(I), NaClO?
questions.explanation: Na is +1 and O is −2, so Cl must be +1 for the compound to be neutral.

questions.q: Which test identifies carbonate ions?

options.A: Add silver nitrate; a white precipitate forms
options.B: Add dilute acid; bubbles of a gas that turns limewater cloudy
options.C: Add barium chloride; a white precipitate forms
options.D: Add sodium hydroxide and warm; a gas turns red litmus blue

questions.explanation: Carbonates react with acid to release carbon dioxide: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O. CO₂ turns limewater milky.

questions.q: Which test identifies sulfate ions?

options.A: Add acidified barium chloride (or nitrate); a white precipitate forms
options.B: Add silver nitrate; a yellow precipitate forms
options.C: Add acid; a gas is released
options.D: Add ammonia; a blue solution forms

questions.explanation: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄, a white precipitate insoluble in acid.

questions.q: Which test identifies ammonium ions?

options.A: Add acid and test the gas with limewater
options.B: Add sodium hydroxide, warm, and test the gas with damp red litmus which turns blue

questions.explanation: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O. Ammonia is the only common alkaline gas, turning damp red litmus blue.

questions.q: In which order should the tests for carbonate, sulfate and halide ions be carried out on an unknown solution?
questions.explanation: Carbonate first (barium and silver carbonates would precipitate otherwise), then sulfate (silver sulfate is slightly insoluble), then halide.

questions.q: Why must the carbonate test be done before the sulfate test?

options.A: Carbonate ions would react with barium ions to give a white precipitate, giving a false positive for sulfate
options.C: The acid used in the sulfate test removes sulfate

questions.explanation: BaCO₃ is also a white precipitate, so carbonate must be removed (by acidifying) before testing for sulfate.

questions.q: What is the ionic equation for the test for chloride ions?
questions.explanation: Silver chloride is a white precipitate. Silver ions are added as silver nitrate solution.

questions.q: Which gas is produced when a carbonate reacts with dilute nitric acid?
questions.explanation: All carbonates release CO₂ with acids, which is identified by turning limewater cloudy.

questions.q: Which reagent is used to confirm the presence of ammonia gas?

options.B: Damp red litmus paper, which turns blue
options.C: Damp blue litmus paper, which turns red

questions.explanation: Ammonia is alkaline and dissolves in the moisture on the litmus to give OH⁻ ions.

questions.q: What is observed when barium nitrate is added to a solution containing sulfate ions?
questions.explanation: Barium sulfate is a dense white insoluble solid. Barium nitrate is preferred when a halide test will follow, because barium chloride would add chloride ions.

questions.q: Which ion gives a cream precipitate with silver nitrate that dissolves in concentrated ammonia but not dilute?
questions.explanation: AgBr is cream and dissolves only in concentrated ammonia.

questions.q: A solution gives no precipitate with barium nitrate, no gas with acid, and a white precipitate with silver nitrate that dissolves in dilute ammonia. Which ion is present?
questions.explanation: The white silver precipitate that dissolves in dilute ammonia is silver chloride.

questions.q: Which definition is correct for the standard enthalpy change of formation?

options.A: The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is formed from its elements under standard conditions, all in their standard states
options.B: The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is burned completely in oxygen
options.C: The enthalpy change when one mole of water forms in a neutralisation
options.D: The enthalpy change when one mole of bonds is broken

questions.explanation: ΔfH° refers to forming one mole of compound from its elements in their standard states at 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K.

questions.q: What is the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state?
questions.explanation: By definition, forming an element from itself involves no change, so ΔfH° = 0 for O₂(g), C(graphite), etc.

questions.q: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of combustion of methane?
questions.explanation: One mole of methane burns completely in oxygen with products in their standard states (water as a liquid at 298 K).

questions.q: In a calorimetry experiment 50.0 g of water is heated by 10.0 °C. What is the energy transferred? (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Which is the main reason that experimental enthalpies of combustion are less exothermic than data-book values?

options.B: Heat loss to the surroundings and incomplete combustion

questions.explanation: Heat lost to the air and the apparatus, evaporation of fuel and incomplete combustion (soot) all reduce the measured temperature rise.

questions.q: What is the sign of the enthalpy change for bond breaking?
questions.explanation: Breaking a bond requires energy (endothermic). Bond making releases energy (exothermic).

questions.q: Using average bond enthalpies, ΔH for a reaction is calculated as
questions.explanation: ΔH = Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds broken) − Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds formed). Energy in minus energy out.

questions.q: Why do calculations using average bond enthalpies give only approximate answers?

options.B: Average values are taken over many different compounds and the actual bond enthalpy in a particular molecule differs
options.C: They ignore the number of bonds

questions.explanation: The C–H bond enthalpy, for example, varies with its environment, so the data-book average is not exactly right for any one molecule.

questions.q: Using Hess's law, ΔrH = ΣΔfH(products) − ΣΔfH(reactants). For the reaction CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O with ΔfH values (kJ mol⁻¹): CH₄ −75, CO₂ −394, H₂O −286, what is ΔrH?
What does Hess's law state?

options.A: Enthalpy change is independent of the route taken, provided the initial and final conditions are the same
options.B: Enthalpy change equals the energy of bonds broken
options.C: Energy is always released in reactions
options.D: The enthalpy of an element is always zero

questions.explanation: Hess's law is a consequence of conservation of energy and lets enthalpy changes be found indirectly.

questions.q: In an enthalpy profile diagram for an exothermic reaction

options.A: the products are higher in energy than the reactants
options.B: the products are lower in energy than the reactants

questions.explanation: Energy is released, so the products are at a lower enthalpy. The activation energy is the hump between reactants and the peak.

questions.q: Which of these describes the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation?

options.A: The enthalpy change when one mole of water is formed from the reaction of an acid and a base under standard conditions
options.B: The enthalpy change when one mole of acid is neutralised
options.C: The enthalpy change when one mole of salt is formed
options.D: The enthalpy change when one mole of base dissolves

questions.explanation: ΔneutH° is defined per mole of water formed, so it is about −57 kJ mol⁻¹ for all strong acid–strong base reactions.

questions.q: Which statement defines activation energy?

options.A: The energy released in a reaction
options.B: The minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur
options.C: The total energy of the reactants

questions.explanation: Only collisions with energy at least equal to the activation energy lead to reaction.

questions.q: Why does increasing the concentration of a reactant increase the rate?

options.B: There are more particles per unit volume, so collisions are more frequent

questions.explanation: More particles in the same volume means more collisions per second. The energy of the particles is unchanged.

questions.q: Why does increasing the temperature increase the rate of reaction?

options.A: Only because the particles collide more often
options.B: Mainly because a greater proportion of particles have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy

questions.explanation: Higher temperature shifts the Boltzmann distribution to the right, so many more collisions have enough energy to react. Collision frequency rises only slightly.

questions.q: On a Boltzmann distribution curve, what does the area under the curve represent?
questions.explanation: Each point gives the number of molecules with a given energy, so the total area is the total number of molecules.

questions.q: What happens to the Boltzmann distribution curve when the temperature is increased?

options.A: The peak moves to the right and gets lower; the area is unchanged
options.B: The peak moves to the left and gets higher
options.C: The curve starts at a higher point
options.D: The area under the curve increases

questions.explanation: At higher temperature the average energy increases, spreading the distribution. The number of molecules does not change.

questions.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of reaction?

options.B: It provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful
options.D: It increases the energy of the particles

questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy without being used up. On the Boltzmann curve, more molecules now exceed the (lower) Ea.

questions.q: Which is an example of a heterogeneous catalyst?

options.D: Chlorine radicals in the ozone layer

questions.explanation: A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants: solid iron with gaseous N₂ and H₂.

questions.q: Which is an example of a homogeneous catalyst?

options.D: Vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process

questions.explanation: Sulfuric acid and the liquid reactants are all in the same phase, so it is homogeneous.

questions.q: Why are catalysts important in industry?

options.A: They increase the yield at equilibrium
options.B: They allow reactions to run at lower temperatures and pressures, saving energy and cost, and reducing CO₂ emissions
options.C: They are consumed in the reaction

questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers Ea so an acceptable rate is reached at lower temperature, which cuts energy use and allows cheaper equipment.

questions.q: Which method would be suitable for following the rate of the reaction between calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid?

options.A: Measuring the change in mass of the flask as CO₂ escapes

questions.explanation: CO₂ is lost from the open flask, so the mass decreases with time. Collecting the gas volume also works.

questions.q: How is the rate at a given time found from a graph of volume of gas against time?

options.B: By drawing a tangent at that time and finding its gradient
options.C: By dividing the total volume by total time

questions.explanation: The gradient of the tangent gives the instantaneous rate. The gradient at t = 0 gives the initial rate.

questions.q: Which statement describes a dynamic equilibrium?

options.B: The forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant
options.C: The concentrations of reactants and products are equal

questions.explanation: Both reactions continue, but because the rates are equal there is no overall change in the amounts present. It requires a closed system.

questions.q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹, which change shifts the equilibrium to the right?
questions.explanation: There are fewer moles of gas on the right (2 vs 4), so increasing pressure favours the forward reaction (Le Chatelier's principle).

questions.q: For an endothermic forward reaction, increasing the temperature

options.A: shifts the equilibrium to the left
options.B: shifts the equilibrium to the right
options.C: has no effect on the position

questions.explanation: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, which absorbs the added heat.

questions.q: What is the effect of a catalyst on the position of equilibrium?

options.C: No effect; equilibrium is reached faster

questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally.

questions.q: For the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), what is the expression for Kc?
questions.explanation: Kc = concentrations of products over reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient.

questions.q: What are the units of Kc for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)?
questions.explanation: Kc = [HI]² / ([H₂][I₂]). The concentration units cancel because there are two on top and two on the bottom.

questions.q: What are the units of Kc for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
questions.explanation: Kc = [NH₃]² / ([N₂][H₂]³): (mol dm⁻³)² / (mol dm⁻³)⁴ = mol⁻² dm⁶.

questions.q: A large value of Kc means

options.A: the equilibrium lies to the left
options.B: the equilibrium lies to the right

questions.explanation: A large Kc means the concentrations of products are much greater than those of reactants at equilibrium.

questions.q: Why is a compromise temperature of about 450 °C used in the Haber process?

options.A: The equilibrium yield is highest at this temperature
options.B: A lower temperature gives a higher yield but too slow a rate; the compromise gives a reasonable yield at an acceptable rate

questions.explanation: The forward reaction is exothermic, so low temperature favours ammonia, but the rate would be far too slow. 450 °C with an iron catalyst balances yield and rate.

questions.q: Why is a pressure of about 200 atm, rather than a much higher pressure, used in the Haber process?

options.A: Higher pressure gives a lower yield
options.B: Higher pressures need expensive, thick-walled equipment and more energy, outweighing the extra yield
options.C: The catalyst is damaged above 200 atm
options.D: Pressure does not affect the yield

questions.explanation: High pressure favours ammonia, but the cost and safety of equipment to withstand very high pressures limit what is economic.

questions.q: Which change alters the value of Kc?
questions.explanation: Kc depends only on temperature. Changes in concentration or pressure shift the position of equilibrium but Kc stays the same.

questions.q: For the equilibrium CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, equilibrium concentrations are all 1.0 mol dm⁻³ except the ester at 4.0 mol dm⁻³. What is Kc?
Which is the correct IUPAC name for CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The longest chain has four carbons (butane) with a methyl group on carbon 2, numbering from the end that gives the lowest locant.

questions.q: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
questions.explanation: Each alkane has 2n + 2 hydrogen atoms, e.g. C₃H₈ for propane.

questions.q: Which pair of compounds are functional group isomers?
questions.explanation: Propanal (aldehyde) and propanone (ketone) share the formula C₃H₆O but have different functional groups. The others are positional or chain isomers.

questions.q: Which type of isomerism is shown by pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane?
questions.explanation: Both are C₅H₁₂ but the carbon skeleton is arranged differently: a straight chain versus a branched chain.

questions.q: What is the molecular formula of hexan-2-one?
questions.explanation: A ketone with six carbons: CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ has 12 hydrogens and one oxygen.

questions.q: Which is a homolytic fission?
questions.explanation: Homolytic fission splits the bond evenly, each atom taking one electron to form two radicals. Heterolytic fission forms ions.

questions.q: Which species is a radical?
questions.explanation: A radical has an unpaired electron, shown by the dot. It is highly reactive.

questions.q: What is the empirical formula of butane, C₄H₁₀?
questions.explanation: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio: 4:10 simplifies to 2:5.

questions.q: Which describes a homologous series?

options.A: Compounds with the same molecular formula
options.B: A series of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, each differing by CH₂
options.C: Compounds with the same number of carbon atoms

questions.explanation: Members of a homologous series show similar chemical properties and a gradual trend in physical properties.

questions.q: How many structural isomers does C₄H₁₀ have?
questions.explanation: Butane and 2-methylpropane are the only two.

questions.q: What is the skeletal formula convention?

options.B: Carbon atoms are at the ends and corners of lines; hydrogens on carbon are omitted but functional groups are shown

questions.explanation: Skeletal formulae show the carbon skeleton as lines, with heteroatoms and their hydrogens drawn in.

questions.q: Which of these is a saturated hydrocarbon?
questions.explanation: Saturated hydrocarbons contain only C–C single bonds and fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. C₅H₁₂ is pentane.

questions.q: What is the bond angle around each carbon atom in an alkane?
questions.explanation: Each carbon has four bonding pairs arranged tetrahedrally, giving 109.5°.

questions.q: Which type of bond is a C–H σ bond?

options.A: Overlap of orbitals above and below the bond axis
options.B: Direct overlap of atomic orbitals along the axis between the two nuclei

questions.explanation: σ (sigma) bonds result from head-on overlap, allowing free rotation about the bond.

questions.q: Why does the boiling point of straight-chain alkanes increase with chain length?

options.B: Larger molecules have more electrons and more surface contact, so London forces between molecules are stronger

questions.explanation: Only induced dipole–dipole forces act between alkane molecules, and these increase with the number of electrons and points of contact.

questions.q: Why does 2,2-dimethylpropane have a lower boiling point than pentane?

options.B: Its branched shape reduces the surface contact between molecules, weakening the London forces

questions.explanation: Branched molecules cannot pack as closely as straight chains, so the intermolecular forces are weaker.

questions.q: Which equation shows the complete combustion of propane?
questions.explanation: Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water: balance C (3), H (8 → 4H₂O), then O (6 + 4 = 10 → 5O₂).

questions.q: Which product of incomplete combustion is toxic because it binds to haemoglobin?
questions.explanation: CO binds irreversibly to haemoglobin, preventing oxygen transport.

questions.q: What conditions are needed for the reaction between methane and chlorine?

options.D: High pressure and a nickel catalyst

questions.explanation: UV light provides the energy for homolytic fission of Cl₂ to form chlorine radicals in the initiation step.

questions.q: Which equation shows the initiation step in the radical substitution of methane by chlorine?
questions.explanation: Initiation is the homolytic fission of the chlorine molecule by UV light.

questions.q: Which equation shows a propagation step in the radical substitution of methane by chlorine?
questions.explanation: Propagation steps consume one radical and produce another, keeping the chain going. The two propagation steps are CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl and CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•.

questions.q: Which is a termination step?
questions.explanation: Termination removes radicals by combining two of them to form a stable molecule.

questions.q: Why is radical substitution of limited use in organic synthesis?

options.B: Further substitution gives a mixture of products (CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄) and, in longer chains, substitution at different positions

questions.explanation: The radicals are not selective, so a mixture of mono-, di-, tri- and tetra-substituted products forms, lowering the yield of any one compound.

questions.q: Why are alkanes relatively unreactive?

options.B: The C–C and C–H σ bonds are strong and non-polar, so the molecules do not attract nucleophiles or electrophiles

questions.explanation: The small electronegativity difference between C and H gives essentially non-polar bonds, and the bonds have high bond enthalpies.

questions.q: What is the shape around each carbon atom in a C=C double bond?
questions.explanation: Each carbon of the double bond has three σ bonds in a plane with 120° angles, and the π bond above and below.

questions.q: How is a π bond formed?

options.B: Sideways overlap of p orbitals above and below the plane of the σ bond
options.D: Overlap of a lone pair with an empty orbital

questions.explanation: The π bond results from sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals and restricts rotation about the double bond.

questions.q: Which compound shows E/Z isomerism?
questions.explanation: E/Z isomerism needs a C=C with two different groups on each carbon. In but-2-ene each carbon has H and CH₃.

questions.q: Which statement about the cis-trans naming system is correct?

options.A: It can be used for all E/Z isomers
options.B: It is a special case of E/Z isomerism used when the two substituents on each carbon are the same
options.C: Cis means the groups are on opposite sides
options.D: Trans is the same as Z

questions.explanation: Cis-trans is only used when there is a hydrogen (or identical group) on each carbon of the C=C. Otherwise the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priority rules give E or Z.

questions.q: In the E isomer of but-2-ene, the two methyl groups are

options.A: on the same side of the double bond
options.B: on opposite sides of the double bond

questions.explanation: E (entgegen) means the higher priority groups are on opposite sides; Z (zusammen) means together.

questions.q: What is the product of the reaction between ethene and bromine?
questions.explanation: Electrophilic addition adds one bromine atom to each carbon of the former double bond.

questions.q: Which observation shows the presence of a C=C double bond?

options.A: Bromine water turns from orange to colourless

questions.explanation: Alkenes decolourise bromine water as the bromine adds across the double bond.

questions.q: What type of mechanism do alkenes undergo with hydrogen bromide?
questions.explanation: The electron-rich π bond attracts the δ+ hydrogen of HBr (the electrophile); a carbocation intermediate then reacts with Br⁻.

questions.q: What is the major product when propene reacts with hydrogen bromide?
questions.explanation: Markownikoff's rule: the H adds to the carbon with more hydrogens, forming the more stable secondary carbocation, so Br ends up on the middle carbon.

questions.q: Why is 2-bromopropane the major product from propene and HBr?

options.A: It has a lower boiling point
options.B: The secondary carbocation intermediate is more stable than the primary because alkyl groups donate electron density (positive inductive effect)
options.C: Br is attracted to the end carbon
options.D: The primary carbocation is more stable

questions.explanation: More alkyl groups around the positive carbon stabilise the carbocation, so that intermediate forms faster and gives the major product.

questions.q: Which reagent and conditions convert ethene to ethanol industrially?

options.A: Steam, phosphoric acid catalyst, 300 °C and 60 atm

questions.explanation: Hydration of ethene by steam over a phosphoric acid catalyst is an electrophilic addition.

questions.q: Which conditions are used to hydrogenate an alkene to an alkane?

options.A: Hydrogen gas with a nickel catalyst at about 150 °C
options.D: Hydrogen at room temperature with no catalyst

questions.explanation: Catalytic hydrogenation is used to harden vegetable oils into margarine.

questions.q: What is the repeat unit of poly(propene)?
questions.explanation: The double bond opens and the monomer CH₂=CHCH₃ becomes the repeat unit with the methyl group as a side chain.

questions.q: Which is an environmental concern about addition polymers?

options.B: They are non-biodegradable and persist in landfill; disposal by incineration can release toxic gases
options.D: They react with oxygen in the air

questions.explanation: Polyalkenes are chemically inert. Recycling, incineration with energy recovery, use as feedstock for cracking, and biodegradable or photodegradable alternatives are responses.

questions.q: How does a radical form in the first step of the reaction between ethene and bromine?

options.A: Bromine does not form radicals in this reaction; the Br₂ molecule is polarised by the π electrons and heterolytic fission gives Br⁺ and Br⁻

questions.explanation: Electrophilic addition involves an induced dipole in Br₂ and heterolytic fission. Radicals are involved in alkane substitution, not alkene addition.

questions.q: Which is a secondary alcohol?
questions.explanation: In propan-2-ol the carbon bearing the OH is attached to two other carbon atoms.

questions.q: Which alcohol cannot be oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
questions.explanation: Tertiary alcohols have no hydrogen on the carbon bearing the OH, so they resist oxidation.

questions.q: What is the product when butan-2-ol is heated with acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
questions.explanation: Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones. Further oxidation does not occur.

questions.q: Which reagent and conditions give propanoic acid from propan-1-ol?

options.A: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heated under reflux

questions.explanation: Refluxing with excess oxidising agent takes the primary alcohol through the aldehyde to the carboxylic acid.

questions.q: What colour change is seen when an alcohol is oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
questions.explanation: Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) is reduced to Cr³⁺ (green).

questions.q: Why do alcohols have higher boiling points than alkanes of similar molecular mass?

options.B: Alcohols form hydrogen bonds between their OH groups

questions.explanation: The polar O–H bond allows hydrogen bonding, a stronger intermolecular force than the London forces in alkanes.

questions.q: Why does solubility in water decrease as the alcohol chain lengthens?

options.B: The non-polar hydrocarbon chain becomes a larger part of the molecule and disrupts hydrogen bonding with water

questions.explanation: Short alcohols mix fully with water because of hydrogen bonding, but a long hydrocarbon chain cannot interact with water.

questions.q: Which reagent and conditions dehydrate an alcohol to an alkene?

options.A: Concentrated sulfuric acid or phosphoric acid, heated under reflux

questions.explanation: Dehydration is an elimination reaction removing H₂O from adjacent carbons, catalysed by a concentrated acid.

questions.q: Which alkenes form when butan-2-ol is dehydrated?
questions.explanation: Water can be eliminated using a hydrogen from either adjacent carbon, giving but-1-ene or but-2-ene, the latter as E and Z isomers.

questions.q: Which reagents convert ethanol into bromoethane?

options.A: Sodium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid (forming HBr in situ), heated
options.D: Hydrogen bromide gas at room temperature only

questions.explanation: The halide ion from NaBr and H₂SO₄ gives HBr, which substitutes the OH group in a nucleophilic substitution.

questions.q: Which equation shows the complete combustion of ethanol?
questions.explanation: Count the oxygens: 2 × 2 + 3 = 7 on the right; one is already in ethanol, so six from 3O₂.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: A four-carbon chain with the OH on carbon 2, numbering to give the lowest locant.

questions.q: Which type of mechanism do haloalkanes undergo with hydroxide ions?
questions.explanation: The δ+ carbon attached to the halogen is attacked by the OH⁻ nucleophile and the halide ion leaves.

questions.q: Why is the carbon atom in a C–Br bond electron deficient (δ+)?

options.A: Bromine is less electronegative than carbon
options.B: Bromine is more electronegative than carbon, so the bonding electrons are drawn towards it

questions.explanation: The polar C–Br bond leaves carbon slightly positive, making it a target for nucleophiles.

questions.q: Which haloalkane is hydrolysed fastest by water?
questions.explanation: Rate depends on the C–halogen bond enthalpy, not the bond polarity. C–I is the weakest bond, so it breaks most easily.

questions.q: In the experiment comparing hydrolysis rates of haloalkanes with aqueous silver nitrate and ethanol, what is observed with 1-iodobutane?
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis releases I⁻ ions, which react with Ag⁺ to give yellow AgI. Because C–I is weakest, this appears first.

questions.q: Why is ethanol used as a solvent in the hydrolysis experiment with silver nitrate?

options.B: Haloalkanes are insoluble in water; ethanol dissolves both the haloalkane and the aqueous silver nitrate

questions.explanation: Ethanol allows the water, haloalkane and silver nitrate to be in one solution so they can react.

questions.q: What is the product when 1-bromopropane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: The OH⁻ replaces the Br in a nucleophilic substitution, giving the primary alcohol.

questions.q: Why are CFCs no longer used in aerosols and refrigerants?

options.B: They are very stable, reach the stratosphere and release chlorine radicals under UV light, which catalyse the breakdown of ozone

questions.explanation: The C–Cl bond breaks homolytically in UV light. One Cl• radical can destroy many thousands of ozone molecules.

questions.q: Which equation shows the formation of a chlorine radical from CF₂Cl₂?
questions.explanation: UV light causes homolytic fission of the weaker C–Cl bond rather than the stronger C–F bond.

questions.q: Which pair of equations shows chlorine radicals catalysing ozone breakdown?

options.A: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂ and ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂

questions.explanation: The chlorine radical is regenerated, so it acts as a catalyst. Overall: O₃ + O → 2O₂.

questions.q: Which radical, produced from nitrogen oxides in aircraft exhausts, also breaks down ozone?
questions.explanation: NO• + O₃ → NO₂• + O₂ and NO₂• + O → NO• + O₂, with the NO• regenerated.

questions.q: Why is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane hydrolysed faster than 1-bromobutane?

options.A: It has a stronger C–Br bond
options.B: Tertiary haloalkanes react via a stable tertiary carbocation (SN1), which forms readily
options.D: It is more soluble in water

questions.explanation: Tertiary haloalkanes can lose the halide first to form a stabilised carbocation, which is faster than the one-step attack needed for primary haloalkanes.

questions.q: What is the role of ozone in the stratosphere?

options.B: It absorbs harmful UV-B radiation, protecting living organisms
options.D: It is a greenhouse gas only

questions.explanation: The ozone layer filters out most UV-B, which would otherwise cause skin cancer and damage crops.

questions.q: Which apparatus is used to heat a reaction mixture for a long time without losing volatile reactants?
questions.explanation: Reflux uses a vertical condenser so vapours condense and return to the flask.

questions.q: What is the purpose of anti-bumping granules?

options.B: To promote smooth boiling by providing nucleation sites for bubbles

questions.explanation: Without them superheated liquid can boil violently (bump) and spray up the condenser.

questions.q: Which technique separates a liquid product from a mixture using differences in boiling point?
questions.explanation: Distillation collects the component boiling at the chosen temperature, which is read from a thermometer at the still-head.

questions.q: Where should the thermometer bulb be placed during distillation?

options.B: Level with the side arm leading to the condenser
options.C: At the top of the condenser

questions.explanation: The thermometer should measure the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser to identify the boiling point of what is being collected.

questions.q: Which reagent is used to remove acidic impurities from a crude organic product in a separating funnel?

options.B: Sodium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate solution

questions.explanation: The carbonate neutralises acid impurities; the CO₂ formed is released by regularly opening the stopper.

questions.q: Which drying agent is suitable for an organic liquid?

options.A: Anhydrous calcium chloride or anhydrous magnesium sulfate

questions.explanation: Anhydrous salts absorb traces of water. The liquid is dry when the solid no longer clumps and runs freely.

questions.q: In a separating funnel, how do you tell which layer is the aqueous layer?

options.B: Add a little water and see which layer increases in volume
options.D: It is always the smaller layer

questions.explanation: The denser liquid is at the bottom. Adding water confirms which layer is aqueous because it joins that layer.

questions.q: Why does the water enter the condenser at the bottom and leave at the top?

options.A: To make the water flow faster
options.B: So the condenser stays full of water and the coolest water meets the hottest vapour, improving condensation

questions.explanation: Counter-current flow keeps the jacket completely filled with cold water.

questions.q: Which flow chart correctly plans a synthesis from an alkene to a carboxylic acid?
questions.explanation: Steam hydration gives the alcohol; a primary alcohol is then oxidised under reflux to the carboxylic acid.

questions.q: Which reagent converts an alcohol to a haloalkane?

options.A: Sodium halide with concentrated sulfuric acid

questions.explanation: HX generated in situ substitutes the OH group.

questions.q: Why is a product purified by redistillation after a reflux reaction?

options.B: To separate the product from unreacted starting material and by-products with different boiling points

questions.explanation: The crude mixture contains several components; distillation collects the fraction boiling at the product's boiling point.

questions.q: Which bond gives a strong, broad absorption at 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹ in an infrared spectrum?
questions.explanation: The O–H of a carboxylic acid is very broad and overlaps the C–H region. An alcohol O–H is at 3200 to 3600 cm⁻¹.

questions.q: Which bond gives a strong, sharp absorption at about 1700 cm⁻¹?
questions.explanation: Carbonyl stretches appear at 1640 to 1750 cm⁻¹ and are strong because of the large dipole.

questions.q: A compound shows an IR peak at 1715 cm⁻¹ but none above 3000 cm⁻¹ apart from C–H. Which could it be?
questions.explanation: A C=O peak without an O–H peak indicates an aldehyde, ketone or ester. Propanone is the ketone.

questions.q: Why do greenhouse gases such as CO₂, CH₄ and H₂O absorb infrared radiation?

options.B: Their bonds vibrate at frequencies that match infrared radiation and the vibrations change the dipole of the molecule

questions.explanation: IR absorption excites bond vibrations (stretching and bending). The absorbed energy is re-emitted in all directions, some back to Earth.

questions.q: What does the molecular ion peak in a mass spectrum give?

options.B: The relative molecular mass of the compound

questions.explanation: The M⁺ peak at the highest m/z (ignoring M+1) corresponds to the whole molecule with one electron removed.

questions.q: Why is there a small peak at M+1 in the mass spectrum of an organic compound?

options.B: Due to molecules containing a ¹³C atom (1.1% natural abundance)
options.C: Due to loss of a hydrogen atom

questions.explanation: About 1.1% of carbon is ¹³C, so a small proportion of molecules are one mass unit heavier.

questions.q: A mass spectrum has a peak at m/z = 29. Which fragment is likely?
A compound has a mass spectrum with peaks at m/z = 15, 43 and 58. Which compound fits?
questions.explanation: Propanone (Mr 58) fragments to CH₃⁺ (15) and CH₃CO⁺ (43). Propanal also has Mr 58 but gives a prominent m/z 29 (CHO⁺ or C₂H₅⁺).

questions.q: Which fingerprint region is used to identify a compound by comparison with a database?
questions.explanation: The complex pattern below 1500 cm⁻¹ is unique to each compound and is matched against known spectra.

questions.q: Which use of infrared spectroscopy is correct?

options.A: Measuring the mass of a molecule
options.B: Breathalysers detecting ethanol by the C–H and O–H absorptions

questions.explanation: Modern breathalysers use IR absorption by ethanol vapour, and IR is also used to monitor air pollution.

questions.q: Which combination identifies the functional group and the molecular mass of an unknown organic compound?
questions.explanation: IR shows which bonds are present (functional group); the mass spectrum gives Mr and fragmentation clues.

questions.q: The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[A]²[B]. What is the overall order?
questions.explanation: Overall order is the sum of the individual orders: 2 + 1 = 3.

questions.q: What are the units of k for a first-order reaction?
questions.explanation: rate = k[A], so k = rate/[A] = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/(mol dm⁻³) = s⁻¹.

questions.q: What are the units of k for a reaction with overall order 2?
questions.explanation: k = rate/[A]² gives (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/(mol dm⁻³)² = mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹.

questions.q: Tripling the concentration of X increases the rate by a factor of 9. What is the order with respect to X?
questions.explanation: 9 = 3², so rate ∝ [X]² and the reaction is second order with respect to X.

questions.q: Which feature of a concentration–time graph shows first-order kinetics?

options.A: A straight line with negative gradient
options.D: A half-life that increases over time

questions.explanation: A first-order reactant has a constant half-life, independent of its concentration.

questions.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 20 s. What is the rate constant? (k = ln 2 / t½)
What shape is a rate–concentration graph for a zero-order reactant?

options.B: A straight line through the origin

questions.explanation: Rate does not depend on the concentration of a zero-order reactant, so the line is horizontal.

questions.q: The rate-determining step of a reaction is

options.B: the slowest step in the mechanism, which controls the overall rate
options.D: the step that releases most energy

questions.explanation: The overall rate cannot be faster than the slowest step. Species in the rate equation appear in or before this step.

questions.q: The mechanism for a reaction has the slow step (CH₃)₃CBr → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻ followed by a fast step with OH⁻. What is the rate equation?
questions.explanation: Only species in the rate-determining step appear. OH⁻ reacts in the fast step so it is zero order (SN1 mechanism).

questions.q: The Arrhenius equation in logarithmic form is
questions.explanation: Taking natural logs of k = Ae^(−Ea/RT) gives ln k = ln A − Ea/RT, a straight line when ln k is plotted against 1/T.

questions.q: From a plot of ln k against 1/T, the activation energy is found from
questions.explanation: Gradient = −Ea/R, so Ea = −gradient × R. The intercept gives ln A.

questions.q: Which experimental method could follow the rate of the reaction between propanone and iodine?

options.B: Colorimetry, as the brown iodine colour fades

questions.explanation: Iodine is the only coloured species, so its concentration can be followed continuously by absorbance.

questions.q: In the iodine clock reaction, what does the measured time represent?

options.A: The time for the reaction to finish completely
options.B: The time for a fixed small amount of iodine to form, so 1/t is proportional to the initial rate
options.D: The time for the catalyst to act

questions.explanation: A fixed amount of thiosulfate removes iodine until it runs out, then the blue-black colour appears. Rate ∝ 1/t.

questions.q: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), what is the expression for Kp?
questions.explanation: Kp uses partial pressures raised to the power of the stoichiometric coefficients.

questions.q: The mole fraction of a gas is

options.B: moles of that gas ÷ total moles of gas
options.C: moles of that gas × total pressure

questions.explanation: Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure.

questions.q: A mixture of 1.0 mol A, 2.0 mol B and 1.0 mol C has a total pressure of 400 kPa. What is the partial pressure of B?
questions.explanation: Mole fraction of B = 2.0/4.0 = 0.50, so p(B) = 0.50 × 400 = 200 kPa.

questions.q: What are the units of Kp for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) with pressures in atm?
questions.explanation: Kp = p(NH₃)² / (p(N₂)p(H₂)³) = atm² / atm⁴ = atm⁻².

questions.q: Which statement about Kc is correct?

options.A: Kc changes when the concentration of a reactant changes
options.C: Kc changes when a catalyst is added

questions.explanation: Equilibrium constants are constant at a given temperature. Concentration and pressure changes shift the position, but Kc is restored.

questions.q: When the temperature of an exothermic reaction at equilibrium is raised
questions.explanation: Equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction (left), lowering the product concentrations relative to reactants, so Kc falls.

questions.q: If Kc = 2.0 for A ⇌ B and [A] is suddenly doubled, what happens?

options.B: The system shifts to make more B until the ratio [B]/[A] returns to 2.0
options.C: The system shifts to make more A

questions.explanation: Adding reactant makes the ratio [B]/[A] less than Kc, so the forward reaction proceeds until the ratio equals Kc again.

questions.q: In a homogeneous equilibrium, which species are included in the Kc expression?

options.B: All reactants and products, which are in the same phase

questions.explanation: A homogeneous equilibrium has everything in one phase. In heterogeneous equilibria, solids and pure liquids are omitted.

questions.q: For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), what is Kp?
questions.explanation: Solids have no partial pressure and are omitted from Kp, leaving only the CO₂.

questions.q: 1.0 mol of ethanoic acid and 1.0 mol of ethanol reach equilibrium with 0.67 mol of ester formed. How many moles of acid remain?
questions.explanation: Each mole of ester uses one mole of acid: 1.0 − 0.67 = 0.33 mol.

questions.q: In the equilibrium H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), a 2.0 dm³ vessel contains 0.20 mol H₂, 0.20 mol I₂ and 1.60 mol HI. What is Kc?
questions.explanation: Concentrations: H₂ = I₂ = 0.10, HI = 0.80 mol dm⁻³. Kc = 0.80² / (0.10 × 0.10) = 64. For this reaction the volume cancels anyway.

questions.q: Which is true when Kc = 1 × 10⁻⁵?

options.A: The reaction goes almost to completion
options.B: The equilibrium lies well to the left; little product forms

questions.explanation: A very small Kc means product concentrations are tiny compared with reactant concentrations.

questions.q: Which is the Brønsted–Lowry definition of an acid?

options.A: A substance that produces hydroxide ions

questions.explanation: A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates H⁺; a base accepts H⁺.

questions.q: In the equilibrium HNO₂ + H₂O ⇌ NO₂⁻ + H₃O⁺, which is the conjugate base of HNO₂?
questions.explanation: The conjugate base is what remains after the acid has donated its proton.

questions.q: What is the pH of a solution with [H⁺] = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³?
What is [H⁺] in a solution of pH 11.2?
What is the pH of 0.025 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide at 298 K? (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶)
Which expression is Kw?
questions.explanation: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K.

questions.q: What is the pH of pure water at a temperature where Kw = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶?
questions.explanation: [H⁺] = √Kw = 2.0 × 10⁻⁷, pH = 6.70. Water is still neutral because [H⁺] = [OH⁻].

questions.q: A weak acid HA (0.20 mol dm⁻³) has Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. What is its pH?
Which approximation is made when calculating the pH of a weak acid?
questions.explanation: Dissociation is small, so the undissociated acid concentration barely changes, and ignoring H⁺ from water means [H⁺] = [A⁻].

questions.q: pKa = −log Ka. Which acid is the strongest?
questions.explanation: The lower the pKa, the larger the Ka and the stronger the acid.

questions.q: Which mixture is a buffer solution?
questions.explanation: A buffer is a weak acid with its conjugate base (or a weak base with its conjugate acid). Strong acids cannot buffer.

questions.q: How can a buffer be made from a weak acid and a strong base?

options.A: Mix equal moles of acid and base
options.B: Add less base than acid, so some weak acid is neutralised to its salt and the rest remains

questions.explanation: Partial neutralisation leaves a mixture of the weak acid and its conjugate base, which is a buffer.

questions.q: In a buffer of ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate, what happens when alkali is added?

options.A: The OH⁻ reacts with ethanoic acid to form ethanoate ions and water, so [H⁺] barely changes
options.B: The OH⁻ reacts with ethanoate ions

questions.explanation: The large reservoir of weak acid removes added OH⁻: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O.

questions.q: For a buffer, pH = pKa when
questions.explanation: Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]; if [A⁻] = [HA] then [H⁺] = Ka and pH = pKa.

questions.q: A buffer contains 0.10 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵) and 0.20 mol dm⁻³ sodium ethanoate. What is its pH?
How does blood keep its pH close to 7.4?

options.A: By the H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻ buffer system

questions.explanation: Carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate ions form a buffer. Excess H⁺ is removed by HCO₃⁻, and excess OH⁻ by H₂CO₃.

questions.q: On a pH titration curve for a strong acid with a strong base, where is the equivalence point?

options.B: pH 7, in the middle of the vertical section

questions.explanation: The vertical region spans roughly pH 3 to 11 for strong–strong, with the equivalence point at pH 7.

questions.q: Which indicator is suitable for a weak acid–strong base titration?
questions.explanation: The vertical section lies in the alkaline region (about pH 7 to 11), so the indicator must change colour within that range.

questions.q: Why is no indicator suitable for a weak acid–weak base titration?

options.B: There is no sharp vertical section on the pH curve, so no indicator changes colour at the equivalence point
options.D: The end point is at pH 7

questions.explanation: The curve changes gradually, so the colour change would occur over a large volume of titrant.

questions.q: What is the pH at the half-neutralisation point in a weak acid–strong base titration?
questions.explanation: At half neutralisation [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa. This is how pKa can be measured from a titration curve.

questions.q: Which definition is correct for lattice enthalpy (OCR)?

options.A: The enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions
options.B: The enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound is broken into gaseous ions
options.C: The enthalpy change when one mole of solid dissolves
options.D: The energy to atomise one mole of compound

questions.explanation: OCR defines lattice enthalpy as the formation of one mole of ionic lattice from gaseous ions, so it is always exothermic (negative).

questions.q: Which equation represents the lattice enthalpy of magnesium chloride?
questions.explanation: Gaseous ions combine to form one mole of the solid lattice.

questions.q: Which has the most exothermic lattice enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Smaller, more highly charged ions attract more strongly. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are both small and doubly charged.

questions.q: Which process does the enthalpy change of atomisation describe?

options.A: Formation of one mole of gaseous atoms from the element in its standard state
options.B: Formation of one mole of gaseous ions
options.C: Breaking one mole of bonds in a gas

questions.explanation: For example ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g), ΔatH = +122 kJ mol⁻¹. Always endothermic.

questions.q: What is the first electron affinity of chlorine?

options.A: The energy to remove one electron from Cl(g)
options.B: The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms each gains one electron to form gaseous 1− ions
options.C: The energy released when Cl₂ forms

questions.explanation: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g), ΔH = −349 kJ mol⁻¹. First electron affinities are exothermic.

questions.q: Why is the second electron affinity of oxygen endothermic?

options.B: The electron is being added to an already negative ion, so there is repulsion to overcome
options.D: The first electron affinity is also endothermic

questions.explanation: O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g) requires energy because the incoming electron is repelled by the negative ion.

questions.q: In a Born–Haber cycle, the enthalpy of formation equals

options.B: the sum of atomisation, ionisation and electron affinity terms plus the lattice enthalpy
options.C: the lattice enthalpy minus the ionisation energy

questions.explanation: Hess's law: ΔfH = ΔatH(metal) + ΔatH(non-metal) + IE(s) + EA(s) + ΔLEH.

questions.q: Which quantity has to be doubled in the Born–Haber cycle for CaF₂?

options.B: Atomisation enthalpy and electron affinity of fluorine

questions.explanation: Two moles of F atoms are needed, each gaining an electron. Calcium needs the first and second ionisation energies once each.

questions.q: The enthalpy change of solution is

options.B: the enthalpy change when one mole of solute dissolves in enough solvent to form a solution where the ions do not interact
options.C: the energy to form gaseous ions

questions.explanation: It can be exothermic or endothermic, depending on the balance of lattice enthalpy and hydration enthalpies.

questions.q: Which equation relates enthalpy of solution to lattice enthalpy and hydration enthalpies (OCR definitions)?
questions.explanation: Dissolving reverses lattice formation (−ΔLEH, endothermic) then hydrates the gaseous ions (exothermic).

questions.q: Which ion has the most exothermic hydration enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Higher charge and smaller radius give a greater attraction to the polar water molecules.

questions.q: Why does hydration enthalpy become less exothermic down Group 1?

options.B: The ionic radius increases so the charge density falls and attraction to water is weaker

questions.explanation: The same 1+ charge spread over a larger ion gives a weaker electrostatic attraction to water.

questions.q: Which change has a positive entropy change?

options.B: Ammonia forming from nitrogen and hydrogen

questions.explanation: Dissolving a solid into free ions in solution increases disorder. The other three changes reduce disorder.

questions.q: What is the sign of ΔS for 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g)?
questions.explanation: Three moles of gas become two moles of gas, so disorder decreases.

questions.q: Entropy is measured in units of
questions.explanation: Standard entropies are quoted in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so must be divided by 1000 before use with ΔH in kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: ΔS for a reaction is calculated as
questions.explanation: Like ΔH from enthalpies of formation, ΔS = total entropy of products minus total entropy of reactants.

questions.q: Which expression gives the free energy change?
questions.explanation: Feasible reactions have ΔG < 0.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +120 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Above what temperature is it feasible?
questions.explanation: ΔG = 0 when T = ΔH/ΔS = 40 000 / 120 = 333 K. Above this, TΔS exceeds ΔH and ΔG is negative.

questions.q: A reaction with ΔH negative and ΔS positive is
questions.explanation: Both terms make ΔG negative: ΔH < 0 and −TΔS < 0.

questions.q: A reaction with ΔH positive and ΔS negative is
questions.explanation: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is positive at every temperature.

questions.q: For ΔH = −100 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −200 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, what is ΔG at 298 K?
Why may a reaction with a negative ΔG not take place at a noticeable rate?

options.B: The activation energy may be very high, so the reaction is kinetically slow

questions.explanation: Thermodynamic feasibility says nothing about rate. Diamond converting to graphite has negative ΔG but a huge activation energy.

questions.q: Why does entropy increase when a solid melts?

options.B: The particles can move more freely, so there are more ways of arranging them (more disorder)

questions.explanation: Entropy is a measure of dispersal of energy and disorder. Liquids are more disordered than solids, gases more than liquids.

questions.q: Which has the highest standard entropy?
questions.explanation: Gases have far more disorder than liquids or solids, so the highest entropy.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of chromium in Cr₂O₇²⁻?
questions.explanation: 7 × −2 = −14; the ion is −2, so 2Cr = +12 and each Cr is +6.

questions.q: In the half-equation MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O, which species is reduced?
questions.explanation: Manganese goes from +7 to +2 by gaining five electrons.

questions.q: In a redox titration, 25.0 cm³ of Fe²⁺ solution needs 20.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄. What is the concentration of Fe²⁺? (MnO₄⁻ : Fe²⁺ = 1 : 5)
Why is no indicator needed in a manganate(VII) titration?

options.B: The purple MnO₄⁻ is decolourised as it reacts; the first permanent pink tinge marks the end point
options.D: An indicator would react with Fe²⁺

questions.explanation: The manganate(VII) is self-indicating: the end point is the first excess drop that stays pink.

questions.q: In iodine–thiosulfate titrations, which indicator is added near the end point?

options.C: Starch, which turns blue-black with iodine

questions.explanation: Starch forms a blue-black complex with iodine. The end point is when the colour disappears as the last iodine is reduced.

questions.q: What is the half-equation for thiosulfate reacting with iodine?
questions.explanation: Thiosulfate is oxidised to tetrathionate. With I₂ + 2e⁻ → 2I⁻, the ratio is 2 thiosulfate : 1 iodine.

questions.q: What is the standard electrode potential of the standard hydrogen electrode?
questions.explanation: It is the reference electrode, defined as 0.00 V under standard conditions.

questions.q: Standard conditions for electrode potentials are
questions.explanation: Temperature 298 K, gas pressure 100 kPa and ion concentrations of 1 mol dm⁻³.

questions.q: E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V and E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V. What is the standard cell potential of a Zn/Ag cell?
questions.explanation: E°cell = E°(positive electrode) − E°(negative electrode) = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V.

questions.q: In the Zn/Ag cell, which electrode is the negative electrode?

options.A: Zinc, because it has the more negative E° and is oxidised
options.B: Silver, because it is a precious metal

questions.explanation: The half-cell with the more negative potential releases electrons (oxidation) and is the negative terminal.

questions.q: Which is the strongest reducing agent? E°: Mg²⁺/Mg −2.37 V; Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V; Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V; Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V.
questions.explanation: The most negative E° corresponds to the species that loses electrons most readily.

questions.q: E°(Cl₂/Cl⁻) = +1.36 V and E°(Br₂/Br⁻) = +1.09 V. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: The more positive couple (Cl₂) is reduced and the less positive (Br⁻) oxidised: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, E°cell = +0.27 V.

questions.q: Why might a predicted feasible redox reaction not happen?

options.B: The activation energy may be high (slow rate) or the conditions may not be standard

questions.explanation: E° values predict thermodynamic feasibility under standard conditions only; they say nothing about rate.

questions.q: Which is a feature of a fuel cell?

options.A: It stores a fixed amount of chemical energy
options.B: It generates a voltage continuously as fuel and oxygen are supplied
options.C: It must be recharged with electricity

questions.explanation: In a hydrogen fuel cell, H₂ and O₂ react to form water and the cell runs as long as fuel is supplied.

questions.q: Which is the overall reaction in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is oxidised at one electrode and oxygen reduced at the other; the only product is water.

questions.q: Which is the definition of a transition element?

options.A: Any element in the d block
options.B: A d-block element that forms at least one ion with a partially filled d subshell
options.C: An element with a full d subshell
options.D: A metal that forms coloured compounds

questions.explanation: Scandium (Sc³⁺ is 3d⁰) and zinc (Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰) are d-block but not transition elements.

questions.q: What is the electron configuration of chromium?
questions.explanation: Chromium is an exception: a half-filled 3d and 4s is more stable than 3d⁴ 4s².

questions.q: What is the electron configuration of Cu²⁺?
questions.explanation: Copper is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Losing the 4s electron and one 3d electron gives 3d⁹.

questions.q: Which is a typical property of transition elements?

options.A: They form only one oxidation state
options.B: They form coloured ions and complexes

questions.explanation: Transition elements show variable oxidation states, form coloured compounds and complex ions, and act as catalysts.

questions.q: Why do transition metal compounds show a range of oxidation states?

options.A: The 4s and 3d electrons are close in energy so different numbers of electrons can be lost
options.C: They have only one outer electron

questions.explanation: Successive ionisation energies rise gradually, so several oxidation states are energetically accessible.

questions.q: Which oxidation state of vanadium is yellow in solution?
questions.explanation: Vanadium colours: +5 (VO₂⁺) yellow, +4 (VO²⁺) blue, +3 green, +2 violet.

questions.q: Which transition metal is used as a catalyst in the Haber process?
questions.explanation: Iron catalyses N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. V₂O₅ is used in the Contact process, nickel for hydrogenation.

questions.q: Which catalyst is used in the Contact process for making sulfuric acid?
questions.explanation: V₂O₅ catalyses 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, cycling between +5 and +4 oxidation states.

questions.q: What is observed when sodium hydroxide is added to a solution of copper(II) sulfate?
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s), pale blue.

questions.q: What is observed when sodium hydroxide is added to a solution of iron(III) chloride?
questions.explanation: Fe³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₃, orange-brown (rust coloured).

questions.q: What colour is the precipitate when sodium hydroxide is added to manganese(II) sulfate solution?
questions.explanation: Mn(OH)₂ is a light brown precipitate that darkens as it is oxidised in air.

questions.q: What is observed when sodium hydroxide is added to chromium(III) chloride solution?

options.A: A green precipitate that dissolves in excess to give a dark green solution
options.B: A green precipitate insoluble in excess

questions.explanation: Cr(OH)₃ is green and amphoteric; in excess NaOH it dissolves to form [Cr(OH)₆]³⁻.

questions.q: What is the shape of a six-coordinate complex such as [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
questions.explanation: Six ligands arranged octahedrally around the central ion with 90° bond angles.

questions.q: What is a ligand?

options.B: A molecule or ion that donates a pair of electrons to a metal ion to form a coordinate bond

questions.explanation: Ligands have at least one lone pair, e.g. H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, CN⁻.

questions.q: What is the coordination number of [CuCl₄]²⁻?
questions.explanation: Coordination number is the number of coordinate bonds to the central ion. Four chloride ligands give 4.

questions.q: What shape is the tetrachlorocuprate(II) ion, [CuCl₄]²⁻?
questions.explanation: Four large chloride ligands arrange tetrahedrally around copper.

questions.q: Which complex is square planar?
questions.explanation: Platinum(II) complexes such as cisplatin are square planar, which allows cis and trans isomers.

questions.q: Which is a bidentate ligand?
questions.explanation: Bidentate ligands have two atoms with lone pairs that each form a coordinate bond, e.g. en (two N atoms) and ethanedioate (two O atoms).

questions.q: How many bidentate ligands are needed to fill an octahedral complex?
questions.explanation: Each bidentate ligand forms two coordinate bonds, so three give the coordination number 6.

questions.q: Which type of isomerism is shown by [Ni(en)₃]²⁺?
questions.explanation: An octahedral complex with three bidentate ligands is chiral and exists as two non-superimposable mirror images.

questions.q: In cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] (cisplatin), the two chloride ligands are
questions.explanation: Cis means adjacent. The trans isomer, with the chlorides opposite, is not an effective anticancer drug.

questions.q: By what process does cisplatin stop cancer cells dividing?

options.A: It forms coordinate bonds to nitrogen atoms on DNA bases, preventing replication
options.D: It stops the cell taking in oxygen

questions.explanation: Ligand substitution replaces the chlorides with N atoms of guanine bases, cross-linking the DNA strands so cancer cells cannot divide.

questions.q: Which octahedral complex can show cis-trans isomerism?
questions.explanation: Two identical ligands in an octahedral complex can be adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans). Six identical ligands give no isomers.

questions.q: What type of bond forms between a ligand and the central metal ion?
questions.explanation: The ligand donates both electrons of the bond from its lone pair.

questions.q: What is observed when excess ammonia is added to copper(II) sulfate solution?

options.A: A pale blue precipitate that remains
options.B: A pale blue precipitate that dissolves to give a deep blue solution

questions.explanation: Ammonia first precipitates Cu(OH)₂, then as a ligand forms deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺.

questions.q: Which equation shows the ligand substitution of [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ with excess ammonia?
questions.explanation: Only four water ligands are replaced, giving the deep blue tetraammine complex.

questions.q: What is observed when concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to aqueous copper(II) sulfate (ligand substitution)?

options.A: The solution turns yellow (green with excess water)

questions.explanation: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ → [CuCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O. The tetrachlorocuprate ion is yellow; mixtures appear green.

questions.q: In the reaction [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ → [CuCl₄]²⁻, what happens to the coordination number?
questions.explanation: Chloride ligands are larger than water, so only four fit around the copper ion, and the shape changes from octahedral to tetrahedral.

questions.q: What colour change occurs when concentrated HCl is added to [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
questions.explanation: Pink [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ becomes blue [CoCl₄]²⁻ as chloride ligands replace water.

questions.q: What is observed when excess ammonia is added to a solution of cobalt(II) ions?

options.A: A blue precipitate that dissolves to form a pale yellow-brown solution, turning darker in air
options.B: A pink solution that stays pink

questions.explanation: Co(OH)₂ forms then dissolves in excess NH₃ to give [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺, which oxidises in air to the +3 complex.

questions.q: Which is the equation for the ligand substitution of [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ with excess ammonia?
questions.explanation: All six water ligands are replaced by ammonia to form the purple hexaamminechromium(III) ion.

questions.q: Haemoglobin contains iron(II) in a complex with a haem group. What is bound to the iron when oxygen is transported?
questions.explanation: Oxygen forms a coordinate bond to Fe²⁺ in the lungs and is released in the tissues.

questions.q: Why is carbon monoxide toxic?

options.B: It binds more strongly to the Fe²⁺ in haemoglobin than oxygen does, and the substitution is irreversible

questions.explanation: CO is a stronger ligand than O₂, so haemoglobin can no longer carry oxygen.

questions.q: Which statement about ligand substitution is correct?

options.A: The oxidation state of the metal always changes
options.B: One ligand is replaced by another; the coordination number may or may not change

questions.explanation: Substitution by similar sized ligands (NH₃ for H₂O) keeps the coordination number; larger Cl⁻ reduces it from 6 to 4.

questions.q: What is the colour of [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺?
questions.explanation: The tetraamminediaquacopper(II) ion is a characteristic deep (royal) blue.

questions.q: What is observed when acidified potassium dichromate(VI) reacts with zinc?

options.A: Orange to green, then green to blue

questions.explanation: Zinc reduces Cr(VI) (orange Cr₂O₇²⁻) to Cr(III) (green Cr³⁺) and then to Cr(II) (blue Cr²⁺).

questions.q: Which reagent oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ in acidic solution?
questions.explanation: MnO₄⁻ is a strong oxidising agent, reduced to Mn²⁺ while Fe²⁺ is oxidised to Fe³⁺.

questions.q: Which equation represents the oxidation of Fe²⁺ by MnO₄⁻?
questions.explanation: Five Fe²⁺ supply the five electrons needed for Mn(VII) → Mn(II), with eight H⁺ forming four waters.

questions.q: What is observed when hydrogen peroxide is added to a chromium(III) solution in alkaline conditions?

options.A: Green to yellow as Cr(III) is oxidised to chromate(VI)

questions.explanation: In alkali, H₂O₂ oxidises Cr³⁺ to the yellow CrO₄²⁻ ion.

questions.q: Cr₂O₇²⁻ and CrO₄²⁻ interconvert depending on pH. Which is correct?

options.B: Acid favours orange dichromate(VI); alkali favours yellow chromate(VI)

questions.explanation: 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O. Both have chromium in +6.

questions.q: Which reagent reduces Cu²⁺ to Cu⁺ in the test for aldehydes?

options.B: An aldehyde reducing Fehling's or Benedict's solution

questions.explanation: The blue Cu²⁺ complex is reduced to a red precipitate of copper(I) oxide.

questions.q: What happens when copper(I) ions are in aqueous solution?

options.B: They disproportionate to Cu(0) and Cu(II)

questions.explanation: 2Cu⁺ → Cu + Cu²⁺. Copper(I) is only stable in insoluble compounds or complexes.

questions.q: What is produced when copper(I) oxide reacts with hot dilute sulfuric acid?
questions.explanation: Cu₂O + H₂SO₄ → Cu + CuSO₄ + H₂O: a brown solid and a blue solution.

questions.q: In the titration of iodine with sodium thiosulfate, what is the mole ratio I₂ : S₂O₃²⁻?
questions.explanation: I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻.

questions.q: Which oxidation state change occurs for manganese in the reaction of MnO₄⁻ with Fe²⁺ in acid?
questions.explanation: In acid, manganate(VII) is reduced to Mn²⁺.

questions.q: What colour change is seen when Fe³⁺ is reduced to Fe²⁺?
questions.explanation: Fe³⁺(aq) is yellow to orange-brown; Fe²⁺(aq) is pale green.

questions.q: Which test identifies the Cu²⁺ ion?

options.A: Sodium hydroxide gives a blue precipitate; excess ammonia gives a deep blue solution
options.B: Sodium hydroxide gives an orange-brown precipitate
options.D: Silver nitrate gives a white precipitate

questions.explanation: Cu(OH)₂ is pale blue; with excess ammonia it dissolves to [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺.

questions.q: Which test distinguishes Fe²⁺ from Fe³⁺?

options.A: Add sodium hydroxide: green precipitate for Fe²⁺, orange-brown for Fe³⁺

questions.explanation: Fe(OH)₂ is pale green; Fe(OH)₃ is orange-brown.

questions.q: Which ion gives a light brown precipitate with NaOH that darkens in air?
questions.explanation: Mn(OH)₂ is buff coloured and oxidises to darker Mn(III)/Mn(IV) oxides.

questions.q: Which ion gives a green precipitate with NaOH that dissolves in excess?
questions.explanation: Cr(OH)₃ is green and amphoteric, forming [Cr(OH)₆]³⁻ in excess alkali. Fe(OH)₂ is green but does not dissolve.

questions.q: Which test identifies carbonate ions in a solution?

options.A: Add dilute nitric acid and bubble the gas through limewater

questions.explanation: Effervescence of CO₂ that turns limewater cloudy confirms carbonate.

questions.q: Which test identifies sulfate ions?

options.A: Add acidified barium nitrate: a white precipitate forms
options.B: Add silver nitrate: a yellow precipitate forms

questions.explanation: BaSO₄ is a white precipitate insoluble in acid.

questions.q: Which test identifies ammonium ions?

options.A: Warm with sodium hydroxide; the gas turns damp red litmus blue

questions.explanation: Ammonia gas is released and is detected by damp red litmus turning blue.

questions.q: Which silver halide is yellow and insoluble in concentrated ammonia?
questions.explanation: Silver iodide is pale yellow and does not dissolve even in concentrated ammonia.

questions.q: What is observed when sodium hydroxide is added to a solution containing Cr³⁺ followed by hydrogen peroxide?

options.A: Green precipitate, then a yellow solution

questions.explanation: Cr(OH)₃ is green; in alkaline conditions H₂O₂ oxidises Cr(III) to yellow CrO₄²⁻.
