questions.q: A solution gives a pale green precipitate with NaOH which slowly turns orange-brown. Which ion is present?
questions.explanation: Fe(OH)₂ (green) is oxidised by air to Fe(OH)₃ (orange-brown).

questions.q: Why is barium nitrate preferred to barium chloride if a halide test will follow?

options.B: Barium chloride would add chloride ions, giving a false positive for chloride

questions.explanation: The halide test uses silver nitrate; any added chloride would precipitate as AgCl.

questions.q: Which statement describes the Kekulé model of benzene?

options.B: A ring with three alternating C=C double bonds
options.D: A planar molecule with six identical bonds

questions.explanation: Kekulé proposed cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. The delocalised model replaced it.

questions.q: Which evidence disproves the Kekulé structure?

options.B: All C–C bond lengths are equal (0.139 nm), between single and double bond lengths
options.D: Benzene burns with a smoky flame

questions.explanation: X-ray diffraction shows one bond length, not alternating short and long bonds. Benzene also resists addition and has a less exothermic hydrogenation enthalpy than expected.

questions.q: How many π electrons are delocalised in benzene?
questions.explanation: Each of the six carbons contributes one p electron to the delocalised ring above and below the plane.

questions.q: Which reagents and conditions are used to form nitrobenzene from benzene?

options.B: Concentrated HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄ at 50 °C

questions.explanation: The sulfuric acid generates the nitronium ion NO₂⁺, the electrophile.

questions.q: What is the electrophile in the nitration of benzene?
questions.explanation: HNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + HSO₄⁻ + H₂O.

questions.q: Which catalyst (halogen carrier) is used in the bromination of benzene?
questions.explanation: A halogen carrier polarises Br₂ to generate the Br⁺ electrophile. Benzene does not react with bromine without a catalyst.

questions.q: What is the product of the Friedel–Crafts alkylation of benzene with chloroethane and AlCl₃?
questions.explanation: Alkylation attaches the alkyl group: C₆H₆ + C₂H₅Cl → C₆H₅C₂H₅ + HCl.

questions.q: Why does phenol react with bromine water but benzene does not?

options.B: A lone pair on the oxygen is delocalised into the ring, increasing the electron density and activating it towards electrophiles

questions.explanation: The activated ring in phenol can polarise Br₂ without a catalyst, giving 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white precipitate) and decolourising the bromine.

questions.q: What is observed when phenol reacts with bromine water?

options.B: The bromine water is decolourised and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms

questions.explanation: Phenol is much more reactive than benzene and substitutes at the 2, 4 and 6 positions.

questions.q: Which statement about the acidity of phenol is correct?

options.A: Phenol reacts with sodium carbonate to release CO₂
options.B: Phenol is a weak acid that reacts with NaOH but not with carbonates
options.C: Phenol is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid

questions.explanation: Phenol is weakly acidic (pKa about 10): it forms sodium phenoxide with NaOH but is too weak to react with Na₂CO₃. Carboxylic acids do release CO₂.

questions.q: Which group directs further substitution to the 2 and 4 positions of a benzene ring?
questions.explanation: Electron-donating groups (OH, NH₂) activate the ring and direct 2,4; electron-withdrawing groups such as NO₂ direct to the 3 position.

questions.q: Which position is favoured for a second substituent on nitrobenzene?
questions.explanation: The NO₂ group is electron-withdrawing and directs incoming electrophiles to the 3 position.

questions.q: Why does benzene undergo substitution rather than addition with electrophiles?

options.B: Addition would disrupt the stable delocalised π system
options.D: Substitution is faster for all hydrocarbons

questions.explanation: Keeping the delocalised ring preserves about 150 kJ mol⁻¹ of stabilisation.

questions.q: Why does cyclohexene react with bromine without a catalyst while benzene does not?

options.B: The localised π bond in cyclohexene has a high electron density that polarises Br₂; benzene's delocalised electrons are spread out

questions.explanation: Delocalisation lowers the electron density at any one point, so benzene cannot induce a dipole in Br₂ strongly enough.

questions.q: Which reagent is used to reduce a carbonyl compound to an alcohol?
questions.explanation: Sodium tetrahydridoborate(III) supplies the hydride ion nucleophile.

questions.q: What is the product of the reduction of propanal with NaBH₄?
questions.explanation: Aldehydes are reduced to primary alcohols.

questions.q: What is the product of the reduction of butanone with NaBH₄?
questions.explanation: Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols.

questions.q: What type of mechanism is the reaction of HCN with a carbonyl compound?
questions.explanation: The CN⁻ nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon, then the O⁻ is protonated.

questions.q: What is the product when propanone reacts with HCN?
questions.explanation: The CN joins the central carbon with the OH, keeping both methyl groups: (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN.

questions.q: Which reagent is used to detect a carbonyl group (aldehyde or ketone)?
questions.explanation: 2,4-DNP gives an orange or yellow precipitate with any aldehyde or ketone, but not with other carbonyl-containing compounds like esters.

questions.q: How can the identity of a carbonyl compound be confirmed using 2,4-DNP?

options.A: By the colour of the precipitate
options.B: By recrystallising the precipitate and measuring its melting point against known values

questions.explanation: Each 2,4-DNP derivative has a characteristic sharp melting point that can be compared with data tables.

questions.q: Which reagent distinguishes an aldehyde from a ketone?

options.B: Tollens' reagent, which gives a silver mirror with aldehydes only

questions.explanation: Aldehydes are oxidised by Tollens' reagent (Ag⁺ reduced to Ag). Ketones are not oxidised.

questions.q: What is Tollens' reagent?
questions.explanation: It is made by adding ammonia to silver nitrate solution.

questions.q: What is the product when ethanal is oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
questions.explanation: Aldehydes are oxidised to carboxylic acids; the dichromate turns from orange to green.

questions.q: In the ¹H NMR spectrum, an aldehyde proton appears at about
questions.explanation: The –CHO proton is strongly deshielded by the carbonyl group.

questions.q: Which infrared absorption indicates a carbonyl group?
questions.explanation: The C=O stretch gives a strong, sharp peak around 1700 cm⁻¹.

questions.q: Why is ethanoic acid soluble in water?

options.B: The COOH group forms hydrogen bonds with water
options.D: It has a long hydrocarbon chain

questions.explanation: Both the C=O and O–H can hydrogen bond. Solubility falls as the chain lengthens.

questions.q: Which reaction confirms the presence of a carboxylic acid rather than a phenol?
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids are strong enough to release CO₂ from carbonates; phenols are not.

questions.q: What are the products when ethanoic acid reacts with magnesium?
questions.explanation: 2CH₃COOH + Mg → (CH₃COO)₂Mg + H₂, a typical acid–metal reaction.

questions.q: Which conditions are used for esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol?

options.A: Heat with a concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst

questions.explanation: The acid-catalysed reaction is reversible and slow, so heating under reflux with H₂SO₄ is used.

questions.q: What is the name of the ester CH₃CH₂COOCH₃?
questions.explanation: The alkyl group (methyl) from the alcohol comes first; the acid part (propanoate) has three carbons.

questions.q: Which reagent converts a carboxylic acid into an acyl chloride?
questions.explanation: RCOOH + SOCl₂ → RCOCl + SO₂ + HCl.

questions.q: What are the products of the acid hydrolysis of methyl ethanoate?
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis reverses esterification, splitting the ester at the C–O bond to give the parent acid and alcohol.

questions.q: What are the products of the alkaline hydrolysis of ethyl propanoate with NaOH?
questions.explanation: Alkaline hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt and the alcohol, and goes to completion.

questions.q: Which product forms when an acid anhydride reacts with an alcohol?

options.A: An ester and a carboxylic acid

questions.explanation: (RCO)₂O + R'OH → RCOOR' + RCOOH.

questions.q: Which is the product of the reaction between propanoyl chloride and water?
questions.explanation: Acyl chlorides hydrolyse vigorously: RCOCl + H₂O → RCOOH + HCl.

questions.q: Which product forms when ethanoyl chloride reacts with phenol?
questions.explanation: Phenols do not esterify with carboxylic acids directly, but acyl chlorides are reactive enough to form the phenyl ester.

questions.q: Which compound is produced when ethanoyl chloride reacts with ammonia?
questions.explanation: CH₃COCl + 2NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ + NH₄Cl: a primary amide.

questions.q: Which is a primary amine?
questions.explanation: A primary amine has one carbon group attached to the nitrogen.

questions.q: Which compound is a secondary amine?
questions.explanation: Two alkyl groups on the nitrogen.

questions.q: Why are amines basic?

options.B: The lone pair on the nitrogen can accept a proton

questions.explanation: Amines are Brønsted–Lowry bases because the nitrogen lone pair forms a bond to H⁺.

questions.q: What is the product when methylamine reacts with hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: CH₃NH₂ + HCl → CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻, an ionic salt.

questions.q: How is ethylamine prepared from bromoethane?

options.A: Heat with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure

questions.explanation: Nucleophilic substitution: CH₃CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br. Excess ammonia limits further substitution.

questions.q: How is phenylamine prepared from nitrobenzene?

options.A: Reduction with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid, then NaOH

questions.explanation: Sn/conc. HCl reduces the NO₂ group to NH₂; NaOH liberates the free amine from its salt.

questions.q: Which is the strongest base?
questions.explanation: The alkyl group increases the electron density on nitrogen. In phenylamine the lone pair is delocalised into the ring, reducing basicity.

questions.q: What is produced when an amine reacts with an acyl chloride?
questions.explanation: RNH₂ + R'COCl → R'CONHR + HCl.

questions.q: Which product forms when phenylamine reacts with bromine water?
questions.explanation: Like phenol, the NH₂ group activates the ring and multiple substitution occurs.

questions.q: Why are quaternary ammonium salts useful?

options.B: Those with long hydrocarbon chains are cationic surfactants used in fabric conditioners and hair products

questions.explanation: The positive head is attracted to negatively charged surfaces, reducing static.

questions.q: What happens to the basic strength when alkyl groups replace the hydrogens on ammonia?

options.B: It increases because the positive inductive effect pushes electrons onto nitrogen

questions.explanation: More electron density on the nitrogen lone pair makes it a better proton acceptor.

questions.q: What is the general formula of an α-amino acid?
questions.explanation: The NH₂ and COOH groups are on the same (α) carbon.

questions.q: What is formed when an amino acid reacts with aqueous NaOH?
questions.explanation: The acid group is neutralised by the base.

questions.q: What is formed when an amino acid reacts with HCl?
questions.explanation: The basic amine group is protonated to form the ammonium chloride salt.

questions.q: Which reaction forms an ester from an amino acid?

options.A: Reaction with an alcohol and acid catalyst

questions.explanation: The COOH group undergoes esterification like any carboxylic acid.

questions.q: What is a chiral centre?

options.A: A carbon atom with four different groups attached
options.D: A carbon with two identical groups

questions.explanation: A carbon with four different groups has no plane of symmetry, giving two non-superimposable mirror images.

questions.q: Which amino acid is not chiral?
questions.explanation: Glycine (R = H) has two hydrogens on the α-carbon.

questions.q: Which is a primary amide?
questions.explanation: A primary amide has NH₂ attached directly to the carbonyl.

questions.q: Which is a secondary amide?
questions.explanation: One alkyl group on the amide nitrogen: N-methylethanamide.

questions.q: Optical isomers

options.A: rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions

questions.explanation: Enantiomers have identical physical properties except their effect on plane-polarised light.

questions.q: Which type of isomerism is shown by 2-aminopropanoic acid (alanine)?
questions.explanation: The α-carbon has H, CH₃, NH₂ and COOH, four different groups.

questions.q: Which best describes a peptide link?

options.B: A secondary amide link –CONH– formed between amino acids

questions.explanation: The COOH of one amino acid condenses with the NH₂ of another.

questions.q: Which type of polymer is formed from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid?
questions.explanation: Ester links form between each OH and COOH, with water lost.

questions.q: Which monomers form nylon-6,6?
questions.explanation: A polyamide: amide links between the diamine and diacid.

questions.q: What small molecule is lost in condensation polymerisation using a dioyl dichloride?
questions.explanation: Acyl chlorides react with alcohols or amines losing HCl.

questions.q: What is the repeat unit of the polyester made from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (Terylene)?
questions.explanation: The repeat unit contains one of each monomer joined by ester links.

questions.q: Which polymer can be hydrolysed back to its monomers?
questions.explanation: The polar ester links are attacked by acid or alkali; addition polymers have only C–C bonds.

questions.q: What are the products of the alkaline hydrolysis of a polyester?

options.A: A diol and the dicarboxylate salt
options.B: A diol and the dicarboxylic acid

questions.explanation: Hot NaOH breaks the ester links, giving the alcohol and the sodium salt of the acid.

questions.q: What are the products of acid hydrolysis of a polyamide?

options.A: A diamine and a dicarboxylic acid
options.C: The diammonium salt and the dicarboxylic acid

questions.explanation: Acid hydrolysis protonates the amine groups, giving the dicarboxylic acid and the diammonium salt.

questions.q: Which polymer is Kevlar?
questions.explanation: Made from benzene-1,4-diamine and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, with hydrogen bonds between chains giving great strength.

questions.q: Which intermolecular force exists between polyamide chains?

options.A: Hydrogen bonding between N–H and C=O

questions.explanation: The N–H···O=C hydrogen bonds give polyamides strength and high melting points.

questions.q: Which statement compares addition and condensation polymerisation correctly?

options.B: Addition polymerisation forms only the polymer; condensation also forms a small molecule such as water or HCl

questions.explanation: In addition polymerisation the monomer's C=C opens and nothing is lost.

questions.q: Which reaction increases the length of a carbon chain?

options.B: Reaction of a haloalkane with KCN in ethanol

questions.explanation: Nucleophilic substitution adds the CN group, giving a nitrile with one extra carbon.

questions.q: What is the product when bromoethane reacts with KCN in ethanol?
questions.explanation: CH₃CH₂Br + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CN + Br⁻: three carbons.

questions.q: Which reagent reduces a nitrile to an amine?

options.B: H₂ with a nickel catalyst (or LiAlH₄)

questions.explanation: R–CN + 2H₂ → R–CH₂NH₂.

questions.q: What is produced when a nitrile is hydrolysed with dilute acid?

options.A: A carboxylic acid and ammonium ions

questions.explanation: RCN + 2H₂O + H⁺ → RCOOH + NH₄⁺.

questions.q: Which reaction forms a hydroxynitrile?

options.A: Carbonyl compound with HCN (or KCN then acid)

questions.explanation: Nucleophilic addition of CN⁻ to C=O gives a hydroxynitrile, lengthening the chain.

questions.q: Which reaction forms a C–C bond to a benzene ring?
questions.explanation: Friedel–Crafts reactions attach an alkyl or acyl group via an AlCl₃ catalyst.

questions.q: What is the electrophile in the Friedel–Crafts acylation with CH₃COCl/AlCl₃?
questions.explanation: The acylium ion, formed when AlCl₃ removes Cl⁻ from the acyl chloride.

questions.q: What is the product of the Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene with propanoyl chloride?
questions.explanation: The acyl group COCH₂CH₃ is attached to the ring: C₆H₅COCH₂CH₃.

questions.q: Which sequence converts ethanal to 2-hydroxypropanoic acid?

options.A: HCN addition then acid hydrolysis of the nitrile

questions.explanation: Ethanal + HCN → CH₃CH(OH)CN; hydrolysis gives CH₃CH(OH)COOH.

questions.q: Why is Friedel–Crafts acylation often preferred to alkylation?

options.B: The product ketone is less reactive than the starting benzene, so multiple substitution is avoided

questions.explanation: Alkyl groups activate the ring, leading to polyalkylation; the acyl group deactivates it.

questions.q: Which practical technique is used to purify an organic solid?
questions.explanation: The impure solid is dissolved in the minimum of hot solvent, filtered hot, cooled to crystallise, filtered and dried.

questions.q: Why is the minimum volume of hot solvent used in recrystallisation?

options.B: To give a saturated solution so the maximum yield of crystals forms on cooling

questions.explanation: Too much solvent means the product stays dissolved on cooling, lowering the yield.

questions.q: How is the purity of a recrystallised solid checked?

options.B: By measuring its melting point: a pure compound melts sharply at the literature value

questions.explanation: Impurities lower the melting point and widen the melting range.

questions.q: What is filtration under reduced pressure used for?

options.B: Rapidly separating a solid product from a solvent using a Buchner funnel

questions.explanation: The vacuum pulls the solvent through quickly and helps dry the crystals.

questions.q: Which reagent converts a primary alcohol into an aldehyde?
questions.explanation: Distilling off the aldehyde prevents further oxidation to the carboxylic acid.

questions.q: Which sequence converts benzene to phenylamine?

options.A: Nitration (conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄) then reduction (Sn/conc. HCl, then NaOH)

questions.explanation: Benzene → nitrobenzene → phenylamine is the standard two-step route.

questions.q: Which sequence converts propene into propanoic acid?

options.A: Hydration to propan-1-ol, then oxidation under reflux

questions.explanation: Note: steam hydration of propene mainly gives propan-2-ol, so the route via the primary alcohol needs an anti-Markownikoff step; in exam terms the alcohol then acid route is the expected answer. Oxidising propan-1-ol under reflux with acidified dichromate gives propanoic acid.

questions.q: Which functional group test uses 2,4-DNP?
questions.explanation: An orange precipitate forms with carbonyl compounds.

questions.q: Which test identifies a carboxylic acid?
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids release CO₂ from carbonates.

questions.q: Which test identifies a primary or secondary alcohol?

options.A: Orange to green with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) on warming

questions.explanation: Primary and secondary alcohols are oxidised; tertiary alcohols give no colour change.

questions.q: Which test identifies an alkene?

options.A: Bromine water turns from orange to colourless

questions.explanation: Electrophilic addition of bromine across the C=C removes the colour.

questions.q: In a multi-step synthesis each of three steps has a 70% yield. What is the overall yield?
In thin-layer chromatography, the stationary phase is

options.B: a thin layer of silica or alumina on a plate

questions.explanation: The mobile phase is the solvent moving up the plate.

questions.q: Rf is defined as

options.A: distance moved by the solvent front ÷ distance moved by the spot
options.B: distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front
options.C: the time taken for the spot to move

questions.explanation: Rf is a ratio with no units, always between 0 and 1.

questions.q: Separation in TLC depends on

options.B: the relative adsorption of components to the stationary phase and their solubility in the mobile phase

questions.explanation: Strongly adsorbed components move less far.

questions.q: In gas chromatography, the mobile phase is
questions.explanation: Nitrogen or helium carries the vaporised sample through the column.

questions.q: What is retention time in gas chromatography?

options.A: The time the sample is heated
options.B: The time for a component to travel through the column to the detector
options.D: The time for the column to cool

questions.explanation: Retention time depends on the component's volatility and interaction with the stationary phase, and is used for identification.

questions.q: How can the concentration of a component be found from a gas chromatogram?

options.B: From the peak area, compared with a calibration curve from standards of known concentration

questions.explanation: Peak area is proportional to the amount present.

questions.q: Why is GC often combined with MS?

options.A: GC separates the components; MS identifies each from its mass spectrum

questions.explanation: GC–MS is used in forensics, environmental analysis and drug testing.

questions.q: Which test distinguishes a primary alcohol from a tertiary alcohol?

options.A: Warm with acidified potassium dichromate(VI): orange to green for primary, no change for tertiary

questions.explanation: Tertiary alcohols cannot be oxidised.

questions.q: Which test identifies a phenol?

options.B: No reaction with Na₂CO₃ but reacts with NaOH, and decolourises bromine water forming a white precipitate

questions.explanation: Phenol is too weak an acid to react with carbonate but is activated towards bromine.

questions.q: What is observed when a haloalkane is warmed with aqueous silver nitrate?

options.A: A precipitate of the silver halide forms as the haloalkane hydrolyses

questions.explanation: The halide ion released reacts with Ag⁺: white (Cl), cream (Br) or yellow (I).

questions.q: Which component in a mixture will have the shortest retention time in GC?

options.A: The one with the strongest attraction to the stationary phase
options.B: The most volatile component with the weakest interaction with the stationary phase

questions.explanation: Volatile components spend more time in the mobile phase and emerge first.

questions.q: What is the reference standard in NMR spectroscopy?
questions.explanation: TMS gives a single sharp peak, is inert and volatile, and its 12 equivalent protons give a strong signal.

questions.q: Why are deuterated solvents such as CDCl₃ used in ¹H NMR?

options.B: Deuterium does not produce a signal in the ¹H spectrum, so the solvent peak does not interfere

questions.explanation: ²H resonates at a different frequency from ¹H.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of ethanol?
questions.explanation: Two carbon environments: CH₃ and CH₂OH.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of propanone?
questions.explanation: The two CH₃ carbons are equivalent (one peak) and the C=O carbon gives the other.

questions.q: A ¹³C peak at δ 160 to 185 indicates

options.B: a C=O in an ester or carboxylic acid

questions.explanation: Ester and acid carbonyl carbons appear at δ 160 to 185; aldehyde and ketone C=O at δ 190 to 220.

questions.q: In ¹H NMR, what determines the number of peaks?

options.B: The number of different proton environments

questions.explanation: Equivalent protons give one signal.

questions.q: In ¹H NMR, the splitting of a peak is given by

options.A: the number of protons in that environment
options.B: the n + 1 rule, where n is the number of protons on adjacent carbon atoms

questions.explanation: Two neighbouring protons give a triplet, three give a quartet.

questions.q: How many peaks, and with what splitting, are in the ¹H NMR spectrum of chloroethane?
questions.explanation: CH₃ is split by two CH₂ protons (triplet); CH₂ is split by three CH₃ protons (quartet).

questions.q: What is the ratio of peak areas in the ¹H NMR spectrum of ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: Three environments: CH₃CO (3H singlet), OCH₂ (2H quartet), CH₂CH₃ (3H triplet).

questions.q: How can an O–H or N–H proton be identified in a ¹H NMR spectrum?

options.B: Shaking with D₂O makes the peak disappear because the proton exchanges with deuterium

questions.explanation: Labile protons exchange with D₂O and deuterium is not seen in the proton spectrum.

questions.q: Which combination of techniques would fully determine the structure of an unknown organic compound?

options.A: Mass spectrometry, IR spectroscopy and NMR spectroscopy together

questions.explanation: MS gives molecular mass and fragments, IR gives functional groups, NMR gives the carbon–hydrogen framework.

questions.q: In a mass spectrum, a peak at m/z = 45 could be due to
questions.explanation: COOH⁺ is 12 + 32 + 1 = 45; C₂H₅O⁺ is 24 + 5 + 16 = 45. CH₃⁺ is 15, C₂H₅⁺ is 29.

questions.q: What is the potential of the standard hydrogen electrode?
questions.explanation: It is the reference, defined as zero.

questions.q: Which set of conditions is correct for a standard hydrogen electrode?

options.A: H₂ at 100 kPa, 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺, 298 K, platinum electrode
options.B: H₂ at 200 kPa, 2 mol dm⁻³ H⁺, 273 K
options.C: O₂ at 100 kPa, 1 mol dm⁻³ OH⁻
options.D: H₂ at 1 kPa, 0.1 mol dm⁻³ H⁺

questions.explanation: Standard conditions with an inert platinum electrode.

questions.q: Why is platinum used as the electrode in the standard hydrogen electrode?

options.B: It is inert and conducts electricity

questions.explanation: Platinum provides a surface for the reaction without taking part.

questions.q: What is the function of the salt bridge?

options.B: To allow ions to move between half-cells and complete the circuit

questions.explanation: It maintains electrical neutrality in each half-cell.

questions.q: E°(Mg²⁺/Mg) = −2.37 V and E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V. What is E°cell?
In the Mg/Cu cell, which is the negative electrode?

options.B: Magnesium, because it has the more negative E° and is oxidised

questions.explanation: Electrons flow from the more negative half-cell.

questions.q: E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V and E°(I₂/I⁻) = +0.54 V. Which reaction is feasible?
questions.explanation: The more positive couple (Fe³⁺) is reduced; I⁻ is oxidised. E°cell = +0.23 V.

questions.q: Which is the strongest oxidising agent? E°: F₂/F⁻ +2.87; Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36; Br₂/Br⁻ +1.09; I₂/I⁻ +0.54 V.
questions.explanation: The most positive E° is the most readily reduced species.

questions.q: Which is the strongest reducing agent? E°: Li⁺/Li −3.04; Na⁺/Na −2.71; Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76; Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V.
questions.explanation: The most negative E° gives up electrons most readily.

questions.q: Why might a reaction with positive E°cell not take place?

options.B: The activation energy is high or conditions are non-standard

questions.explanation: E° predicts thermodynamic feasibility only.

questions.q: How does increasing [Cu²⁺] affect the electrode potential of the Cu²⁺/Cu half-cell?
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu shifts right, increasing the tendency to gain electrons.

questions.q: Which statement relates E°cell to ΔS total?

options.A: Positive E°cell means negative ΔS total
options.B: Positive E°cell means positive ΔS total and K > 1
options.C: E°cell is unrelated to ΔS total

questions.explanation: Both indicate a thermodynamically feasible reaction.

questions.q: What is the overall reaction in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is oxidised and oxygen reduced; only water is produced.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of a hydrogen fuel cell over a petrol engine?

options.B: The only product is water, so no CO₂ is released at the point of use
options.C: No energy is needed to make hydrogen
options.D: It does not need a catalyst

questions.explanation: Fuel cells are clean at the point of use, though hydrogen production may release CO₂.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of hydrogen fuel cells?

options.B: Hydrogen is difficult to store and transport, and is often made using fossil fuels
options.D: They cannot be used in vehicles

questions.explanation: Storage of a flammable gas and the energy source for producing hydrogen are the main issues.

questions.q: Why is sulfuric acid used to acidify manganate(VII) titrations?

options.A: It is a strong oxidising agent
options.B: It does not react with MnO₄⁻, unlike HCl which would be oxidised to Cl₂

questions.explanation: Chloride ions would be oxidised by MnO₄⁻, giving a false titre.

questions.q: Why can a potassium manganate(VII) titration be carried out without an added indicator?

options.B: The purple MnO₄⁻ is decolourised until excess gives a permanent pink colour
options.D: The end point is at pH 7

questions.explanation: Self-indicating: the first drop of excess MnO₄⁻ remains pink.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of Fe²⁺ solution required 20.0 cm³ of 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄. What is [Fe²⁺]?
What is the mole ratio of thiosulfate to iodine in an iodine–thiosulfate titration?
questions.explanation: 2S₂O₃²⁻ + I₂ → S₄O₆²⁻ + 2I⁻.

questions.q: What colour change marks the end point of an iodine–thiosulfate titration with starch?
questions.explanation: Starch–iodine complex disappears as the last iodine is reduced.

questions.q: Why is starch added near the end point rather than at the start?

options.B: The starch–iodine complex forms slowly and a large amount would give an inaccurate end point

questions.explanation: Added early, the complex does not break down readily.

questions.q: Which half-equation shows the oxidation at the negative electrode of an alkaline hydrogen fuel cell?
questions.explanation: In alkaline conditions hydrogen reacts with hydroxide ions, releasing electrons.

questions.q: How many moles of thiosulfate react with the iodine produced from 1 mol of Cu²⁺ (2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → 2CuI + I₂)?
questions.explanation: 1 mol Cu²⁺ gives 0.5 mol I₂, which needs 1 mol S₂O₃²⁻.

questions.q: Which change makes a redox reaction more feasible?

options.B: Increasing the concentration of the species being reduced

questions.explanation: This makes the reduction electrode potential more positive, raising Ecell.

questions.q: Which element is not classified as a transition metal?
questions.explanation: Zn²⁺ has a full 3d¹⁰ subshell; transition metals must form an ion with a partially filled d subshell.

questions.q: What is the electron configuration of Cu⁺?
questions.explanation: Copper [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ loses its 4s electron.

questions.q: Why are copper(I) compounds colourless?

options.B: The 3d subshell is full, so no d–d electron transitions are possible

questions.explanation: Colour needs a partially filled d subshell.

questions.q: How is a coordinate (dative) bond formed in a complex ion?

options.B: The ligand donates a lone pair of electrons to the metal ion

questions.explanation: Ligands are electron pair donors.

questions.q: What is the coordination number of [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺?
questions.explanation: Six coordinate bonds from six water ligands.

questions.q: What is the shape of [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺?
questions.explanation: Two ligands give a linear complex.

questions.q: Which ligand is bidentate?
questions.explanation: Ethanedioate has two oxygen atoms that each donate a lone pair.

questions.q: How many coordinate bonds does EDTA⁴⁻ form?
questions.explanation: EDTA is hexadentate: two N and four O donor atoms.

questions.q: Why are transition metal complexes coloured?

options.B: Ligands split the d orbitals; electrons absorb visible light to move between the levels and the complementary colour is seen

questions.explanation: d–d transitions absorb light of energy ΔE = hν.

questions.q: Which factor does not affect the colour of a complex?
questions.explanation: Colour depends on the d-orbital splitting, set by oxidation state, ligands and geometry.

questions.q: What is the colour change when excess ammonia is added to copper(II) sulfate solution?

options.B: Pale blue to deep blue, via a pale blue precipitate

questions.explanation: Cu(OH)₂ precipitate dissolves forming [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺.

questions.q: Which equation shows the ligand exchange of [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ with concentrated hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Larger Cl⁻ ligands give a tetrahedral four-coordinate yellow complex.

questions.q: Why does the coordination number change when Cl⁻ replaces H₂O around Cu²⁺?

options.B: Chloride ions are larger, so only four fit around the metal ion

questions.explanation: Steric reasons: the bulky chloride ligands limit the number that can bond.

questions.q: Why is the replacement of six water ligands by one EDTA⁴⁻ favourable?

options.B: The number of particles increases from 2 to 7, so ΔS system is large and positive

questions.explanation: The chelate effect is entropy driven.

questions.q: What is observed when sodium hydroxide is added to iron(III) sulfate solution?
questions.explanation: Fe(OH)₃ is orange-brown and insoluble in excess NaOH.

questions.q: What is observed when excess sodium hydroxide is added to chromium(III) sulfate solution?

options.B: Grey-green precipitate that dissolves to give a green solution

questions.explanation: Cr(OH)₃ is amphoteric and dissolves to form [Cr(OH)₆]³⁻.

questions.q: Which colour is the vanadium(IV) ion VO²⁺?
questions.explanation: +5 yellow, +4 blue, +3 green, +2 violet.

questions.q: Which reagent reduces vanadium(V) to vanadium(II)?
questions.explanation: Zinc is a strong enough reducing agent to take vanadium through all the lower states.

questions.q: What colour change is seen when hydrogen peroxide oxidises an alkaline chromium(III) solution?
questions.explanation: Cr³⁺ is oxidised to the yellow chromate(VI) ion CrO₄²⁻.

questions.q: What happens when acid is added to yellow chromate(VI) solution?
questions.explanation: 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O.

questions.q: Which catalyst is used in the Contact process and which oxidation states does it cycle between?
questions.explanation: V₂O₅ oxidises SO₂ (V +5 to +4) and is reoxidised by O₂.

questions.q: How does Fe²⁺ catalyse the reaction between S₂O₈²⁻ and I⁻?

options.B: It is oxidised to Fe³⁺ by S₂O₈²⁻, then Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻ and is regenerated
options.D: It forms a complex with iodine

questions.explanation: A homogeneous catalyst using variable oxidation states; two oppositely charged ions no longer need to collide.

questions.q: Why is the reaction between MnO₄⁻ and C₂O₄²⁻ slow at first, then speeds up?

options.B: Mn²⁺ product acts as an autocatalyst

questions.explanation: Autocatalysis: Mn²⁺ is oxidised to Mn³⁺ which then oxidises ethanedioate.

questions.q: Which complex is used as an anticancer drug?
questions.explanation: Cisplatin binds to DNA, preventing cell division.

questions.q: A reaction has the rate equation rate = k[A][B]². What is its overall order?
questions.explanation: Sum of the orders: 1 + 2 = 3.

questions.q: What are the units of the rate constant for a second-order reaction?
questions.explanation: k = rate/[A]² = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/(mol dm⁻³)².

questions.q: What are the units of the rate constant for a zero-order reaction?
questions.explanation: rate = k, so k has the units of rate.

questions.q: Doubling [X] has no effect on rate; doubling [Y] doubles the rate. What is the rate equation?
questions.explanation: X is zero order and Y is first order.

questions.q: Doubling [A] quadruples the rate. What is the order with respect to A?
questions.explanation: Rate ∝ [A]².

questions.q: Which graph is a straight line through the origin?

options.A: Rate against concentration for first order
options.B: Concentration against time for first order
options.C: Rate against concentration for zero order
options.D: Rate against concentration² for first order

questions.explanation: rate = k[A] gives a straight line through the origin.

questions.q: A reactant has a constant half-life. What is its order?
questions.explanation: Only first-order reactants have a half-life independent of concentration.

questions.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 100 s. What is k?
What is the rate-determining step?
questions.explanation: The slowest step controls the overall rate.

questions.q: For a reaction with rate = k[RBr], which mechanism is consistent?

options.B: SN1, with slow ionisation of RBr followed by fast attack by the nucleophile

questions.explanation: Only RBr appears in the rate equation, so the nucleophile reacts after the slow step.

questions.q: Which haloalkane is most likely to react by an SN2 mechanism?
questions.explanation: Primary haloalkanes are unhindered and do not form stable carbocations.

questions.q: In the iodination of propanone, rate = k[CH₃COCH₃][H⁺]. What does this tell you about iodine?

options.A: Iodine is in the rate-determining step
options.B: Iodine is zero order and reacts after the rate-determining step

questions.explanation: Changing [I₂] does not change the rate.

questions.q: In a clock reaction, how is the rate related to the time t?
questions.explanation: A fixed amount of product forms in time t, so the average rate is proportional to 1/t.

questions.q: Which form of the Arrhenius equation gives a straight line?
questions.explanation: ln k = ln A − Ea/RT, gradient −Ea/R.

questions.q: A plot of ln k against 1/T has gradient −6000 K. What is Ea? (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
questions.explanation: Ea = −gradient × R = 6000 × 8.31 = 49 860 J mol⁻¹ = 49.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: How does the rate constant change when temperature increases?
questions.explanation: k rises exponentially with T according to the Arrhenius equation.

questions.q: Which factor does not affect the rate constant k?
questions.explanation: k depends on temperature and Ea; concentration appears separately in the rate equation.

questions.q: Which method could follow the rate of the reaction between bromine and methanoic acid?

options.B: Colorimetry, as the orange bromine fades

questions.explanation: Bromine is the only coloured species.

questions.q: Why is a large excess of one reactant used when finding the order with respect to another?

options.B: Its concentration stays effectively constant so the other reactant's order can be found
options.C: To make the reaction zero order overall

questions.explanation: The excess reactant's concentration is absorbed into an apparent rate constant.

questions.q: What does a concentration–time graph with a straight line of negative gradient show?
questions.explanation: Constant rate regardless of concentration.

questions.q: Which species appear in the rate equation of a multi-step reaction?

options.B: Only those involved in the rate-determining step and steps before it

questions.explanation: Species that react after the slow step do not affect the rate.

questions.q: For the reaction 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, rate = k[NO]²[O₂]. What are the units of k?
questions.explanation: Third order overall.

questions.q: What is A in the Arrhenius equation?

options.B: The pre-exponential factor related to collision frequency and orientation

questions.explanation: A accounts for how often collisions with the right orientation occur.

questions.q: How does a catalyst affect the Arrhenius plot of ln k against 1/T?

options.B: Shallower gradient because Ea is lower

questions.explanation: Gradient = −Ea/R, so a lower Ea gives a less steep line.

questions.q: Which molecule contains a chiral centre?
questions.explanation: The second carbon has H, OH, CH₃ and C₂H₅: four different groups.

questions.q: Which statement describes a racemic mixture?

options.B: An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers that does not rotate plane-polarised light
options.C: A mixture of E and Z isomers
options.D: A compound with two chiral centres

questions.explanation: The optical rotations cancel.

questions.q: Why does the SN1 hydrolysis of a chiral haloalkane give a racemic mixture?

options.B: The planar carbocation can be attacked from either side

questions.explanation: Attack above or below the plane gives both enantiomers equally.

questions.q: Which reagent gives a positive result with an aldehyde but not with a ketone?
questions.explanation: Only aldehydes are oxidised, giving a silver mirror.

questions.q: What is observed when propanal is warmed with Fehling's solution?
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ is reduced to Cu₂O by the aldehyde.

questions.q: Which compound gives a positive iodoform test (yellow precipitate with I₂/NaOH)?
questions.explanation: Methyl ketones (CH₃CO–) give CHI₃.

questions.q: What is formed when 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine reacts with a ketone?
questions.explanation: The orange 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone can be purified and its melting point measured to identify the ketone.

questions.q: Which reagent reduces a ketone to a secondary alcohol?
questions.explanation: Lithium tetrahydridoaluminate supplies the H⁻ nucleophile.

questions.q: What type of mechanism is the reaction of HCN with propanone?
questions.explanation: CN⁻ attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon.

questions.q: What is the product of propanone with HCN?
questions.explanation: (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN.

questions.q: Which reagent converts a carboxylic acid to an acyl chloride?
questions.explanation: RCOOH + PCl₅ → RCOCl + POCl₃ + HCl.

questions.q: What is the product when ethanoic acid reacts with LiAlH₄?
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids are reduced to primary alcohols.

questions.q: Which test distinguishes a carboxylic acid from a phenol?

options.B: Sodium carbonate solution: the acid gives CO₂ bubbles

questions.explanation: Phenol is too weak an acid to release CO₂ from carbonate.

questions.q: What is the name of CH₃COOCH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The alcohol part (ethyl) first, then the acid part (ethanoate).

questions.q: Which conditions favour a high yield of ester from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol?

options.B: Heat with concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst and distil off the ester

questions.explanation: Removing the ester shifts the equilibrium right.

questions.q: What are the products of the alkaline hydrolysis of methyl propanoate?
questions.explanation: Alkaline hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt and alcohol, and goes to completion.

questions.q: What is produced when ethanoyl chloride reacts with water?
questions.explanation: Vigorous hydrolysis with steamy fumes of HCl.

questions.q: What is produced when ethanoyl chloride reacts with methylamine?
questions.explanation: CH₃COCl + CH₃NH₂ → CH₃CONHCH₃ + HCl.

questions.q: Why are acyl chlorides more reactive than carboxylic acids?

options.B: The carbonyl carbon is more δ+ because of two electronegative atoms, and Cl⁻ is a good leaving group

questions.explanation: Both O and Cl withdraw electrons.

questions.q: Why do carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than alcohols of similar Mr?
questions.explanation: Two hydrogen bonds link pairs of molecules.

questions.q: Which product forms when ethanoic anhydride reacts with ethanol?
questions.explanation: (CH₃CO)₂O + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + CH₃COOH.

questions.q: Why is KCN with a little acid used rather than pure HCN for addition to carbonyls?

options.B: HCN is a toxic gas and a weak acid; KCN gives a higher [CN⁻]

questions.explanation: The reaction needs cyanide ions; HCN alone dissociates very little.

questions.q: What is the product when ethanal is oxidised by acidified dichromate(VI)?
questions.explanation: Aldehydes are oxidised to carboxylic acids; orange to green.

questions.q: Which is a use of esters?
questions.explanation: Esters are volatile with pleasant smells and are good solvents.

questions.q: Which evidence contradicts the Kekulé structure of benzene?

options.B: All C–C bonds are the same length

questions.explanation: Kekulé's structure would have alternating long and short bonds.

questions.q: How does the enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene compare with three times that of cyclohexene?
questions.explanation: The difference is the delocalisation (resonance) energy that stabilises benzene.

questions.q: Which electrophile is involved in the nitration of benzene?
questions.explanation: Generated from concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids.

questions.q: Which conditions are used for the nitration of benzene?

options.B: Concentrated HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 50 °C

questions.explanation: Higher temperatures give dinitration.

questions.q: What is the role of FeBr₃ in the bromination of benzene?

options.B: Halogen carrier that generates the Br⁺ electrophile

questions.explanation: Br₂ + FeBr₃ → Br⁺ + FeBr₄⁻.

questions.q: What type of mechanism does benzene undergo with electrophiles?
questions.explanation: Substitution preserves the stable delocalised ring.

questions.q: What is the product of the Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene with ethanoyl chloride?
questions.explanation: C₆H₅COCH₃, with AlCl₃ catalyst.

questions.q: Why does phenol react with bromine water while benzene does not?

options.B: The oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring, increasing electron density and activating it

questions.explanation: Phenol gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol and decolourises bromine water without a catalyst.

questions.q: Which statement about phenol is correct?

options.A: It reacts with sodium carbonate releasing CO₂
options.B: It reacts with NaOH to form sodium phenoxide but not with carbonates
options.C: It is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid

questions.explanation: Phenol is a very weak acid.

questions.q: How is phenylamine made from nitrobenzene?

options.B: Reduction with tin and concentrated HCl, then NaOH

questions.explanation: Sn/HCl reduces NO₂ to NH₂; NaOH liberates the free amine.

questions.q: Place these in order: which is the strongest base, ethylamine, ammonia, phenylamine or ethanamide?
questions.explanation: Alkyl groups increase electron density on N; in phenylamine the lone pair is delocalised into the ring.

questions.q: Explain why phenylamine is less basic than ammonia.

options.B: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available

questions.explanation: Reduced electron density on the nitrogen.

questions.q: What is produced when ethylamine reacts with ethanoyl chloride?
questions.explanation: Amines react with acyl chlorides to form N-substituted amides.

questions.q: What is observed when excess butylamine is added to copper(II) sulfate solution?

options.B: Pale blue precipitate that dissolves to form a deep blue solution

questions.explanation: Amines act as ligands like ammonia.

questions.q: What reagent is used to make a Grignard reagent from bromoethane?
questions.explanation: Water must be excluded because it destroys the Grignard reagent.

questions.q: What is formed when a Grignard reagent reacts with carbon dioxide followed by dilute acid?
questions.explanation: RMgBr + CO₂ then H⁺ → RCOOH, adding one carbon.

questions.q: What is formed when CH₃MgBr reacts with propanone followed by dilute acid?
questions.explanation: Grignard + ketone gives a tertiary alcohol: (CH₃)₃COH.

questions.q: Which monomers form a polyamide?

options.A: A diol and a dicarboxylic acid
options.B: A diamine and a dicarboxylic acid
options.D: An amino acid and an alcohol

questions.explanation: Amide links form with loss of water, e.g. nylon-6,6.

questions.q: Which small molecule is released when a polyester forms from a diol and a dioyl dichloride?
questions.explanation: Acyl chlorides react with OH groups releasing HCl.

questions.q: How do amino acids exist in neutral aqueous solution?
questions.explanation: The acidic COOH protonates the basic NH₂ within the molecule.

questions.q: What is formed when an amino acid reacts with hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: The basic NH₂ group accepts a proton.

questions.q: What is a peptide link?

options.B: A secondary amide group –CONH– joining amino acids

questions.explanation: Formed by condensation between COOH and NH₂.

questions.q: Which reagent is used to locate amino acid spots on a chromatogram?
questions.explanation: Ninhydrin gives purple spots; amino acids are otherwise colourless.

questions.q: Which reaction decreases the carbon chain length?

options.C: The iodoform reaction of a methyl ketone

questions.explanation: The CH₃ group is removed as CHI₃, leaving a carboxylate with one fewer carbon.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of butanone?
questions.explanation: CH₃, C=O, CH₂ and CH₃ are all different environments.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of 2-methylpropane?
questions.explanation: Three equivalent CH₃ carbons and one CH.

questions.q: A ¹³C peak at δ 205 suggests

options.C: a ketone or aldehyde carbonyl carbon

questions.explanation: Ketone and aldehyde C=O appear at δ 190 to 220.

questions.q: How many proton environments does ethanol have in its ¹H NMR spectrum?
questions.explanation: CH₃, CH₂ and OH are three environments.

questions.q: What does the integration (area) of a ¹H NMR peak show?

options.B: The relative number of protons in that environment

questions.explanation: Peak areas are proportional to the numbers of equivalent protons.

questions.q: A ¹H NMR peak is split into a triplet. How many protons are on the adjacent carbon(s)?
questions.explanation: n + 1 rule: a triplet means n = 2.

questions.q: What splitting pattern does the CH₃ group in chloroethane show?
questions.explanation: It has two neighbouring protons on the CH₂.

questions.q: Which compound shows a single peak in its ¹H NMR spectrum?
questions.explanation: Both CH₃ groups in propanone are equivalent and have no neighbouring protons.

questions.q: Why is TMS used as the standard in NMR?

options.B: It gives a single sharp peak at δ 0, is inert and volatile

questions.explanation: Its 12 equivalent protons give one strong reference signal.

questions.q: Why is CDCl₃ used as a solvent in ¹H NMR?

options.B: Deuterium gives no signal in the ¹H spectrum

questions.explanation: Deuterated solvents do not interfere with the proton spectrum.

questions.q: What happens to an O–H peak when D₂O is added?
questions.explanation: The O–H proton exchanges with deuterium.

questions.q: In the ¹H NMR spectrum of ethyl ethanoate, what is the ratio of the peak areas?
questions.explanation: CH₃CO (3H), OCH₂ (2H), CH₃ (3H).

questions.q: What chemical shift is typical for an aldehyde proton?
questions.explanation: Strongly deshielded by the carbonyl.

questions.q: A compound C₂H₄O₂ shows ¹H NMR singlets at δ 2.1 (3H) and δ 11.5 (1H). What is it?
questions.explanation: CH₃ singlet and COOH singlet at very high shift.

questions.q: Which substance acts as the mobile phase in gas chromatography?

options.B: An inert carrier gas such as nitrogen or helium

questions.explanation: The sample is vaporised and carried through the column by the gas.

questions.q: What is the stationary phase in HPLC?

options.B: A fine solid packed in a column under high pressure

questions.explanation: High-performance liquid chromatography uses small particles, needing high pressure.

questions.q: What is retention time?

options.A: The time to prepare the sample
options.B: The time between injection and detection of a component
options.C: The time the column is heated

questions.explanation: Characteristic of a compound under fixed conditions.

questions.q: How is the amount of a component found from a chromatogram?

options.B: From the area under its peak compared with standards

questions.explanation: Peak area is proportional to the quantity present.

questions.q: Why is GC combined with MS?

options.A: GC separates the components and MS identifies each one
options.D: To avoid using a carrier gas

questions.explanation: GC–MS allows identification of unknowns in mixtures.

questions.q: Which component has the shortest retention time in GC?

options.B: The most volatile with weakest attraction to the stationary phase

questions.explanation: Volatile components spend more time in the gas phase and emerge first.

questions.q: Which combination identifies the structure of an unknown organic compound?
questions.explanation: Mr and fragments, functional groups, and the C–H framework.

questions.q: Which proton environment appears at δ 3.3 to 4.3?
questions.explanation: Protons on a carbon bonded to oxygen are deshielded to this region.

questions.q: Why do protons in different environments have different chemical shifts?

options.B: The surrounding electrons shield them to different extents from the applied field

questions.explanation: Electronegative groups withdraw electron density and shift peaks downfield.

questions.q: A ¹H NMR spectrum shows a doublet (6H) and a septet (1H). Which group is present?
questions.explanation: Two equivalent CH₃ (split by 1H into a doublet) and a CH split by 6H into a septet.

questions.q: An atom has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 17 electrons. What is its mass number?
questions.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 17 + 18 = 35.

questions.q: Which pair of species are isotopes?
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

questions.q: Which statement about isotopes of the same element is correct?

options.B: They have the same number of neutrons
options.C: They have the same electron configuration
options.D: They have the same mass number

questions.explanation: Isotopes have identical electron arrangements, so identical chemical properties; only neutron number (and mass) differs.

questions.q: Boron has isotopes ¹⁰B (19.9%) and ¹¹B (80.1%). What is its relative atomic mass?
In a time-of-flight mass spectrometer, which ions reach the detector first?

options.C: Those with the greatest charge density

questions.explanation: All ions are given the same kinetic energy, so lighter ions travel faster along the flight tube.

questions.q: Why are atoms ionised in a mass spectrometer?

options.B: So they can be accelerated by an electric field and detected

questions.explanation: Only charged particles can be accelerated and deflected by electric fields and generate a current at the detector.

questions.q: How many peaks appear in the mass spectrum of Br₂ (isotopes ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br, roughly equal abundance)?
questions.explanation: ⁷⁹Br⁷⁹Br (158), ⁷⁹Br⁸¹Br (160) and ⁸¹Br⁸¹Br (162), in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1.

questions.q: Which equation represents the first ionisation energy of sodium?
questions.explanation: First ionisation energy refers to one mole of gaseous atoms losing one mole of electrons.

questions.q: Which Period 3 element has the highest first ionisation energy?
questions.explanation: Argon has the greatest nuclear charge in Period 3 with electrons in the same shell, and a full, stable outer shell.

questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of boron lower than that of beryllium?

options.B: Boron's outer electron is in a 2p orbital, which is higher in energy and more shielded than the 2s

questions.explanation: The 2p electron is slightly further from the nucleus and shielded by the 2s electrons, so it is removed more easily.

questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of oxygen lower than that of nitrogen?

options.B: Oxygen's electron is removed from a paired 2p orbital where repulsion makes removal easier
options.C: Nitrogen has a full outer shell

questions.explanation: Nitrogen has three singly occupied 2p orbitals; in oxygen one 2p orbital holds a pair whose mutual repulsion lowers the energy needed.

questions.q: The successive ionisation energies of an element are (kJ mol⁻¹): 738, 1451, 7733, 10541. In which group is it?
questions.explanation: The large jump after the second electron shows two electrons in the outer shell.

questions.q: Which is the electron configuration of a chromium atom?
questions.explanation: Chromium has a half-filled 3d and 4s, which is more stable than 3d⁴ 4s².

questions.q: Which is the electron configuration of the Fe²⁺ ion?
questions.explanation: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². The 4s electrons are lost first.

questions.q: How many electrons can a p subshell hold?
questions.explanation: Three p orbitals, each holding two electrons.

questions.q: What is the shape of a p orbital?
questions.explanation: p orbitals are dumbbell shaped, aligned along the x, y and z axes.

questions.q: Which Period 3 element (Na to Ar) has the highest melting point?
questions.explanation: Silicon has a giant covalent structure with many strong covalent bonds.

questions.q: Why do the melting points of the Period 3 metals rise from sodium to aluminium?

options.B: The metallic bonding strengthens as the ions have a higher charge and more delocalised electrons

questions.explanation: Na⁺ with one electron, Mg²⁺ with two, Al³⁺ with three: stronger attraction in the metallic lattice.

questions.q: Why is the melting point of sulfur higher than that of phosphorus?

options.B: S₈ molecules are larger than P₄ so have stronger London forces

questions.explanation: Both are simple molecular; the larger S₈ molecule has more electrons so stronger London forces.

questions.q: Why does atomic radius decrease across Period 2?

options.B: Nuclear charge increases with the same shielding, pulling the electrons closer

questions.explanation: Electrons enter the same shell while the number of protons rises.

questions.q: To which block of the periodic table does calcium belong?
questions.explanation: Calcium's highest energy electrons are in the 4s subshell.

questions.q: Which species has the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶?
questions.explanation: Mg (12 electrons) loses two to give 10 electrons, the configuration of neon.

questions.q: What is the general trend in first ionisation energy down Group 1?
questions.explanation: More shells mean greater radius and shielding, outweighing the extra nuclear charge.

questions.q: Which statement explains why the Ar of chlorine is not a whole number?

options.A: Chlorine atoms contain fractions of protons
options.B: Chlorine is a mixture of isotopes with different masses

questions.explanation: The weighted mean of ³⁵Cl (about 75%) and ³⁷Cl (about 25%) is 35.5.

questions.q: Which compound has the highest melting point?
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are small and doubly charged, giving the strongest electrostatic attraction in the lattice.

questions.q: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten but not when solid?

options.B: The ions are free to move when molten but fixed in the solid lattice
options.C: The compound becomes covalent when molten

questions.explanation: Charge is carried by mobile ions, which can only move when the lattice has broken down.

questions.q: Which ion has the smallest ionic radius?
questions.explanation: All four have 10 electrons. Al³⁺ has the most protons (13), pulling the electrons closest.

questions.q: Which is a dative covalent bond?

options.B: The N–H bond formed when NH₃ accepts H⁺

questions.explanation: In NH₄⁺, both electrons in the new N–H bond come from the nitrogen lone pair.

questions.q: What is the shape of a BF₃ molecule?
questions.explanation: Three bonding pairs and no lone pairs on boron give 120° angles.

questions.q: What is the bond angle in methane?
questions.explanation: Four bonding pairs repel equally to give a tetrahedral shape.

questions.q: What is the shape of a sulfur hexafluoride molecule, SF₆?
questions.explanation: Six bonding pairs give an octahedral shape with 90° angles.

questions.q: Why is the bond angle in NH₃ smaller than in CH₄?

options.B: The lone pair on nitrogen repels more strongly than bonding pairs, squeezing them closer

questions.explanation: Lone pair–bond pair repulsion is greater than bond pair–bond pair repulsion.

questions.q: What is the shape of the H₂O molecule and its bond angle?
questions.explanation: Two bonding pairs and two lone pairs; each lone pair reduces the angle by about 2.5°.

questions.q: What is the shape of PCl₅?
questions.explanation: Five bonding pairs: three at 120° in a plane and two at 90° above and below.

questions.q: Which molecule is non-polar?
questions.explanation: CO₂ is linear and symmetrical, so the two C=O dipoles cancel.

questions.q: Which is the most electronegative element?
questions.explanation: Electronegativity increases across a period and up a group; fluorine is top right.

questions.q: Which molecule has the strongest London forces?
questions.explanation: More electrons and a larger surface area give stronger instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces.

questions.q: Why does pentane boil at a higher temperature than its isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane?

options.B: Its branched shape reduces the surface contact between molecules, weakening London forces

questions.explanation: Same molecular formula, but the compact branched molecule has fewer points of contact.

questions.q: Which compound can form hydrogen bonds with water?
questions.explanation: Methanol has an O–H group: a δ+ H and a lone pair on oxygen.

questions.q: Why is ice less dense than liquid water?

options.B: Hydrogen bonds hold the water molecules in an open lattice that is less dense than the liquid

questions.explanation: In ice each water molecule is hydrogen bonded to four others in an open tetrahedral arrangement.

questions.q: Why is the boiling point of HF higher than that of HCl?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding between HF molecules is much stronger than the London and dipole forces in HCl.

questions.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity?

options.B: Each carbon uses only three electrons in bonding; the fourth is delocalised and free to move

questions.explanation: The delocalised electrons between the layers carry the charge.

questions.q: Which statement explains why metals are malleable?

options.B: Layers of positive ions can slide over each other while the delocalised electrons maintain the bonding

questions.explanation: The non-directional attraction between ions and delocalised electrons is kept when layers slide.

questions.q: Which best describes the bonding in sodium chloride?

options.A: Shared electron pairs between Na and Cl
options.B: Electrostatic attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a lattice

questions.explanation: Ionic bonding: electrons transferred from sodium to chlorine.

questions.q: Which evidence supports the existence of ions in solids?

options.B: Electron density maps show spherical regions with no electron density between them

questions.explanation: Separate spheres with zero density between them show discrete ions rather than shared electrons.

questions.q: Why is iodine a solid but chlorine a gas at room temperature?

options.B: Iodine molecules have more electrons so stronger London forces

questions.explanation: The intermolecular forces, not the covalent bond strength, determine the state.

questions.q: Which has a permanent dipole?
questions.explanation: Trichloromethane is tetrahedral but with different groups, so the bond dipoles do not cancel.

questions.q: What is the bond angle in a trigonal bipyramidal molecule between the planar bonds?
questions.explanation: Three bonds lie in a plane at 120°; the two axial bonds are at 90° to this plane.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of manganese in the manganate(VII) ion, MnO₄⁻?
questions.explanation: Four oxygens = −8; the ion is −1, so Mn = +7.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in SO₃²⁻?
questions.explanation: Three oxygens = −6; overall −2, so S = +4.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of hydrogen in NaH?
questions.explanation: In metal hydrides hydrogen is the more electronegative element and is −1.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of oxygen in H₂O₂?
questions.explanation: In peroxides each oxygen is −1 so that the two hydrogens (+2) balance.

questions.q: In the reaction Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, which species is oxidised?
questions.explanation: Zinc goes from 0 to +2, losing electrons.

questions.q: Which is the oxidising agent in 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂?
questions.explanation: Fe³⁺ gains electrons (is reduced), so it oxidises the iodide.

questions.q: Which is a disproportionation reaction?
questions.explanation: Chlorine is both reduced (0 to −1) and oxidised (0 to +1).

questions.q: What is the name of NaClO₃?
questions.explanation: Three oxygens (−6) and sodium (+1) give chlorine +5.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of nitrogen in NO₃⁻?
questions.explanation: −6 from oxygen, overall −1, so N = +5.

questions.q: Which half-equation shows reduction?
questions.explanation: Reduction is gain of electrons.

questions.q: How many electrons are transferred in the half-equation Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O?
questions.explanation: Each Cr goes from +6 to +3 (gain of 3), and there are two Cr atoms.

questions.q: How many moles of Fe²⁺ are oxidised by one mole of MnO₄⁻ in acid?
questions.explanation: Mn goes from +7 to +2 (5 electrons); each Fe²⁺ supplies one electron.

questions.q: In the reaction 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O, what are the final oxidation numbers of chlorine?
questions.explanation: Chloride is −1; chlorate(V) is +5.

questions.q: Which species acts as a reducing agent when it reacts with chlorine?
questions.explanation: Bromide ions donate electrons to chlorine: 2Br⁻ + Cl₂ → Br₂ + 2Cl⁻.

questions.q: In 2H₂S + SO₂ → 3S + 2H₂O, what happens to sulfur in H₂S?
questions.explanation: Sulfur in H₂S goes from −2 to 0 (oxidation); sulfur in SO₂ goes from +4 to 0 (reduction).

questions.q: Which change is a reduction?
questions.explanation: The oxidation number falls from +2 to 0.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of carbon in CO₃²⁻?
questions.explanation: Three oxygens = −6; overall −2, so C = +4.

questions.q: Which element always has an oxidation number of −1 in compounds?
questions.explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and always −1 in compounds.

questions.q: In the reaction Mg + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂, which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: H⁺ gains electrons (reduced to H₂), so it is the oxidising agent.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of iron in Fe₂O₃?
questions.explanation: Three oxygens = −6, shared across two iron atoms gives +3 each.

questions.q: Which equation correctly balances the half-equation for the oxidation of water to oxygen?
questions.explanation: Oxygen goes from −2 to 0; two water molecules give four electrons.

questions.q: When chlorine is bubbled through water, which statement is correct?

options.B: Chlorine disproportionates to form HCl and HClO

questions.explanation: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO: chlorine goes to −1 and +1.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of vanadium in VO₂⁺?
questions.explanation: Two oxygens = −4; overall +1, so V = +5.

questions.q: In the equation Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O, what is the change in oxidation number of nitrogen?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen in HNO₃ is +5; in NO₂ it is +4. (Only two of the four nitrate groups are reduced.)

questions.q: Which Group 2 metal reacts most vigorously with water?
questions.explanation: Reactivity increases down the group as ionisation energies fall.

questions.q: What is produced when magnesium reacts with steam?
questions.explanation: Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂; with cold water the hydroxide forms very slowly.

questions.q: Which Group 2 hydroxide is the least soluble?
questions.explanation: Hydroxide solubility increases down the group.

questions.q: Which Group 2 sulfate is the least soluble?
questions.explanation: Sulfate solubility decreases down the group; BaSO₄ is used in the test for sulfate.

questions.q: Which Group 2 carbonate decomposes at the lowest temperature?
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ is the smallest cation with the highest charge density, so it polarises the carbonate ion most.

questions.q: What is observed when calcium nitrate is heated strongly?

options.A: A white solid and a colourless gas
options.B: Brown fumes and a gas that relights a glowing splint

questions.explanation: 2Ca(NO₃)₂ → 2CaO + 4NO₂ (brown) + O₂.

questions.q: Which flame colour is produced by barium compounds?
questions.explanation: Ba: apple green; Ca: brick red; Sr: crimson; K: lilac.

questions.q: Why do metal compounds give coloured flames?

options.B: Electrons are excited and emit light of a particular frequency as they fall back to lower energy levels

questions.explanation: The energy gap between levels corresponds to visible light of a specific colour.

questions.q: What is the trend in electronegativity down Group 7?
questions.explanation: Larger atoms with more shielding attract the bonding pair less strongly.

questions.q: Why does the boiling point of the halogens increase down the group?

options.B: More electrons give stronger London forces between molecules

questions.explanation: Intermolecular London forces increase with the number of electrons.

questions.q: What is observed when chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution?
questions.explanation: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂; iodine gives a brown solution.

questions.q: Why can bromine displace iodide but not chloride?

options.B: Bromine is a stronger oxidising agent than iodine but weaker than chlorine

questions.explanation: Oxidising ability decreases down Group 7.

questions.q: What is observed when concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid potassium iodide?

options.B: Purple vapour, a yellow solid and a gas smelling of bad eggs

questions.explanation: I⁻ is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce H₂SO₄ to SO₂, S and H₂S, forming I₂.

questions.q: Which halide ion is the strongest reducing agent?
questions.explanation: The large iodide ion loses its outer electron most easily.

questions.q: What is observed when concentrated sulfuric acid is added to sodium chloride?
questions.explanation: Chloride is not a strong enough reducing agent to reduce sulfuric acid, so only HCl forms.

questions.q: Which products form when chlorine reacts with cold dilute sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O (bleach).

questions.q: What is the colour of the precipitate formed when silver nitrate is added to a bromide solution?
questions.explanation: AgBr is cream and dissolves in concentrated but not dilute ammonia.

questions.q: Why is dilute nitric acid added before silver nitrate in the halide test?

options.B: To remove carbonate ions that would also give a precipitate

questions.explanation: Silver carbonate is also insoluble and would give a false positive.

questions.q: Which silver halide dissolves in dilute ammonia?
questions.explanation: AgCl is the most soluble of the three and dissolves in dilute ammonia.

questions.q: What is observed when hydrogen chloride gas meets ammonia gas?
questions.explanation: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl, a white solid formed as fine particles.

questions.q: What is observed in the test for sulfate ions?

options.A: White precipitate with acidified barium chloride

questions.explanation: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄, white and insoluble in acid.

questions.q: Which gas turns damp red litmus paper blue?
questions.explanation: Ammonia is alkaline; it is released when ammonium salts are warmed with NaOH.

questions.q: Why do Group 2 metals react more vigorously with acids down the group?

options.B: Their first and second ionisation energies decrease, so electrons are lost more easily

questions.explanation: Larger atoms with more shielding lose their outer electrons more easily.

questions.q: What is the trend in thermal stability of Group 1 and Group 2 nitrates?
questions.explanation: Larger cations polarise the nitrate ion less, so more heat is needed to decompose it.

questions.q: How many moles are in 11.0 g of carbon dioxide?
What is the mass of 0.20 mol of calcium carbonate?
What volume of hydrogen at RTP is produced when 0.10 mol of magnesium reacts with excess acid?
questions.explanation: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, 1 : 1, so 0.10 mol H₂ = 0.10 × 24 = 2.4 dm³.

questions.q: What is the concentration when 4.0 g of NaOH is dissolved to make 250 cm³ of solution?
A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon by mass. What is its empirical formula?
A compound has empirical formula CH₂O and Mr = 60. What is its molecular formula?
questions.explanation: Empirical mass = 30; 60/30 = 2, so C₂H₄O₂.

questions.q: In the ideal gas equation pV = nRT, what unit must volume be in?
questions.explanation: SI units: Pa, m³, mol, K. 1 cm³ = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m³.

questions.q: What is the volume of 0.50 mol of gas at 100 kPa and 298 K? (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ Na₂CO₃ reacts with HCl. How many moles of HCl are needed?
questions.explanation: n(Na₂CO₃) = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol; Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl, so 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol HCl.

questions.q: What is the atom economy for making hydrogen in CH₄ + 2H₂O → CO₂ + 4H₂?
questions.explanation: Mr products: CO₂ 44 + 4H₂ 8 = 52. Desired product 8. 8/52 × 100 = 15.4%.

questions.q: Which type of reaction always has 100% atom economy?
questions.explanation: All the reactant atoms end up in the single product.

questions.q: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 5.0 g and produces 3.5 g. What is the percentage yield?
What is the percentage uncertainty in a titre of 20.00 cm³ read from a burette with ±0.05 cm³ per reading?
questions.explanation: Two readings: ±0.10 cm³ total. 0.10/20.00 × 100 = 0.50%.

questions.q: How can the percentage uncertainty of a mass measurement be reduced?

options.B: Use a larger mass on the same balance

questions.explanation: The absolute uncertainty is fixed, so a larger reading gives a smaller percentage.

questions.q: Which results are concordant?
questions.explanation: Concordant titres agree within 0.10 cm³.

questions.q: Why is the first (rough) titration excluded from the mean?

options.B: It is only used to find the approximate end point and is not accurate

questions.explanation: The rough titre is added quickly and overshoots; only accurate concordant titres are averaged.

questions.q: What is the first step in preparing a standard solution?

options.A: Fill the volumetric flask to the mark

questions.explanation: The solid is weighed, dissolved in a beaker, transferred with washings to a volumetric flask, then made up to the mark.

questions.q: A hydrated salt MgSO₄·xH₂O loses 51.2% of its mass on heating. What is x?
questions.explanation: Take 100 g: 48.8 g MgSO₄ = 0.407 mol; 51.2 g water = 2.84 mol; ratio 7.

questions.q: How many atoms are present in 0.10 mol of CO₂?
questions.explanation: 0.10 × 6.02 × 10²³ molecules × 3 atoms = 1.8 × 10²³.

questions.q: Which is the correct ionic equation for the reaction of silver nitrate with sodium chloride?
questions.explanation: Spectator ions Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are cancelled.

questions.q: In a reaction between 0.30 mol of Al and 0.30 mol of O₂ (4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃), which is the limiting reagent?
questions.explanation: 0.30 mol Al needs 0.225 mol O₂; O₂ is in excess, so Al is limiting.

questions.q: What mass of Al₂O₃ forms from 0.30 mol of Al in excess oxygen?
questions.explanation: 0.30 mol Al gives 0.15 mol Al₂O₃ (Mr 102): 15.3 g.

questions.q: Which quantity is the same for 1 dm³ of any ideal gas at the same temperature and pressure?
questions.explanation: Avogadro's law: equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules.

questions.q: Why is a standard solution made up in a volumetric flask rather than a beaker?

options.B: A volumetric flask has a precise graduation line, giving an accurate volume
options.C: A beaker would react with the solution

questions.explanation: Volumetric flasks are calibrated to one accurate volume.

questions.q: Which is the correct name for CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: Longest chain is four carbons (butane) with a methyl on carbon 2 (lowest number).

questions.q: Which pair are functional group isomers?
questions.explanation: Both are C₃H₆O but one is an aldehyde and the other a ketone.

questions.q: Which of these alkenes shows E/Z isomerism?
questions.explanation: Each carbon of the C=C in but-2-ene has two different groups (H and CH₃).

questions.q: Why can E/Z isomers not interconvert at room temperature?

options.A: The C–C σ bond is too strong
options.B: Rotation about the C=C would require breaking the π bond

questions.explanation: The π bond prevents rotation about the double bond.

questions.q: What type of reaction is the reaction of methane with chlorine in UV light?
questions.explanation: UV light causes homolytic fission of Cl₂; chlorine radicals substitute hydrogen atoms.

questions.q: Which is a termination step in the chlorination of methane?
questions.explanation: Two radicals combine to form a stable molecule, ending the chain.

questions.q: Which pollutant is formed from nitrogen and oxygen in a car engine?
questions.explanation: At the high temperature in the engine, N₂ and O₂ from the air react to form nitrogen oxides.

questions.q: What does a catalytic converter do to carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide?

options.B: Converts them to carbon dioxide and nitrogen

questions.explanation: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂ on a platinum/rhodium surface.

questions.q: What is the mechanism for the reaction of ethene with bromine?
questions.explanation: The electron-rich π bond attacks the electrophilic Br δ+.

questions.q: What is the major product when HBr reacts with propene?
questions.explanation: The secondary carbocation intermediate is more stable, so Br⁻ adds to the middle carbon.

questions.q: Why is a secondary carbocation more stable than a primary one?

options.B: Two alkyl groups push electrons towards the positive carbon, spreading the charge

questions.explanation: The positive inductive effect of alkyl groups stabilises the carbocation.

questions.q: What is observed when ethene is bubbled through bromine water?
questions.explanation: Electrophilic addition forms colourless 1,2-dibromoethane (actually 2-bromoethanol too).

questions.q: What is the product when ethene reacts with steam in the presence of phosphoric acid?
questions.explanation: Hydration: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH, 300 °C and 60 to 70 atm.

questions.q: What is formed when ethene reacts with cold, dilute, acidified potassium manganate(VII)?
questions.explanation: The purple solution is decolourised as the diol forms.

questions.q: What is the repeat unit of poly(chloroethene), PVC?
questions.explanation: The monomer CH₂=CHCl opens its double bond.

questions.q: Which method of disposing of waste polymers recovers the monomers?
questions.explanation: Cracking breaks the polymer into small molecules that can be used as feedstock.

questions.q: Why is incineration of PVC a problem?
questions.explanation: The chlorine in PVC forms hydrogen chloride, which must be removed by scrubbing.

questions.q: Which haloalkane hydrolyses fastest with aqueous silver nitrate?
questions.explanation: The C–I bond is the weakest, so it breaks most easily.

questions.q: What is the role of OH⁻ in the reaction of 1-bromopropane with aqueous KOH?
questions.explanation: OH⁻ donates a lone pair to the δ+ carbon, replacing Br⁻ to form propan-1-ol.

questions.q: Which conditions favour elimination over substitution for bromoethane with KOH?
questions.explanation: In ethanol the hydroxide acts as a base, removing H⁺ to form ethene.

questions.q: What is formed when bromoethane reacts with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure?
questions.explanation: Nucleophilic substitution by NH₃ gives the primary amine.
