questions.q: What is observed when a tertiary alcohol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
questions.explanation: Tertiary alcohols are not oxidised, so no colour change.

questions.q: What is the product when butan-2-ol is oxidised?
questions.explanation: Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones.

questions.q: Which reagent converts ethanol to chloroethane and gives white fumes?
questions.explanation: Phosphorus(V) chloride reacts with the OH group releasing HCl fumes.

questions.q: Which peak in a mass spectrum gives the relative molecular mass?

options.B: The peak at the highest m/z (ignoring M+1)

questions.explanation: The molecular ion peak M⁺ is at the highest m/z, apart from the small ¹³C isotope peak.

questions.q: What causes the M+1 peak in a mass spectrum?
questions.explanation: ¹³C has 1.1% natural abundance, so a small peak appears one unit above M.

questions.q: Which fragment ion has m/z 29?
questions.explanation: C₂H₅⁺: 24 + 5 = 29. (CHO⁺ is also 29.)

questions.q: A compound shows a molecular ion at m/z 58 and a large peak at m/z 43. What is it likely to be?
questions.explanation: Propanone (58) loses CH₃• to give CH₃CO⁺ at 43. Butane also gives 43 but the question points to the carbonyl.

questions.q: How many molecular ion peaks are seen for chloroethane?
questions.explanation: ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl give peaks at m/z 64 and 66 in a 3 : 1 ratio.

questions.q: What is the ratio of the M and M+2 peaks for a compound containing one bromine atom?
questions.explanation: ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br are almost equally abundant.

questions.q: Why does infrared radiation cause molecular vibrations?

options.B: Its frequency matches the natural vibration frequency of bonds

questions.explanation: Bonds absorb IR at their characteristic frequencies and vibrate with greater amplitude.

questions.q: A strong, sharp IR absorption at about 1700 cm⁻¹ is caused by which bond?
questions.explanation: The carbonyl stretch is at 1630 to 1820 cm⁻¹.

questions.q: Which absorption suggests an alcohol?
questions.explanation: The hydrogen-bonded O–H stretch in alcohols is broad at 3200 to 3550 cm⁻¹.

questions.q: Which combination of IR absorptions indicates a carboxylic acid?

options.A: C=O at 1700 and very broad O–H at 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹

questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids show both the carbonyl and a very broad acid O–H.

questions.q: What is the fingerprint region used for?

options.B: Identifying a compound by matching with a database spectrum

questions.explanation: The pattern below 1500 cm⁻¹ is unique to each compound.

questions.q: Which molecule does not absorb infrared radiation?
questions.explanation: N₂ has no dipole change during vibration, so it does not absorb IR. This is why it is not a greenhouse gas.

questions.q: Which use of IR spectroscopy is correct?
questions.explanation: Breathalysers measure IR absorption by ethanol's C–H bonds.

questions.q: How does IR spectroscopy explain the greenhouse effect?

options.B: Bonds in CO₂, CH₄ and H₂O absorb IR emitted by the Earth, trapping heat

questions.explanation: C=O, C–H and O–H bonds absorb infrared radiation.

questions.q: Which peaks would distinguish propan-1-ol from propanal?

options.B: Propanal has a C=O peak at about 1700 cm⁻¹ and no broad O–H
options.D: Propanal has a broad O–H peak

questions.explanation: The alcohol has a broad O–H at 3200 to 3550 and no C=O.

questions.q: Which species is detected in a mass spectrometer?
questions.explanation: Only positive ions are accelerated and detected; radicals are not.

questions.q: What is the m/z of the molecular ion of ethanol?
questions.explanation: C₂H₅OH has Mr 46.

questions.q: Which fragmentation gives m/z 31 for ethanol?
Which statement about fragmentation is correct?

options.A: Only one fragment forms per molecule
options.B: The molecular ion breaks into a cation and a radical
options.D: Fragmentation does not occur in organic compounds

questions.explanation: M⁺ → X⁺ + Y•; only the cation is detected.

questions.q: What is m/z?

options.A: Mass divided by charge of the ion

questions.explanation: Most ions are 1+, so m/z is numerically equal to the mass of the ion.

questions.q: Which fragment at m/z 45 is typical of a carboxylic acid?
Which analytical technique would best distinguish butan-1-ol from butanoic acid?

options.B: Infrared spectroscopy, by the C=O and very broad O–H of the acid

questions.explanation: Both have O–H, but only the acid has a C=O and the very broad acid O–H region.

questions.q: Why is high resolution mass spectrometry useful?

options.B: It distinguishes compounds with the same integer Mr using precise masses

questions.explanation: Compounds such as C₃H₈O (60.0575) and C₂H₄O₂ (60.0211) can be told apart.

questions.q: In the IR spectrum of an ester, which absorptions would you expect?

options.A: C=O at about 1740 and C–O at 1000 to 1300 cm⁻¹, no O–H

questions.explanation: Esters have a carbonyl and C–O bonds but no hydroxyl group.

questions.q: Which statement describes an exothermic reaction?

options.A: ΔH is positive and heat is absorbed
options.B: ΔH is negative and heat is released
options.D: The products have more energy than the reactants

questions.explanation: Exothermic reactions release heat to the surroundings; products are at a lower enthalpy.

questions.q: Which are standard conditions for enthalpy changes?
questions.explanation: Standard pressure is 100 kPa; temperature is stated, usually 298 K.

questions.q: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethanol?
questions.explanation: One mole of compound formed from its elements in their standard states.

questions.q: Which equation shows the reaction to which the standard enthalpy change of combustion of methane applies?
questions.explanation: One mole of substance completely burned in oxygen.

questions.q: What is the standard enthalpy change of formation of oxygen gas?
questions.explanation: An element in its standard state has ΔfH = 0 by definition.

questions.q: Which equation represents the enthalpy change of atomisation of bromine?
questions.explanation: Atomisation forms one mole of gaseous atoms from the element in its standard state.

questions.q: In a calorimetry experiment, 100 cm³ of solution rises by 5.0 °C. How much heat was released? (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)
0.025 mol of fuel releases 1500 J when burned. What is ΔH combustion?
Why is the experimental enthalpy change of combustion usually less exothermic than the data book value?

options.B: Heat is lost to the surroundings and combustion may be incomplete

questions.explanation: Heat loss, incomplete combustion and evaporation of fuel all reduce the measured value.

questions.q: Which statement is Hess's law?

options.A: Enthalpy change depends on the route
options.B: The enthalpy change is independent of the route taken
options.C: Enthalpy is always conserved as heat

questions.explanation: A consequence of the conservation of energy.

questions.q: Which expression gives ΔrH from enthalpies of formation?
questions.explanation: Products minus reactants for formation data.

questions.q: Which expression gives ΔrH from enthalpies of combustion?
questions.explanation: Reactants minus products for combustion data (the arrows point down to the combustion products).

questions.q: ΔfH values: CO₂ −394, H₂O −286, C₂H₆ −85 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔcH of ethane (C₂H₆ + 3½O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O)?
What is the definition of mean bond enthalpy?

options.A: The energy to break one bond
options.B: The average energy needed to break one mole of a given type of bond in gaseous molecules
options.C: The energy released when a bond breaks
options.D: The energy to form one mole of molecules

questions.explanation: Averaged over many compounds containing that bond.

questions.q: Using bond enthalpies, ΔH is calculated as
questions.explanation: Breaking bonds is endothermic (positive), forming bonds is exothermic (negative).

questions.q: Bond enthalpies: C–H 413, Cl–Cl 243, C–Cl 346, H–Cl 432 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl?
Why do bond enthalpy calculations give different values from Hess's law?

options.B: Mean bond enthalpies are averages and do not apply to the specific molecule

questions.explanation: Actual bond strengths vary with molecular environment.

questions.q: Why is the enthalpy of neutralisation of ethanoic acid less exothermic than that of hydrochloric acid?

options.B: Energy is needed to dissociate the weak acid

questions.explanation: Some of the energy released is used to break the O–H bond in the undissociated weak acid.

questions.q: Why is a polystyrene cup used in solution calorimetry?

options.B: It is an insulator with a low heat capacity

questions.explanation: Reduces heat loss and absorbs little heat itself.

questions.q: What is the purpose of plotting a temperature–time graph and extrapolating?

options.B: To estimate the maximum temperature rise, correcting for heat loss

questions.explanation: Extrapolating the cooling line back to the time of mixing gives the corrected ΔT.

questions.q: 50 cm³ of 2.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl is neutralised by 50 cm³ of 2.0 mol dm⁻³ NaOH, releasing 5.7 kJ. What is ΔH neutralisation?
questions.explanation: n(water) = 0.10 mol; 5.7/0.10 = 57 kJ mol⁻¹, exothermic.

questions.q: The enthalpy of formation of a compound is −100 kJ mol⁻¹. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The compound is less stable than its elements
options.B: The compound is more stable than its elements

questions.explanation: A negative ΔfH means energy is released when it forms, so it is lower in energy than its elements.

questions.q: In an enthalpy profile diagram for an endothermic reaction, where are the products?

options.A: At the same level as the reactants

questions.explanation: Energy is absorbed, so the products have higher enthalpy.

questions.q: What is the sign of ΔH for bond breaking?
questions.explanation: Energy must be supplied to overcome the attraction between the bonded atoms.

questions.q: Which two conditions must be met for a collision to lead to a reaction?

options.A: Correct orientation and energy at least equal to the activation energy

questions.explanation: Collision theory: sufficient energy and the correct orientation.

questions.q: How does increasing concentration increase the rate of reaction?

options.B: There are more particles per unit volume so collisions are more frequent

questions.explanation: More frequent collisions lead to more successful collisions per second.

questions.q: Why does a small increase in temperature cause a large increase in rate?

options.B: Many more particles have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy

questions.explanation: The main effect is the increased proportion of molecules with E ≥ Ea; collision frequency rises only slightly.

questions.q: On a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, what does the area under the curve represent?
questions.explanation: Each point gives the number of molecules with that energy; the total area is the total number.

questions.q: What happens to the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve when temperature increases?

options.A: The peak moves to the right and gets lower
options.B: The peak moves to the left and gets higher
options.C: The area under the curve increases

questions.explanation: More molecules have higher energies; the total number is unchanged.

questions.q: Where does the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve start?

options.A: At a positive value on the y-axis

questions.explanation: No molecules have zero energy.

questions.q: How does a catalyst speed up a chemical reaction?

options.B: It provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy

questions.explanation: More molecules have energy greater than the lower Ea.

questions.q: Which is a homogeneous catalyst?
questions.explanation: Homogeneous catalysts are in the same phase as the reactants (all liquid here).

questions.q: Which is a heterogeneous catalyst?

options.A: H⁺ in the hydrolysis of esters
options.B: Cl• radicals in the ozone layer
options.C: Vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process
options.D: Fe²⁺ in redox reactions in solution

questions.explanation: Solid V₂O₅ catalyses the reaction between gases.

questions.q: How does a heterogeneous catalyst work?

options.B: Reactants adsorb onto the surface where bonds weaken, react, then products desorb

questions.explanation: Adsorption at active sites lowers the activation energy.

questions.q: Why does a catalyst not change the enthalpy change of a reaction?

options.B: It only changes the route, not the energy of the reactants or products
options.C: It only works at high temperatures

questions.explanation: ΔH depends only on the enthalpies of reactants and products.

questions.q: Which best describes activation energy?

options.A: The energy released by a reaction
options.B: The minimum energy colliding particles need to react
options.C: The average energy of the particles

questions.explanation: Particles must overcome this barrier for bonds to start breaking.

questions.q: Why does powdered zinc react faster with acid than a lump of zinc?

options.B: Powder has a larger surface area so more collisions occur per second
options.C: Powder has a lower activation energy

questions.explanation: More zinc atoms are exposed to the acid at any moment.

questions.q: Which method could follow the rate of a reaction that produces hydrogen gas?

options.B: Collecting the gas in a gas syringe at intervals

questions.explanation: Volume of gas against time gives the rate.

questions.q: What does the gradient of a tangent to a concentration–time curve represent?

options.A: The rate of reaction at that time

questions.explanation: Rate = change in concentration / change in time.

questions.q: Why does the rate of a reaction fall as it proceeds?

options.B: Reactant concentration decreases so collisions are less frequent

questions.explanation: Fewer reactant particles mean fewer collisions per second.

questions.q: Which statement about catalysts in industry is correct?

options.A: They are consumed in the reaction
options.B: They allow lower temperatures and pressures, reducing energy costs
options.C: They increase the yield at equilibrium

questions.explanation: Lower energy use is cheaper and better for the environment.

questions.q: Why are catalysts important for sustainability?

options.B: They reduce energy demand and so fossil fuel use and CO₂ emissions

questions.explanation: Lower activation energy means lower temperatures are needed.

questions.q: Which of these increases the rate of a gaseous reaction?

options.B: Increasing the volume of the container

questions.explanation: Higher pressure brings the molecules closer together, so collisions are more frequent.

questions.q: How does a catalyst affect the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution?

options.A: It shifts the peak to the right
options.B: It does not change the curve but lowers Ea, so more molecules exceed it

questions.explanation: The energy distribution is unchanged; the Ea line moves left.

questions.q: Which has no effect on the rate of reaction?
questions.explanation: Whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic does not determine its rate.

questions.q: What is the effect of a catalyst on the activation energy?
questions.explanation: The catalysed route has a lower energy barrier.

questions.q: Why does the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve never touch the x-axis at high energy?

options.B: There is no upper limit to the energy a molecule can have
options.D: All molecules have the same energy

questions.explanation: A very small number of molecules can have very high energies.

questions.q: In the depletion of ozone, what role does the chlorine radical play?

options.B: Catalyst, regenerated at the end of the cycle

questions.explanation: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂; ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂. The chlorine radical is regenerated.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a system in dynamic equilibrium?

options.B: Forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates and concentrations stay constant
options.C: The concentrations of reactants and products are equal

questions.explanation: Both reactions continue but there is no net change.

questions.q: Why must the system be closed for equilibrium to be established?

options.B: So that no substances can enter or leave

questions.explanation: If products escape, the reverse reaction cannot occur.

questions.q: For an exothermic forward reaction, what happens to the yield of products when the temperature is increased?
questions.explanation: Equilibrium shifts in the endothermic (reverse) direction to oppose the temperature rise.

questions.q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), what is the effect of increasing pressure?
questions.explanation: Four moles of gas become two; the system shifts to the side with fewer gas moles.

questions.q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), what is the effect of increasing pressure on the position of equilibrium?
questions.explanation: Equal moles of gas on each side, so pressure has no effect on position.

questions.q: How does adding a catalyst affect the position of an equilibrium?
questions.explanation: Both rates increase equally; equilibrium is reached faster with the same composition.

questions.q: Which is the correct Kc expression for 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃?
questions.explanation: Products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient.

questions.q: What are the units of Kc for 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃?
questions.explanation: (mol dm⁻³)² / (mol dm⁻³)³ = mol⁻¹ dm³.

questions.q: Which of these changes will alter the value of Kc?
questions.explanation: Kc is constant at constant temperature.

questions.q: Why is 450 °C used in the Haber process rather than a lower temperature?

options.B: A lower temperature gives a higher yield but the rate would be too slow

questions.explanation: A compromise between yield (favoured by low T) and rate (favoured by high T).

questions.q: Why is 200 atm rather than a much higher pressure used in the Haber process?

options.B: Very high pressures are expensive and dangerous

questions.explanation: High pressure favours ammonia but costs rise steeply with stronger equipment.

questions.q: What happens to the yield of ammonia if it is removed from the Haber process as it forms?

options.B: Rises, as the equilibrium shifts right to replace it

questions.explanation: Removing a product shifts the equilibrium towards the products.

questions.q: Which statement about Le Chatelier's principle is correct?

options.A: The position of equilibrium shifts to oppose any change made to the system

questions.explanation: The system responds to minimise the effect of the change.

questions.q: In 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), the forward reaction is exothermic. What is observed on heating?
questions.explanation: Equilibrium shifts left (endothermic direction), making more brown NO₂.

questions.q: What is the effect of adding water to the esterification equilibrium CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O?
questions.explanation: Water is a product, so adding it shifts the equilibrium to the left.

questions.q: Which conditions are used in the Contact process for 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃?
questions.explanation: The yield is already about 99% so high pressure is unnecessary.

questions.q: In an equilibrium with Kc = 1 × 10⁻⁸, where does the equilibrium lie?
questions.explanation: A very small Kc means very little product.

questions.q: Which is a homogeneous equilibrium?
questions.explanation: All species are in the same phase.

questions.q: What is the effect of increasing concentration of a reactant on Kc?

options.C: No change in Kc; the position shifts right

questions.explanation: The concentrations change until the ratio equals Kc again.

questions.q: For an endothermic forward reaction, how does increasing temperature affect the yield?
questions.explanation: The equilibrium shifts in the endothermic (forward) direction.

questions.q: What effect does doubling all concentrations have on the position of equilibrium for A + B ⇌ C + D?
questions.explanation: The ratio [C][D]/[A][B] is unchanged.

questions.q: Which expression is Kc for CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O?
questions.explanation: Products over reactants; water is included as it is not the solvent here.

questions.q: Why is a catalyst used in the Haber process?

options.A: To increase the yield of ammonia
options.B: To reach equilibrium faster at a lower temperature

questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds up both reactions equally so the compromise temperature can be lower.

questions.q: Which statement about equilibrium concentrations is correct?

options.B: They stay constant once equilibrium is reached

questions.explanation: Constant concentrations are the macroscopic sign of equilibrium.

questions.q: What is the mole fraction of nitrogen in a mixture of 2 mol N₂, 6 mol H₂ and 2 mol NH₃?
In a mixture at 500 kPa, the mole fraction of oxygen is 0.3. What is its partial pressure?
Which is the Kp expression for 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g)?
questions.explanation: Products over reactants with powers from the equation.

questions.q: What are the units of Kp for 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) with pressures in kPa?
questions.explanation: kPa / kPa² = kPa⁻¹.

questions.q: What are the units of Kc for N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂?
questions.explanation: (mol dm⁻³)²/(mol dm⁻³) = mol dm⁻³.

questions.q: 1.0 mol of PCl₅ dissociates to 30% in a 10 dm³ vessel: PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂. What is Kc?
questions.explanation: Equilibrium: PCl₅ 0.70, PCl₃ 0.30, Cl₂ 0.30 mol. Concentrations ÷ 10: 0.070, 0.030, 0.030. Kc = 0.030²/0.070 = 0.0129.

questions.q: For an exothermic reaction, what happens to Kc when temperature rises?
questions.explanation: Equilibrium shifts left, lowering the product : reactant ratio.

questions.q: Which statement about Kp and pressure is correct?

options.C: Kp is unchanged; the partial pressures adjust so their ratio stays equal to Kp

questions.explanation: Only temperature changes an equilibrium constant.

questions.q: For a reaction where Kc = 4.0 and the reaction is A ⇌ B, what is [B] if [A] = 0.5 mol dm⁻³ at equilibrium?
Which relationship links ΔS total to K?
questions.explanation: A positive ΔS total gives K greater than 1.

questions.q: What does Kc = 1 × 10⁶ tell you about a reaction?

options.B: The equilibrium lies far to the right

questions.explanation: Products dominate at equilibrium.

questions.q: In the equilibrium CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), what is Kp?
questions.explanation: Solids are omitted.

questions.q: 2.0 mol of HI in a 1 dm³ vessel decompose: 2HI ⇌ H₂ + I₂. At equilibrium 0.4 mol H₂ is present. What is Kc?
Which experimental step is essential before analysing an equilibrium mixture by titration?

options.B: Quenching the reaction, e.g. by cooling or dilution

questions.explanation: Quenching stops the reaction so concentrations do not change during analysis.

questions.q: In the esterification equilibrium experiment, why is the HCl catalyst subtracted from the titre?

options.B: The NaOH neutralises the HCl as well as the ethanoic acid

questions.explanation: The titre measures total acid; the known HCl must be removed to find ethanoic acid.

questions.q: For an endothermic reaction, how does Kp change as temperature increases?
questions.explanation: Equilibrium shifts to the right (endothermic direction).

questions.q: In a Kp calculation, what must the partial pressures add up to?
questions.explanation: Partial pressures sum to the total pressure; mole fractions sum to 1.

questions.q: Which change will not affect Kc?
questions.explanation: Catalysts have no effect on the equilibrium constant.

questions.q: For A(g) + B(g) ⇌ C(g), 1.0 mol of A and 1.0 mol of B are mixed and 0.6 mol of C forms. How many moles of A remain?
questions.explanation: 1.0 − 0.6 = 0.4 mol of A (and of B).

questions.q: Why does increasing the concentration of a product cause a shift to the left?

options.B: The ratio of products to reactants exceeds Kc, so the reverse reaction proceeds until the ratio equals Kc again

questions.explanation: Kc is fixed; the concentrations readjust.

questions.q: The reaction N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ has Kp = 0.15 atm at 298 K and 1.5 atm at 350 K. What does this show?
questions.explanation: Kp increases with temperature, so the forward reaction is endothermic.

questions.q: Which is true about the magnitude of Kc and the rate of reaction?

options.B: Kc gives no information about rate

questions.explanation: Equilibrium constants are thermodynamic; rate is kinetic.

questions.q: How is Kc for the reverse reaction related to Kc for the forward reaction?
questions.explanation: Kc(reverse) = 1/Kc(forward).

questions.q: For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ at equilibrium: p(SO₂) = 20 kPa, p(O₂) = 10 kPa, p(SO₃) = 200 kPa. What is Kp?
What is a Brønsted–Lowry base?
questions.explanation: Bases accept protons; acids donate them.

questions.q: What is the conjugate base of HSO₄⁻?
questions.explanation: Remove one proton from HSO₄⁻.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ HNO₃?
What is the pH of 0.010 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid, assuming complete dissociation?
What is [H⁺] in a solution of pH 4.5?
Which is the expression for Ka of a weak acid HA?
questions.explanation: Products of dissociation over undissociated acid.

questions.q: Which acid is the strongest?
questions.explanation: Lowest pKa means largest Ka.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.20 mol dm⁻³ propanoic acid (Ka = 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³)?
Which assumption is made when calculating the pH of a weak acid?

options.B: [H⁺] = [A⁻] and the equilibrium concentration of HA equals its initial concentration

questions.explanation: Dissociation is so small that [HA] barely changes; water's H⁺ is ignored.

questions.q: What is the value of Kw at 298 K?
questions.explanation: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶.

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.050 mol dm⁻³ KOH?
What is the pH of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ Ba(OH)₂, assuming full dissociation?
How does the pH of pure water change as temperature rises?
questions.explanation: Kw increases with temperature (endothermic dissociation), so [H⁺] rises and pH falls, but water stays neutral.

questions.q: At what pH is the equivalence point for a strong acid–strong base titration?
questions.explanation: Equal moles of strong acid and base give a neutral salt solution.

questions.q: Which indicator is suitable for a strong acid–weak base titration?
questions.explanation: The vertical region is in the acidic range (about pH 3 to 7), matching methyl orange (3.1 to 4.4).

questions.q: Which indicator should be chosen for the titration of ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: The vertical region is at pH about 7 to 11, matching phenolphthalein (8.3 to 10).

questions.q: Why can an indicator not be used to find the end point of a weak acid–weak base titration?

options.B: There is no sharp change in pH at the equivalence point
options.D: Indicators only work with strong acids

questions.explanation: A gradual pH change gives no sharp colour change.

questions.q: How can pKa be found from a weak acid–strong base titration curve?
questions.explanation: At half-neutralisation [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

questions.q: Which mixture would make a buffer?
questions.explanation: A weak acid with its conjugate base.

questions.q: A buffer contains 0.10 mol dm⁻³ methanoic acid (Ka = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴) and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ sodium methanoate. What is its pH?
What happens when a small amount of HCl is added to an ethanoate buffer?

options.B: H⁺ reacts with CH₃COO⁻ to form CH₃COOH, so pH barely changes

questions.explanation: The large reservoir of conjugate base removes the added H⁺.

questions.q: Which equilibrium controls the pH of blood?
questions.explanation: The carbonic acid/hydrogencarbonate buffer keeps blood pH at about 7.4.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ HCl is mixed with 25.0 cm³ of 0.050 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. What is the pH?
How is a buffer made by partial neutralisation?

options.A: Add excess NaOH to a weak acid
options.B: Add less NaOH than the moles of weak acid, leaving some acid and forming its salt
options.C: Mix a strong acid and strong base
options.D: Add water to a weak acid

questions.explanation: The remaining weak acid and the salt formed make the buffer.

questions.q: Which equation represents the lattice energy of sodium chloride?
questions.explanation: Edexcel defines lattice energy as the formation of one mole of solid from gaseous ions (exothermic).

questions.q: Which has the most exothermic lattice energy?
questions.explanation: Small, doubly charged ions attract most strongly.

questions.q: Why is the second electron affinity of oxygen positive?

options.B: An electron is added to a negative ion, so repulsion must be overcome
options.D: The first electron affinity is also positive

questions.explanation: O⁻ + e⁻ → O²⁻ requires energy.

questions.q: In a Born–Haber cycle for KBr, which term must be included once but for CaBr₂ twice?

options.A: First ionisation energy of the metal

questions.explanation: Two Br atoms (and two electron affinities) are needed for CaBr₂.

questions.q: Which equation calculates lattice energy from a Born–Haber cycle?

options.B: ΔLE = ΔfH − Σ(atomisation + ionisation + electron affinity)

questions.explanation: Hess's law around the cycle.

questions.q: Why does the experimental lattice energy of AgI differ from the theoretical value?

options.B: AgI has significant covalent character, which the purely ionic model ignores
options.C: The theoretical value assumes covalent bonding

questions.explanation: Polarisation of the large I⁻ by Ag⁺ gives extra bonding not in the ionic model.

questions.q: Which cation is the most polarising?
questions.explanation: Small size and high charge give the highest charge density.

questions.q: Which anion is the most polarisable?
questions.explanation: The large I⁻ has its outer electrons far from the nucleus and easily distorted.

questions.q: Which equation represents the enthalpy change of hydration of Mg²⁺?
questions.explanation: Gaseous ions to aqueous ions.

questions.q: How is enthalpy of solution related to lattice energy and hydration enthalpies (Edexcel definitions)?
questions.explanation: The lattice must be broken (reverse of lattice energy) and the gaseous ions hydrated.

questions.q: Which of these Group 1 ions has the most exothermic hydration enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Smallest ion, highest charge density.

questions.q: ΔLE(NaCl) = −780, ΔhydH(Na⁺) = −406, ΔhydH(Cl⁻) = −364 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔsolH?
Which process has a negative entropy change?

options.C: Ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases forming solid ammonium chloride

questions.explanation: Two gases become one solid: a large decrease in disorder.

questions.q: What are the units of entropy?
questions.explanation: Entropy values are in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so divide by 1000 to combine with kJ.

questions.q: Which equation gives ΔS surroundings?
questions.explanation: Exothermic reactions increase the entropy of the surroundings.

questions.q: A reaction is feasible when
questions.explanation: ΔS total = ΔS system + ΔS surroundings must be positive.

questions.q: For a reaction ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS system = −199 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔS total at 298 K?
At what temperature does ΔS total = 0 for a reaction with ΔH = +50 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS system = +125 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹?
questions.explanation: T = ΔH/ΔS system = 50 000/125 = 400 K. Above this the reaction is feasible.

questions.q: Why is the dissolving of ammonium nitrate feasible even though it is endothermic?

options.B: ΔS system is large and positive, outweighing the negative ΔS surroundings

questions.explanation: The solid becomes free ions in solution, a large increase in disorder.

questions.q: Which equation relates ΔG to ΔS total?
questions.explanation: A positive ΔS total corresponds to a negative ΔG.

questions.q: Why might a reaction with positive ΔS total not occur at a measurable rate?

options.B: The activation energy is too high

questions.explanation: Feasibility is thermodynamic; the rate may be negligible.

questions.q: How does the entropy of a substance change as temperature increases?
questions.explanation: Particles have more energy and more ways of arranging it.

questions.q: Which of these forms of water has the highest standard entropy?
questions.explanation: Gases are the most disordered.

questions.q: For an exothermic reaction with positive ΔS system, when is it feasible?
questions.explanation: Both ΔS system and ΔS surroundings are positive at every temperature.
